en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Minor Exposition (*Cūḷaniddesa*) within the Minor Collection (*Khuddakanikāya*).
The Exposition of the Pārāyana Chapter:
1. The Explanation of the Discourse to Ajita the Young Brahmin.
Regarding the first discourse in the Pārāyana Chapter, the explanation of the *Ajitasutta*:
“By what is the world shrouded? (Thus asked the Venerable Ajita.
By what does it not shine forth?
What do you say is its defilement? And what is its great terror?”

Having excluded what has already been stated and what is obvious in the first question and the successive questions asked by the young brahmin Ajita, as well as in their explanations, we shall speak only of the distinctive points.
In this context, "covered" (*nivuta*) means concealed. "What do you say is its defilement? (*kissābhilepanaṃ brūsī*) means:
what do you declare to be the defilement of this world?

*Āvuta* means covered. *Nivuta* means concealed. *Ovuta* means covered from below. *Pihita* means covered from above. *Paṭicchanna* means not opened. *Paṭikujjita* means covered face-downward. *Nappakāsati* means it does not shine forth.
*Nappabhāsati* means it does not produce the radiance of knowledge. *Na tapati* means it does not produce the heat of knowledge.
*Na virocati* means it does not produce the brilliance of knowledge. *Na ñāyati* means it is not known.
"It is not discerned" means it is not made known (*nappaññāyate*).
"By what is it smeared? means by what is it anointed? The words *saṃlitto* and *upalitto* have been expanded by means of prefixes.
You have explained [the meaning] by way of definition (*niddesa*), taught it by way of further explanation (*paṭiniddesa*), and set it forth in various ways while awakening the meaning.
He established [the teaching]. To show the reason for that meaning, he "opened" it; to show its literal form, he "analyzed" it;
and by removing its concealed state and its profundity, he "clarified" it, creating a foundation for the knowledge of his listeners.
Thus, the meaning should be understood as follows: through all these modes, he "proclaimed" it, dispelling the darkness of ignorance of the listeners.
2. “Because of stinginess and negligence it does not shine forth”: because of stinginess (*macchariya*) and because of negligence (*pamāda*), it does not manifest.
For stinginess does not allow its virtues, such as generosity (*dāna*), to shine forth, while negligence prevents its virtues, such as moral discipline (*sīla*), from doing so.
"Craving is its smearing" means that craving (*taṇhā*) is like the monkey’s smearing for this world, just as a monkey is smeared [with lac]. "Suffering" refers to the suffering of birth and so forth.
"Of those phenomena" means of those phenomena such as form and so forth. "The origin is discerned from the beginning" means that arising is discerned first.
"Cessation is discerned through passing away" means that dissolution is discerned through destruction.
"Resultant [consciousness] is dependent on karma" means that the result of wholesome and unwholesome [karma] is dependent on karma because it proceeds without abandoning that karma.
It is called "resultant" (*vipāka*). "Kamma dependent on resultant" refers to wholesome and unwholesome kamma;
it is called "kamma dependent on resultant" because it exists having made room for the resultant. "Matter dependent on name" refers to matter in the fivefold plane (*pañcavokāra*);
it is called "matter dependent on name" because it proceeds without ever abandoning name. "Matter dependent on matter"...
In the fivefold plane of existence (pañcavokāra), because name (nāma) proceeds without ever abandoning form (rūpa), it is called "name dependent on form" (rūpasannissitaṃ nāma).
3. "They flow everywhere as streams" means that in all the sense-bases (āyatana), such as form and so forth, the streams of craving and the like flow.
"What is the obstruction? means: what is the hindrance, what is the protection for them? "Speak of restraint" (saṃvaraṃ brūhi) refers to that restraint which is designated as their obstruction.
"Speak. By this he asks about abandonment with remainder. "By what are the streams closed?"—by what phenomenon (*dhamma*) are these streams closed and cut off?
By this he asks about abandonment without remainder.
"They flow" means they arise. "They leak" means they flow while moving downward. "They run" means they proceed as a continuous flow. "They circulate" means they revolve again and again.
4. "Mindfulness is their obstruction": mindfulness, which follows after insight and investigates the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states, is the obstruction to those streams.
"I call it the restraint of the streams": the intention is that I call that very mindfulness the restraint of the streams.
"By wisdom these are closed up": by means of the wisdom that effects the penetration of impermanence and so forth regarding forms and the rest.
By means of the wisdom of the path, these streams are completely closed off.
"They are cut off" means they are severed. "And their origin" means the condition.
"And their passing away" means the non-existence of those that have arisen, or the non-arising of those not yet arisen. "And their gratification" means the benefit. "And their danger" means...
"And the fault" means [the cause of] defilement. "And the escape" means the departure [from it].
"And wisdom" refers to this wisdom spoken by you in the verse of inquiry, as well as mindfulness and whatever remaining name-and-form there is—where does all this cease?
Being asked this question of mine, please explain it. Thus [he spoke].

The summarized meaning should be understood as follows: "Where does this cease? means where does this name-and-form (nāmarūpa) no longer exist? "It is stilled" means it is extinguished (nibbāti). "It goes to its end" means it reaches non-existence. "It subsides" means it settles down. 6.
Furthermore, because the fifty sections of this [work] are comprised under the very name *Paññāsati*, therefore...
These have not been stated separately. This is the summary of the meaning here: that which you asked me, Ajita—the question, "Where does this come to an end?"—that I shall tell you:
where name-and-form cease without remainder, there this comes to an end.
For with the cessation of each respective consciousness, this comes to an end right there, neither before nor after.
"Right here, with the cessation of consciousness, this ceases; through the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of each respective [factor];
it does not go beyond that"—this is what is meant.
"By the cessation of volitional consciousness through the knowledge of the path of stream-entry" means by the wisdom associated with the path of stream-entry.
By way of ceasing through the impossibility of arising for a consciousness associated with wholesome or unwholesome volition. In that regard, cessation is twofold:
cessation of the non-clung-to (*anupādinnaka*) and cessation of the clung-to (*upādinnaka*).

For, by means of the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimagga*), five types of consciousness cease—namely, the four associated with views and that accompanied by doubt—and these give rise to matter. That is the aggregate of non-clung-to matter.
Those consciousnesses are the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*); the associated feeling, perception, and mental formations are the three formless aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*).

In that regard, if the stream-enterer’s path of stream-entry had not been cultivated, those five types of consciousness would have reached the state of being overwhelmed by the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) regarding the six objects.
However, the path of stream-entry prevents the arising of such obsession in them.

By obstructing [the flow] and effecting the demolition of the dam, it renders [the defilements] incapable of arising; thus, it is said that it causes the cessation of what has not yet been grasped (*anupādinnaka*).

By the path of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmi-magga*), six types of consciousness cease—namely, the four dissociated from views and the two accompanied by displeasure—by way of gross sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
By the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmi-magga*), those same [consciousnesses] cease by way of subtle sensual lust and ill-will.
Six types of consciousness cease. By means of the path of Arahantship, five unwholesome types of consciousness cease—namely, the four dissociated from views and that accompanied by restlessness.

In that regard, if those Noble Ones had not developed those paths, those consciousnesses would have reached the state of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) regarding the six objects. However, because they have developed those paths, the arising of obsession [is prevented].
By obstructing the stream and effecting its eradication, they render it incapable of arising again and thus cause the cessation of what is not yet grasped (*anupādinnaka*).
In this way, the cessation of the ungrasped is to be understood.

Furthermore, if the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) had not been cultivated by a stream-enterer, then—excluding the seven [remaining] existences—it would have continued through the beginningless cycle of rebirth (*anamatagga*).
The occurrence of the appropriated aggregates within the cycle of existence would continue. Why? Because the causes for that occurrence still exist.
However, as that path arises, it eradicates these five defilements: the three fetters, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt.
Now, [if one asks] from where [could there be] seven more births for a stream-enterer, setting aside...
In this beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, the turning of the wheel of what is grasped will continue to proceed.
Thus, the path of stream-entry, by making the turning of the wheel of what is grasped non-proceeding, is said to "cease" what is grasped.
If the path of once-returning had not been cultivated by a once-returner, [then] apart from two existences, in five...
The cycle of existence consisting of what has been grasped would continue to proceed. Why? Because of the presence of the causes for its proceeding.
However, as that path arises, it eradicates these four defilements: the gross fetters of sensual lust and aversion, and the gross underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion.
Now, from where [would] two [defilements] remain for a once-returner?
Setting aside one existence, it will proceed through the five existences as the turning of what has been acquired (*upādinnakappavatta*).
Thus, the path of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmimagga*), by making the turning of what has been acquired non-proceeding, is said to "cease" what has been acquired.
If the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*) had not been cultivated for a non-returner, then—setting aside one existence—in a second existence...
The process of existence involving what is acquired would continue. Why? Because the causes for its continuation exist.
However, as that path arises, it eradicates these four defilements: the fetters of subtle sensual lust and ill will, and the underlying tendencies of subtle sensual lust and ill will.
Now, how could there be [rebirth] for a non-returner, except for one remaining birth?

In the second existence, the continuity of what is clung-to (upādinnaka) would proceed. Thus, the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga), by causing the continuity of what is clung-to not to proceed, is said to "cease" what is clung-to.
If the path of arahantship (arahattamagga) had not been cultivated for an arahant, the continuity of what is clung-to in the fine-material and immaterial realms would [have proceeded].

It would proceed. Why? Because the causes for its proceeding exist. However, as that Path arises, it eradicates these eight defilements: lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Now, from where could the proceeding of a rebirth-process involving grasping arise again for one whose taints are destroyed?
Thus, the path of arahantship, by making the process of what is acquired cease, is said to "cease what is acquired.
Furthermore, herein, the path of stream-entry ceases existence in the states of misery; the path of once-returning ceases a portion of the sensual-sphere existence within the happy destinies;
the path of non-returning ceases the sensual-sphere existence; and the path of arahantship ceases existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms—thus it ceases all forms of existence.
They say this. In this way, the cessation of the acquired (*upādinnaka*) should be understood.

Therein, by the phrase "by the cessation of volitional consciousness" (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena*), he shows the cessation of the unacquired (*anupādinnaka*). By the phrase "name-and-form which might arise—here these cease," however, he shows the cessation of the acquired.

Therein, "setting aside seven existences" means excluding seven existences for one wandering from the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) back to the sense-sphere existence. "In the beginningless saṃsāra"—
“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense-bases,
occurring without interruption, is called ‘saṃsāra’”—

thus has the cycle of saṃsāra been described. In this cycle, those things that would arise as name-and-form— wherein "name" has the characteristic of bending and consists of the four [mental] aggregates—
Name, which has the characteristic of cognizing, and form—consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives—these phenomena might arise.
"In this they cease" means that in this path of stream-entry, these phenomena of name-and-form reach cessation by way of being incapable of further arising.
"By the knowledge of the path of once-returning": herein, one returns to this world only once more by way of rebirth-linking.
A once-returner; the path of that [once-returner] is the once-returner path. By means of the knowledge associated with that path.
"Excluding two births" means excluding two births by way of rebirth-linking within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) itself.
"In five births" means in the five remaining births. "These cease here" means these states cease here in the once-returner path.

They cease in the manner already described. "Excluding one existence" means, in the highest sense, having set aside one existence either in the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*) or the immaterial sphere (*arūpadhātu*).
"In the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere" refers to both the fine-material and immaterial spheres in the second existence.
Regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): here, in a fine-material existence there is name-and-form, whereas in an immaterial existence there is name alone.
“They cease here”: here, on the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*), these phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) cease in the manner already described. “An arahant”:
this refers to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) and who has received the name “arahant” because he is far removed (*āraka*) from the defilements (*kilesa*).

“In the element of Nibbāna without residue”: for the element of Nibbāna is twofold—both with residue (*saupādisesa*) and without residue (*anupādisesa*). Therein, [residue] is that which is grasped as “I” and “mine.”
"It is grasped as fuel," thus it is *upādi*; this is a designation for the five aggregates (*khandha*). That which remains, that which is left over, is *upādisesa*.
That which exists together with a remainder of clinging is *saupādisesa*. That in which there is no remainder of clinging is *anupādisesa*.
"By means of that *anupādisesa* element of Nibbāna" refers to one who is attaining final Nibbāna, like a fire whose fuel has been exhausted.

For one who is attaining Nibbāna, for one entering the state of non-occurrence. Regarding the phrase "by the cessation of the final consciousness," this refers here to the cessation of inhalation and exhalation.

There are three kinds of finality: the finality of existence (*bhava-carima*), the finality of jhāna (*jhāna-carima*), and the finality of death (*cuti-carima*). For among existences, inhalation and exhalation occur in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), but they do not occur in the fine-material or immaterial existences (*rūpa- and arūpabhava*). Therefore, that [cessation] is the finality of existence. Among the jhānas...
The first three jhānas continue to proceed, but they do not proceed in the fourth. Therefore, that is called the "final jhāna.
However, those [mental factors] that arise together with the sixteenth consciousness prior to the death-consciousness cease along with the death-consciousness.
That is called the "final death-consciousness. This is what is intended here by the term "final. For any Buddhas or Paccekabuddhas...
Or, whether they be noble disciples or others, down to even a tiny ant, all pass away with the neutral (abyākata) life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta) as their suffering-truth.
Therefore, "by the cessation of the final consciousness" means by the cessation of the death-consciousness (cuti-citta).
By "wisdom, mindfulness, and name," one should understand the inclusion of the four immaterial aggregates (arūpa-khandha). And "form" (rūpa)...
By this, it should be understood that the four great elements and the twenty-four derived forms are included.
Now, showing the means for its cessation, he said: "With the cessation of consciousness, herein this is brought to an end.

In this context, "consciousness" refers both to the final consciousness and to the volitional (kamma-) formation consciousness. Through the abandoning and cessation of the volitional formation consciousness—
Right here it is brought to a halt, it ceases, and like the flame of a lamp, it passes into a state of non-designation (*apaṇṇattika*).
Because it serves as the condition for the non-arising of the final consciousness, it is brought to a halt by way of non-arising through the cessation of non-arising.
At this point, the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*)—which was elucidated by the phrase "suffering is its great terror"—and the phrase "those which are streams" [are concluded].

By the phrase "this is the truth of origin" (*samudayasacca*), [the origin is indicated]; by "these two are closed off by wisdom" (*paññāya ete pidhīyare*), the truth of the path (*maggasacca*); and by "it is ceased without remainder" (*asesaṃ uparujjhati*), the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*).

Thus, even though he had heard the Four Noble Truths, because he had not yet attained the plane of the Noble Ones (*ariyabhūmi*), he asked again about the practice of those in training and those beyond training (*sekkhāsekkhapaṭipada*) by reciting the verse beginning with "And those who have discerned the Dhamma" (*ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse*). In that context, "those who have discerned the Dhamma" (*saṅkhātadhammā*) refers to [discerning] by way of impermanence and so forth.
"Those who have thoroughly investigated the Dhamma"—this is a designation for the Arahants.
"Learners" refers to the remaining noble persons who are still training in virtue and the other perfections. "Many" means numerous beings.
"Tell me, being asked, their prudent conduct"—that is, being asked by me regarding those learners and non-learners, you, being prudent and wise, should explain their practice.
"Their aggregates are reckoned" means that for them the five aggregates have been taught by making them non-relinking, or they have been established by way of a summary.
The same method applies to the elements and so forth. "Iriyanti" means application. "Cariyanti" means activity.
"Vuttinti" means occurrence. "Ācaranti" means conduct. "Gocaranti" means condition. "Vihāranti" means the manifestation of the postures. "Paṭipadanti" means insight.

8. Now, because all defilements must indeed be abandoned by one in training (sekkha), beginning with the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), the Blessed One shows the practice of one in training with the half-stanza beginning, “Regarding sensual pleasures” (kāmesu). Its meaning is as follows:
one should not covet sense-objects (vatthu-kāma) with the defilement of desire (kilesa-kāma); and abandoning those states that cause turbidity of the mind, such as bodily misconduct and so forth—

"One should be undisturbed in mind. However, because the one beyond training (*asekkha*) is skilled (*kusala*) regarding all phenomena due to having thoroughly examined all conditioned things and so forth by way of impermanence and the rest;

and because, being mindful through the foundations of mindfulness such as the contemplation of the body, he has attained the state of a monk (*bhikkhu*) by having shattered the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the like, and thus wanders as a wanderer in all postures—therefore, [the Blessed One said] "skilled" in the half-stanza.
This shows the practice of one beyond training (*asekkha-paṭipadā*).

"One should not covet" means one should not fall into greed. "One should not be obsessed" means one should not fall into lust. "One should not be bound" means one should not cling through the power of lust.
"One should abandon the defilements that cause turbidity" means one should abandon the defilements reckoned as affliction, which cause the agitation of the mind.
"All phenomena are non-self" is stated including *nibbāna* within its scope. "Whatever has the nature of arising" means whatever has the characteristic of being conditioned.
"Together with the conclusion of the verse" means precisely along with the end of the verse.

"Those who have the same intention as the brahmin" means those who share the same aspiration (*ajjhāsaya*) with the young man Ajita through his noble intention. "Of one application" means by way of the applications of body, speech, and mind.

*Ekappayogā*: Having a single application. *Ekādhippāyā*: Those who have a single intention (*adhippāya*) or inclination (*ruci*) are "those of one intention"; the meaning is that they have a single taste. *Ekavāsanavāsitā*:
Perfumed by a single latent tendency (*vāsanā*), meaning their cultivation was developed together with him in the past dispensation of the Buddha.

*Anekapāṇasahassānaṃ*: Of many thousands of living beings (*pāṇa*), namely thousands of beings consisting of both gods and humans. *Virajaṃ vītamalaṃ*: Free from dust and devoid of stain, meaning it is devoid of the dust of passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
And it is free from the stains of passion and so forth.
Here, "the eye of the Dhamma" (dhammacakkhu) refers to the path of stream-entry; elsewhere, it refers to the three lower paths.
To show the cause for its arising, [it is said]: "Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation."
He said: "For having made that cessation the object, it arises by way of its function as such a penetration of all conditioned things.

'The mind of that brahmin was liberated from the taints through non-clinging' means that at the moment of the Path, the mind of that Ajita brahmin and his thousand disciples was being liberated from the taints of sense-desire and so forth, without grasping through craving and the like."

At the moment of the fruit [of his attainment], he was liberated. Simultaneously with the attainment of *arahantship*, at the very moment the Venerable Ajita attained *arahantship*, the deerskins, matted hair, bark garments, triple staffs, water-pots, and other such items of the thousand disciples vanished.

All of them, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power (*iddhi*) and having hair only two finger-breadths long, became "Come, monk" (*ehi bhikkhu*) types of monks and stood paying homage to the Blessed One.
They sat down with palms joined. In the Pāḷi, however, only the Elder Ajita is mentioned.
Therein, "by practice in accordance with the meaning" means by the practice that one has obtained as one's own expectation; the sense is: by way of attaining Nibbāna. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One brought the teaching to its conclusion with Arahantship as its summit.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Ajita-māṇava-sutta* in the *Cūḷaniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*, titled *Saddhammappajjotikā*, is completed. 2.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Tissametteyya-māṇava-sutta*.

9. In the second exposition, the *Tissametteyyasutta-niddesa*—after the passage “content with anger” had been concluded—the Blessed One, having understood that Mogharāja was beginning to ask, “How is it that the King of Death does not see one who contemplates the world?
replied, “Mogharāja, wait; his faculties have not yet reached maturity. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
“Let another ask,” he refused. Then Tissa Metteyya, wishing to ask about his own doubt, spoke the verse beginning with “Anger.
In that context, “one who is contented with anger” refers to what sentient being here is satisfied. “Quiverings” refers to the fluctuations of craving and views.
“Having directly known both extremes” means having fully understood both ends. “Is not smeared by wisdom” means he is not defiled by insight.
“Fulfilled in purpose”: because his purpose is fulfilled by thoughts of renunciation and so forth, he is one whose heart’s desire is fulfilled.

“Shaken by craving”: moved by craving. The same method applies to “shaken by views” and the rest. “Shaken by sensual desire”: moved and agitated by the defilements of sensual desire. There is also a reading “shaken by action” (*kamm-iñjita*), but that is not good.
“A great man” (*mahāpurisa*): a great person. “The supreme man” (*uttamapurisa*): the foremost person. “The preeminent man” (*padhānapurisa*): the best person.
An "alāmaka" person is an eminent person. A "jeṭṭhaka" person is a leading person.
A "not inferior" person is a supreme person. A person who has reached the pinnacle of men is a preeminent person. A person desired by all is an excellent person.
“Sibbinimaccagā”: he has transcended craving; having transcended it, he stands firm. “Upaccagā”: he has thoroughly transcended.

In explaining this meaning, the Blessed One spoke the two verses beginning with “Kāmesu. Therein, “brahmacariyavā kāmesu” means one who lives the holy life for the sake of [overcoming] sensual desires;
having seen the danger in sensual desires, he is endowed with the holy life of the Path.
This has been stated. By this much, he shows contentment. By the words "free from craving" (*vītataṇho*) and so forth, he shows imperturbability (*aniñjitataṃ*).

Therein, "extinguished through reflection" (*saṅkhāya nibbuto*) means extinguished by the extinction of passion and other defilements after having investigated phenomena by way of impermanence and so on.

"From association with what is not the true Dhamma" (*asaddhammasamāpattiyā*) means from connection with base states. "Abstention" (*ārati*) means delighting at a distance. "Refraining" (*virati*) means [abstaining] from that.
"Without delighting": having turned away from it, not delighting by means of that. "Abstention" (*veramaṇī*): the destruction of enmity (*vera*).

"Non-performance" (*akiriyā*): the cutting off of performance. "Non-doing" (*akaraṇa*): the delimitation of doing. "Non-transgression" (*anajjhāpatti*): the state of not falling into [offense]. "Non-exceeding the limit" (*velā-anatikkamo*): non-exceeding the boundary (*sīmā*).
The remainder is clear because it follows the method explained in various other places.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta also by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, this brahmin too was established in Arahantship together with his thousand students, and the Dhamma-eye arose in many thousands of others.
The rest is exactly as before.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Tissametteyya-māṇava-sutta* in the *Cūḷaniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*, titled *Saddhammappajjotikā*, is completed. 3.
Exposition of the *Puṇṇaka-māṇava-sutta*.
12. In the third section, the exposition of the Puṇṇaka Sutta—“Unshaken” (aneja): this too was spoken after refuting Mogharāja by means of the same method as before.
Therein, “one who sees the roots” (mūladassāvin) means one who sees the unwholesome roots and so forth. “Sages” (isayo) refers to those with matted hair named *isi*.
“Sacrifice” (yañña) refers to the object to be given. “They prepared” (akappayiṃsu) means they sought out.
"Hetudassāvī" (one who sees the cause) and all the following terms are synonyms for "cause" (*kāraṇa*).

For a cause is called "hetu" because it moves toward (*hinoti*) or proceeds toward its own fruit; therefore it is called a cause. Because it brings forth that fruit—as if saying, "Come, take this!"—it is called a "nidāna" (source).
The five phrases beginning with "sambhavadassāvī" (one who sees the origin) [are explained as follows].

These are precisely the methods shown below. Because it comes—that is, proceeds—dependent upon that, and because that fruit arises or originates from that, it is therefore called both a "condition" (paccaya) and an "origination" (samudaya).

Or alternatively, "any other happy destinies whatsoever" refers to those such as Uttaramātā and others who are excluded from the four states of misery (apāya), yet are men of little power and wretched condition.

And it should be understood that they are oppressed by suffering due to the scarcity of food and clothing. Or, as for "any other miserable states," these should be understood as [the realms of] King Yama, nāgas, supaṇṇas, petas, those with great psychic power (*mahiddhika*), and so forth.
"For the production of a personal existence" means for the sake of obtaining a personal existence (*attabhāva*) by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the three places.
"He knows" means he knows by means of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). "He sees" means...
He sees with the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*).

"Unwholesome" (*akusala*) means produced through lack of skill (*akosalla*). They "partake of the unwholesome," thus they are "associated with the unwholesome" (*akusalabhāgiya*). They "exist on the side of the unwholesome," thus they are "belonging to the side of the unwholesome" (*akusalapakkhika*).
All these have ignorance as their root and cause; thus they are "rooted in ignorance" (*avijjāmūlaka*). They converge in ignorance.
They converge and proceed together through ignorance; thus, they are "converging in ignorance" (*avijjāsamosaraṇā*).

"The eradication of ignorance" (*avijjāsamugghātā*) means that when ignorance has been destroyed by the path of Arahantship, all those unwholesome states (*akusaladhammā*) of the aforementioned kind undergo eradication;

they all reach the state of being destroyed. "Rooted in heedfulness" (*appamādamūlakā*): non-negligence, which is the non-forgetting of mindfulness (*sati*), is their root or cause; thus, they are "rooted in heedfulness. Regarding heedfulness...
They "converge" by proceeding correctly; thus, they have heedfulness as their point of convergence (*appamādasamosaraṇā*). It is said that "heedfulness is declared the foremost of those qualities";
therefore, although it itself belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), it is called "foremost" by virtue of being the foundation for the phenomena belonging to all four planes of existence.

"Able" (*alamatta*) means one whose mind is capable. "By me asked" (*mayā pucchitaṃ*) means "asked by me. "Carry this burden" (*vahassetaṃ bhāraṃ*) means "carry this burden that has been brought. "Whosoever have gone forth into the seers' going-forth" (*ye keci isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitā*); there is also a reading: "those who have gone forth into the seers' going-forth" (*isipabbajjā pabbajitā*).
"Ājīvaka disciples, the Ājīvaka deities": those who hear and listen to the words of the Ājīvakas are the Ājīvaka disciples;
"of those Ājīvaka disciples," [it means] the Ājīvakas accept their gifts, and they themselves are the Ājīvaka deities.
This applies in all cases. "Those who are the ones worthy of offerings for whom": those such as the Ājīvakas and others, up to the ends of the quarters, for whom...
They are suitable as objects of giving for the kṣatriyas and others. "They are their deities" means those Ājīvikas and others are the deities of those kṣatriyas and others.
"Those who seek sacrifice" means they desire the object of giving (*deyyadhamma*). "Search" means they look for it. "Seek out" means they procure it.
Or, "these are many sacrifices" means these are indeed numerous sacrifices. Or, "these are many sacrificers" refers to [those who perform] the object of giving.
These *puthuka* are indeed those who perform sacrifices; or these *puthuka* are those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), meaning they are truly suitable for the gifts to be given.
To demonstrate them in detail, he explains at length by way of the method beginning with, "How are these sacrifices manifold?
(13) "Desiring" means longing for form and so forth. "This state" (*itthatta*) means desiring this very condition, that is, the state of being human and so on.
"Desiring" (icchantā) is what is meant. "Seated upon old age" (jaraṃ sitā) means dependent on old age. And here, by way of old age, the entire suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) is expressed.
By this, it is shown that they were dependent on the suffering of the round and, not being liberated from it, they continued to fashion [their worlds].
"Hoping for the acquisition of form" (rūpapaṭilābhaṃ āsīsamānā) means longing for the attainment of excellence in the sense-sphere of visible forms. The same applies to sounds and the rest.

The method [is as follows]: "Obtaining a personal existence in a great noble khattiya family" means aspiring for rebirth—the acquisition of a personal existence—in a great noble khattiya family that has attained excellence. The same method applies to the great noble brahmin families and so forth.
"Among the gods of the Brahmā-world" is said here with reference to their previous existence. "Therein" refers to the khattiya families and the rest.

"Dependent on aging" (*jarānissitā*) means supported by aging. The same method applies to "dependent on illness" (*byādhinissitā*) and so forth. By these [terms], the entire suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is shown to be exhausted.
14. "Are they diligent, Blessed One, in the path of sacrifice? Have they crossed over birth and aging, O Venerable Sir?"—here, "sacrifice" itself is the "path of sacrifice.
This is what is meant: "Are they, being diligent in sacrifice, performing the sacrifice..."
"They have transcended the suffering of saṃsāra.
Those who "give a sacrifice" or "perform a sacrifice" do so by way of giving gifts that are worthy of being given. "Relinquish" means they let go.
"Make aspirations" means they long for the acquisition of form and so forth. "Praise" means [they praise] in the manner beginning with, "A pure gift has been given," and so on.
They praise sacrifices and the like. "They long for" means they utter speech for the sake of obtaining forms and so forth. "They sacrifice" means they give.

"They long for sensual pleasures based on gain" means that, depending upon the gain of forms and so forth, they repeatedly long for sensual pleasures themselves, saying, "O, may these also be ours!"—the meaning is that they increase craving therein. "Devoted to sacrificing."

"Devoted to sacrifice. "Stained by the lust for existence": thus, being stained precisely by the lust for existence through these aspirations and so forth—or having become stained by the lust for existence while performing these aspirations and so forth—they did not cross over, they did not transcend the suffering of the cycle of birth and so on.
"Or they praise sacrifice" means they extol giving; "or the fruit" means the acquisition of form and so forth. "In those worthy of offerings..."
It flows forth toward those endowed with noble birth and other such qualities. "Purely given" means having been made pure, it is given.
"Pleasing" means that which increases the mind's delight. "Exquisite" means possessing nutritive essence (*ojā*). "At the proper time" means at the appropriate moment for each respective occasion.
"Suitable" means given while avoiding what is unsuitable. "Blameless" means faultless. "Constantly" means again and again. "One whose mind is serene while giving" refers to the one who gives.
"A mind that releases is serene. They "praise" and "extol" means they make their virtues manifest.
They "eulogize" means they speak of their praise-worthiness. They "commend" means they bring about confidence.
"On account of this" means on account of the cause given from this human world. "Reciters" (*ajjhāyaka*) are those who repeat the *mantras*. "Bearers of the *mantras*" (*mantadhara*)...
"Reciting the mantras. "Of the three Vedas" means of the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, and *Sāmaveda*.

"Masters" (*pāragū*) means those who have gone to the further shore by means of striking the lips and performing the ritual acts. "Together with the *Nighaṇḍu* and the *Keṭubha*" means of those [Vedas] along with the *Nighaṇḍu* and the *Keṭubha*.
"*Nighaṇḍu*" is the treatise that elucidates synonyms for trees and so forth. "*Keṭubha*" is the poetic elaboration of ritual procedures for poets.

The *sattha* (scripture) brings benefit. "Together with the analysis of syllables" means for those [teachings] that possess the analysis of syllables. "Analysis of syllables" refers to phonology (*sikkhā*) and etymology (*nirutti*).

Regarding the phrase "those for whom history is the fifth": having made the *Atharvaveda* the fourth, "history" (*itihāsa*)—which consists of ancient narratives associated with such expressions as "Thus it was, thus it was"—is the fifth among these.
"With history as the fifth" refers to those [scholars] who have mastered the Vedas with history as the fifth.
They study and know the *pada* (word-texts) and the remainder of the grammar; thus they are called *padakā* and *veyyākaraṇā*.
"Lokāyata" is said to be the science of sophistry (*vitaṇḍavāda*). "The marks of a Great Man" refers to that which illuminates the characteristics of Great Men such as the Buddhas.
A treatise measuring twelve thousand granthas, wherein there were what are called the Buddha-mantras consisting of sixteen thousand verses and phrases.
By means of these [mantras], it was explained: "Those endowed with this characteristic are called Buddhas;
by this, Pratyekabuddhas; by this, the Chief Disciples; by this, the eighty Great Disciples; by this, the Mother of the Buddha; by this, the Father of the Buddha; by this, the Chief Attendant..."

"The foremost attendant, the wheel-turning monarch"—this is the distinction that is known. "Without deficiency" (*anavaya*) means they are not deficient in these worldly doctrines and marks of a Great Man, but rather fulfill them;
what is meant is that they are not "deficient" (*avaya*). Those who are "deficient" are those who are unable to sustain [the teachings] either in meaning or in text.
"Free from lust" (*vītarāga*) means those by whom lust has been abandoned. By this, those established in the fruit of Arahantship are indicated.

"Those who have spoken thus. "Practicing for the removal of lust" refers to those on the path to Arahatship. "Free from hatred" refers to those established in the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
"Practicing for the removal of hatred" refers to those on the path to Non-returning. "Free from delusion" refers to those established in the fruit of Arahatship.
"Practicing for the removal of delusion" refers to those on the path to Arahatship. "Endowed with virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation..."
They are endowed with these four qualities—virtue and the rest—which are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

By the phrase "endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation," it should be understood that they are said to be endowed with the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*), and that is indeed mundane.
"They yearn" means they aspire. "They long" means they expect. "They intensely long" means they expect exceedingly. "Engaged in the practice of sacrifice" means they are devoted to them.
When the object of giving is being bestowed during the formal recitation (*anuyoga*), they are engaged by way of application.
16. "Then who else indeed? means: then now, who other [than me] has crossed over?

17. "Having reckoned" means having investigated with knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "The higher and the lower" means both the higher (*parāni*) and the lower (*oparāni*), such as the state of another self (*parattabhāva*) and one's own state of self (*sakattabhāva*), etc.
"Both those on this side and those on the other"—this is what is meant. "Smokeless" means free from the smoke of bodily misconduct and the like.
"Untroubled" means free from the troubles of passion and the like. "He has crossed over"—such an Arahant as this has crossed over birth and old age.

"One's own forms" refers to one's own physical forms; "others' forms" refers to the physical forms of others. "Bodily misconduct has been blown away"—the threefold bodily misconduct has been rendered smokeless. "Blown away" means destroyed.
For conceit, O brahmin, is like a load of a *khāri* measure. Just as a load of a *khāri* being carried on the shoulder,
even while held aloft, touches the ground at every step it takes, so too conceit— elevated by relying on grounds for conceit such as birth, lineage, and family—
arouses envy here and there and causes one to sink into the four states of misery.
Therefore he said: "Pride, O Brahmin, is indeed a burden of a khāri for you. Anger is smoke:
in the sense of being an impurity to the fire of your knowledge, anger is smoke; for by that, the fire of your knowledge is defiled and does not shine.
Falsehood is ashes: in the sense of being devoid of essence, lying is called ashes. For just as a fire covered by ashes does not blaze, so too [is it] for you because of falsehood.
He shows that knowledge is concealed. He says: "The tongue is a ladle (*sujā*).

Just as you have a ladle made of gold, silver, copper, wood, or clay for the purpose of performing sacrifices, so too do I have an abundant tongue as a ladle for the purpose of performing the sacrifice of the Dhamma.
Just as you have a place of sacrifice on the riverbank, so too [is this] in the sense of being a place for performing the sacrifice of the Dhamma.
The heart is the locus of light. "Self" (*attā*) refers to consciousness (*citta*).

"Birth" (*jāti*) is so called by way of being born; this is its specific individual nature (*sabhāvapaccatta*) here. It is "origination" (*sañjāti*) by way of arising, the prefix having been added to the word.

It is "descent" (*okkanti*) by way of entering [the womb]. Or, it is "birth" (*jāti*) in the sense of being born. That [birth] occurs by way of the non-completion of the sense bases (*aparipuṇṇāyatana*).

It is "joined" (*yuttā*). In the sense of being born, it is "birth" (*sañjāti*); that is joined by way of the fullness of the sense bases (*āyatana*). In the sense of descending, it is "descent" (*okkanti*); that is joined by way of the egg-born and the womb-born.
For these [beings] descend into and enter both the shell of the egg and the membrane of the womb;
as if descending and entering, they take rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). In the sense of manifesting, it is "manifestation" (*abhinibbatti*).

This [birth] is applicable by way of moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) and spontaneously born (*opapātika*). For those two arise having become manifest. This, first of all, is the conventional discourse (*sammutikathā*).
Now follows the discourse on the ultimate meaning (*paramatthakathā*). For it is only the aggregates (*khandhā*) that appear in the ultimate sense, not "beings" (*sattā*).
And therein, "of the aggregates": in a one-aggregate existence, of one; in a four-aggregate existence, of four; in a five-aggregate existence...
The inclusion of all five [aggregates] should be understood. "Manifestation" (*pātubhāvo*) means arising.

Regarding "of the sense-bases" (*āyatanānaṃ*), it should be understood here as a collective term for the sense-bases in which one is reborn in various places. "Acquisition" (*paṭilābho*) is simply the manifestation within the continuity of existence (*santati*).

For it is precisely when they are manifesting that they are said to be "acquired. Furthermore, this [acquisition] is characterized by the initial production [of aggregates] in each respective state of existence.
Birth has the function of producing; its manifestation is the emergence here from a past existence, or alternatively, its manifestation is the diversity of suffering by way of its fruit.

Aging is the individual essence (*sabhāvapaccatta*). "The state of decaying" (*jīraṇatā*) is a description of its mode of manifestation. The three terms beginning with "brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*) are descriptions of its functions when time has passed;
the latter two are descriptions of its natural state. For by this term, "this aging," it is illuminated according to its individual essence.
This is its individual intrinsic nature (*sabhāvapaccatta*). By the term "aging" (*jīraṇatā*), it is described according to its mode; thus, this is a description of its mode.
By the term "brokenness" (*khaṇḍicca*), it is described according to its function of causing the teeth and nails to become broken when the [period of] time has elapsed.

By the term "graying" (*pālicca*), it is described according to its function of causing the hair of the head and body to become gray. By the term "wrinkling" (*valittacatā*), it is described by way of its causing the flesh to wither...
It is so called because its function is to produce wrinkles. Thus, these three—namely, "brokenness" and so forth—are descriptions of its functions when time has passed.
Through the observation of these transformations, "manifest aging" (pākaṭajarā) is demonstrated.
For just as the path taken by water, wind, or fire is made manifest by the state of grass and trees being broken down, crushed, or scorched; [so too is aging made manifest through these signs].

It becomes manifest, yet that path traversed is not merely those things such as water; in the same way, the path traversed by aging through the brokenness of teeth and so forth is manifest and is perceived even when one opens one's eyes, yet aging itself is not merely the brokenness of teeth and so forth.
For aging is not something cognizable by the eye-consciousness.

However, by these two terms—“the waning of life” (*āyuno saṃhāni*) and “the ripening of the faculties” (*indriyānaṃ paripāko*)—the natural state consisting of the exhaustion of life and the ripening of the eye and other faculties is illustrated specifically in relation to the passage of time.
Therefore, it should be understood that these latter two are descriptions of the natural state.
In this context, since the life-span of one who has reached old age diminishes, aging is [described as] "of life..."
The term "deterioration" (*saṃhānī*) is used here by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit [of aging].
For when the faculties such as the eye are in their youth, they are very clear and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects of their own domain;

however, when one has reached old age, these faculties become fully ripened, agitated, and dull, such that they are incapable of grasping even coarse objects of their own domain. Therefore, [it is said]: "Of the faculties..."
"Ripening" is stated by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit.
Furthermore, all this aging (jarā) thus described is twofold: manifest and concealed.

Among these, aging regarding material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) is called "manifest aging," because the state of decay and so forth is visible in the teeth and other parts. However, aging regarding immaterial phenomena (arūpa-dhamma) is...

Because such a transformation is not visible, it is called "concealed aging. In this regard, that state of being broken and so forth which is seen is actually just the *vaṇṇa* (color/appearance) of teeth and other parts that are easily discernible as such.

Having seen that with the eye and reflected upon it through the mind-door, one knows aging by thinking, "These teeth have been struck by aging. [This is like] the horns of a cow and so forth tied up in a watering place.
It is like perceiving the presence of water below after having looked [at the surface].
Furthermore, this aging is twofold: "without interval" (avīci) and "with interval" (savīci).

In that regard, it is like the gradual fading of gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, the sun, and so forth among living beings such as humans; and like the gradual withering of flowers, fruits, sprouts, and so forth among non-living things. Between these instances—
Because the specific changes in complexion and so forth are difficult to discern, aging is called "uninterrupted aging" (*avīcijarā*); the meaning is that it is continuous aging.

However, in other cases among those already mentioned, because the specific changes in complexion and so forth are easily discernible from time to time, aging is called "interrupted aging" (*savīcijarā*).
Therein, interrupted aging should be illustrated by way of both the clung-to (*upādinnaka*) and the unclung-to (*anupādinnaka*): for instance, in the case of young children...
First of all, what are called milk-teeth appear; they are not firm. When those have fallen out, teeth appear again;
these are white from the very beginning, but when struck by the wind of old age, they become black. Hair, moreover, may be reddish-brown, black, or white from the very beginning.
The skin, however, is still blood-red in those who are growing.
In those growing white things, the whiteness becomes apparent; in black things, the blackness becomes apparent. And when struck by the wind of old age, it takes on wrinkles.
Just as all grain is white at the time of sowing but later turns green, so too, when struck by the wind of old age, it becomes pale-white.
It is certainly appropriate to illustrate this with the sprout of a mango as well. Furthermore, this [aging] has the characteristic of the maturation of the aggregates.
Old age has the function of bringing about death; its manifestation is the destruction of youth. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta also by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship;
at the conclusion of the teaching, this brahmin also became established in Arahantship together with his thousand pupils, and the Dhamma-eye arose in many thousands of others.
It arose. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Puṇṇaka-māṇava-sutta* in the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the sub-commentary on the *Cūḷaniddesa*, is completed.
4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Mettagū Māṇava Sutta 18.

Regarding the fourth discourse, the Mettagū Sutta: “I consider you a master of knowledge (vedagū) and one who has developed himself (bhāvitatta)” means that I consider you thus as a “master of knowledge” and as “one who has developed himself.
“Not limited” (aparitta) means not small. “Great” (mahanta) means not insignificant. “Profound” (gambhīra) means not shallow. “Immeasurable” (appameyya) means [incapable] of being measured.
“Unassailable” means it cannot be overcome. “Difficult to fathom” means it is hard to plunge into or enter. “Possessing many jewels, like the ocean”:

because it is a source of many jewels of the Dhamma, it possesses manifold gems and is thus like the great ocean; it is "possessing many jewels" and resembles the sea. “He does not become dejected” means he does not have a downcast face.

“With a mind that is not fixed” means his mind is not hardened by hatred. “With a mind that is not cowed” means his mind is not contracted. “With a mind that is not corrupted” means his mind is not putrid.
"In what is seen, only what is seen" means that regarding the object of form within the domain of the eye, there is only what is seen;
that object alone will exist, and there is no agent or instigator. That which is seen by the eye is simply the sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*).

This same method applies to hearing and the other senses as well. Furthermore, "the seen" refers to the sphere of visible form by way of seeing, the sphere of sound by way of hearing, and [the sphere of odor] by way of smelling.
He shows the sense bases of the nose, tongue, and body. For the nose, he shows the base of odors; for the tongue, the base of flavors;
for the body, the base of tangibles—namely earth, fire, and air—and by way of what is cognized, he shows the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*).
"Not clinging to what is seen" means being free from the clinging of lust regarding what is seen by eye-consciousness. "Not falling away" means being free from anger and non-opposition.
"Independent" means not clinging through craving. "Unbound" means not fettered by conceit. "Completely liberated" means released from all objects.
"Dissociated" means remaining having become detached from the defilements.
"The eye exists for the Blessed One" means that the natural physical eye of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is found.
"Passati" means he sees or looks upon. "Cakkhunā rūpaṃ" means a visible form as an object for eye-consciousness. "Chandarāgo" means the desire of craving.

"Dantaṃ nayanti samitiṃ" means that when people go into the midst of a great crowd at places such as pleasure gardens or circular arenas, they lead only a tamed ox or a tamed noble horse, having yoked it to a vehicle. "Rājā" refers to such places indeed.
Even when traveling, the king mounts only a tamed elephant. Regarding "among men": even among men, one who is tamed by the four noble paths and is free from malice is the best.
Regarding "one who endures reproach": even when such transgressive speech is spoken repeatedly, he endures it;
he does not flare up nor is he distressed. Such a tamed person is the best—this is the meaning.
*Muletsa* refers to those born from a mare and a donkey. *Ājānīya* refers to those capable of quickly understanding whatever task a trainer of tame horses commands them to perform.
*Sindhava* refers to horses born in the kingdom of Sindhu. *Mahānāga* refers to great elephants, so called because they are like tuskers.
*Attadanta*: these—whether mules, Sindhu horses, or tuskers—are indeed well-tamed, not untamed.
But he who, through his own self-taming, is self-subdued—meaning tamed by means of what is known as the four paths—and is free from worldly attachments, is even better than that;
the meaning is that he is superior to all of these.
For no person [is equal] by means of those vehicles—that is, by means of these supreme vehicles such as the elephant-vehicle and so forth.
Because it has never been gone to even in a dream, one would not go in that manner toward the direction of Nibbāna,

which is designated as "the ungone. Just as a person who is tamed— tamed by the restraint of the faculties in the prior stage and well-tamed by the cultivation of the Noble Path in the subsequent stage—
who is tamed, free from worldly trappings, and possessed of wisdom, goes to that direction never before gone and reaches the plane of the tamed.
Therefore, the meaning is that self-taming alone is more excellent.
"They do not waver in various circumstances" means they do not shake or tremble amidst the ninefold divisions of pride.
"Completely liberated from renewed existence" means they are well-freed from the defilements of karma through the liberation of total eradication. "Having reached the stage of the tamed."

They stand having attained the fruit of arahantship. "Those who have conquered in the world" refers to those aforementioned ones whose taints are exhausted; they are called "victorious conquerors" in the world of beings.
"One whose faculties are developed" refers to that one whose taints are exhausted, whose five faculties beginning with faith have been increased by reaching the fruit of arahantship.
"Internally and externally" refers to the internal sense bases such as the eye, and the external sense bases such as visible forms.
And they have been rendered free from attachment. "In the whole world" means in the entire world-system (*sakkalate-dhātuke loke*).

"Having become disillusioned with this world and the next" means having transcended both this present selfhood and the selfhood in the future world, he stands as one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).

"He awaits his time, cultivated and self-controlled" means that this one whose taints are exhausted, being self-controlled through the faculties such as the eye and possessing developed mind, yearns for the time of death.
"Of those phenomena whose initial origination is discerned" means that the arising of those phenomena, such as the aggregates, is discerned.
"Cessation by way of passing away" means that their very non-existence is discerned through the process of passing away.
"Resultant [state] dependent on karma" means that the result is dependent on wholesome or unwholesome karma, because it proceeds without relinquishing that karma.
Even fruition (vipāka) is said to be dependent upon karma alone. "Matter dependent on mind" (nāmasannissitaṃ rūpaṃ) becomes so because it proceeds by taking up all matter within the mind;
thus, it is called "dependent on mind. "Followed by birth" means that everything, beginning with karma, has entered into birth.
"Pervaded by aging" means spread over by aging. "Overcome by illness" means [overcome] by the suffering of illness.
"Trampled": struck down by death, brought down and beaten by Māra. "Without refuge":
because there is no protection even from sons and others, it is a state of non-protection, unguarded, or a security that cannot be found. "Without shelter": unfit for one to cling to or rely upon;
even for those who have clung to it, it does not perform the function of a shelter. "Without a resort": it does not remove fear for those who depend upon it.

It does not destroy fear. "Becoming a non-refuge" means that it is a non-refuge precisely because of its own non-existence prior to arising; the meaning is that it becomes a non-refuge at the very moment of its arising. 19. Regarding "Do you ask? (*apucchasī*):
here, *a-* is a particle used merely for metrical completion; the sense is simply "you ask. "I shall explain" (*pavakkhāmi*).
I shall explain it just as they understand it, and as one who understands explains it.
"Suffering arises with acquisition (*upadhi*) as its source": various sufferings such as birth arise with craving and other forms of acquisition as their source.

"Craving-acquisition" means craving itself is the craving-acquisition. "View-acquisition" means the views of eternalism and annihilationism themselves are the view-acquisition. [Likewise] the defilements such as lust (*rāga*).

The defilements themselves are the substrate of defilement (*kilesūpadhi*). Meritorious and other types of kamma are themselves the substrate of kamma (*kammūpadhi*). The three kinds of misconduct are themselves the substrate of misconduct (*duccaritūpadhi*).
Edible food and the other nutriments are themselves the substrate of nutriment (*āhārūpadhi*). Hostility and resentment are themselves the substrate of resentment (*paṭighūpadhi*).

The four elements, such as earth, which are produced by kamma and grasped by kamma, are themselves the four clung-to elements (*upādinnadhātu*), which are the substrates. The six internal bases, beginning with the eye, [are likewise].
The six internal sense bases (*āyatana*) themselves are acquisitions (*upadhi*).

The six groups of consciousness, beginning with eye-consciousness, are also acquisitions. Furthermore, all suffering is suffering in the sense of being oppressive; thus, all suffering pertaining to the three planes is an acquisition in the sense of being difficult to bear.
20. Thus, regarding the verses beginning with "He who indeed is unwise" concerning the sufferings that originate from the cause of acquisitions (*upadhi*):

therein, "one who understands" means one who knows conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) by way of their impermanence and so forth. "Contemplating the origin of suffering as birth" means contemplating that the cause of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is "acquisitions.
There is nothing further to be said in the commentary (*niddesa*) on this verse.

21. “Sokapariddavañca” means both sorrow (*soka*) and lamentation (*parideva*). “For this Dhamma has been known by you just as beings know it” means that this Dhamma has been understood by you through the process of making it known, exactly as sentient beings perceive it.

In this context, “they cross over” means they cross the flood of views (*diṭṭhogha*) by means of the first path. “They emerge” means they emerge and cross the flood of sensual desire (*kāmogha*) by means of the second path, through the process of attenuating it.
“They go forth across” means they do so by means of the third path, through the process of abandoning that very [flood] without remainder.

They cross over specifically. "They transcend" means they correctly transcend by means of the fourth path through the abandoning of the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) and the flood of ignorance (*avijjā-ogha*).
"They go beyond" means they abide having attained the fruit.
22. "I shall proclaim the Dhamma to you": I shall teach you the Dhamma of Nibbāna and the Dhamma of the practice leading to Nibbāna.
"In this very life" (*diṭṭhe dhamme*) means in the very phenomena of suffering and so forth that are seen, or in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"Not subject to dispute" (*anītika*) means directly evident to oneself. "Having understood which" (*yaṃ viditvā*) means having understood which phenomenon by way of such methods as "all conditioned things are impermanent.
In that regard, "beautiful in the beginning" (*ādikalyāṇa*) means: even setting aside the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion, I shall proclaim your Dhamma; and that—
Whether praising it briefly or at length, I shall praise it precisely as being excellent in its beginning and so forth. This means:
having made it auspicious, excellent, and blameless in the beginning, I shall praise it; likewise in the middle, and having made it auspicious and blameless in the end, I shall praise it.
For even a single verse that the Blessed One taught is entirely auspicious on all sides.
By the first quarter of the Dhamma, it is excellent in the beginning; by the second and third quarters, it is excellent in the middle;

and by the final quarter, it is excellent in the end. A discourse with a single sequence of sections is excellent in the beginning through its introduction (*nidāna*), excellent in the end through its conclusion (*nigamana*), and excellent in the middle through the remainder.
A discourse with multiple sequences of sections is excellent in the beginning through the first sequence and [excellent in the end] through the final one.
It is "good in the end" because of its conclusion; it is "good in the middle" by virtue of the remaining [sections].
Furthermore, it is "good in the beginning" because it has a specific origin (*sanidāna-uppatti*);

it is "good in the middle" because the meaning is unerring due to its suitability for those to be trained (*veneyya*) and because it is endowed with reasons and examples; and it is "good in the end" through the conclusion, which generates faith in the listeners.
And it is excellent in the conclusion.

For the entire Dhamma of the Dispensation is excellent in the beginning by virtue of morality, which constitutes its own benefit; it is excellent in the middle by means of serenity, insight, the paths, and the fruits;
and it is excellent in the conclusion by means of Nibbāna. Or alternatively, it is excellent in the beginning by way of morality and concentration, and by way of insight and the paths...
It is beautiful in the middle through the fruits [of practice] and beautiful in the end through Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is beautiful in the beginning because of the Buddha’s perfect awakening;
beautiful in the middle because of the Dhamma’s intrinsic excellence; and beautiful in the end because of the Saṅgha’s correct practice.

Or, for one who has heard it and is practicing accordingly, it is beautiful in the beginning through the full awakening that is to be attained; [beautiful in the middle through] the awakening of a Pacceka-Buddha...
It is beautiful in the middle and beautiful in its conclusion through the enlightenment of a disciple.
When it is being heard, because it suppresses the hindrances, it brings about what is beautiful even by way of its hearing; thus it is "beautiful in the beginning.
When it is being practiced, because it brings about the bliss of serenity and insight, it brings about what is beautiful even by way of practice.

It is "beautiful in the middle" because one who practices accordingly, when the fruit of practice is accomplished, brings about the state of suchness (*tādibhāva*); thus, by means of the fruit of practice as well, it brings about what is beautiful, and is therefore "beautiful in the conclusion.
Furthermore, when the Blessed One teaches this Dhamma, he reveals both the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsanabrahmacariya*) and the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*).

He illuminates it through various methods. It is "possessing the meaning" (sāttha) by virtue of its perfection of meaning, and "possessing the phrasing" (sabyañjana) by virtue of its perfection of phrasing.
It is "possessing the meaning" through its conjunction with the words of the meaning, consisting of its making known, manifesting, explaining, analyzing, clarifying, and establishing.

It is "possessing the phrasing" through the perfection of its syllables, words, phrases, modes, etymologies, and definitions. [It is profound] through the profundity of its meaning and the profundity of its penetration.
It is "with meaning" (*sāttha*) because of the profundity of the doctrine (*dhamma*) and the profundity of the teaching (*desanā*).

It is "with phrasing" (*sabyañjana*) because it is the domain of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) and the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*). It is "with meaning" because it is to be understood by the wise and inspires confidence in those who are similar to them.
It is "with phrasing" because it is credible and inspires confidence in worldly people. It is "with meaning" because its intention is profound.
It is "with phrasing" because it is expressed with clear words. It is "absolutely complete" because it is entirely perfect due to the absence of anything that needs to be added.
It is "pure" because it is faultless due to the absence of anything that needs to be removed.
Furthermore, it is "possessed of meaning" because of the excellence of the realization through practice; it is "with phrasing" because of the excellence of the tradition through study.
It is "entirely complete" because it is endowed with the five aggregates of dhamma beginning with virtue (*sīla*).
It is "pure" because it is free from defilements, functions for the sake of crossing over [the flood of existence], and is indifferent to worldly gain.

It is "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*) because it is embraced by the three trainings, because it is to be practiced by those who have become sublime and excellent, and because it is the very state of their practice.
Having thus shown the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma), he now said, "The four foundations of mindfulness," in order to show the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma).
Having shown the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), he said, "And Nibbāna," in order to show the supramundane state produced [thereby].
And I shall praise the practice leading to Nibbāna, which consists of the preliminary qualities of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and insight (vipassanā).

"Seen as suffering": when suffering is seen by way of its own intrinsic characteristic (*sarasalakkhaṇa*), I shall reveal the truth of suffering. This same method applies to the origin and the other truths as well. "I rejoice in that":
I long for those words of yours which illuminate the Dhamma in the manner described. "The supreme Dhamma": I rejoice in that supreme Dhamma.
In this context, "the shattering of the great mass of darkness" means the cutting away of the great heap of ignorance (*avijjā*). By way of the characteristic of impermanence...
He seeks by way of the characteristic of suffering. He searches all around by way of the characteristic of non-self.
"The breaking up of the great perversion" means the shattering of the twelvefold perversion, such as "beauty in the ugly" and so forth.
"The plucking out of the great dart of craving" refers to the great thorn of craving in the sense of its piercing within.
"Plucking out": the untying of the "robe of views. Views themselves are called a "robe" (*saṅghāṭa*) in the sense of being sewn together because they proceed without interruption;
its "untying" is the turning back from that robe of views. "Felling the banner of conceit":

the felling of the banner of conceit, which has the characteristic of loftiness in the sense of being raised high. "The subsiding of formative activity": of formative activity such as merit (*puñña*), etc.
"Quelling" means crossing over the flood; it is the crossing over and emerging from the flood of sensual desire and so forth, which causes one to sink into the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"Laying down the burden" means casting off and discarding the burden of the five aggregates, beginning with form.
"Severing the round of saṃsāra" means the cutting off of the round of saṃsāra—the succession of aggregates and so forth—by destroying its cause.
"The extinguishing of the fever" means the extinction of the fever of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"The allaying of the burning" means the pacification and subsiding of the burning of the defilements. "The raising of the banner of the Dhamma" means the raising up and establishing of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.
"The ultimate, the deathless Nibbāna": it is the ultimate in the sense of being supreme. There is... [no further text provided].
It is called "deathless" (*amata*) because it is dead, meaning that which is designated as death has ceased.

It is also called "antidote" (*agada*) because it is the opposite of the poison of the defilements (*kilesa*). It is called "nibbāna" because it is the extinction (*nibbuta*) that serves as the opposite of the suffering of saṃsāra.

It is called "nibbāna" because there is no craving (*taṇhā*), which is a kind of "flame" (*āna*), here. "By beings of great influence" means by beings such as Sakka who possess great majesty. "Sought after" means searched for. "Where is the God of Gods? means where is the one who transcends the gods. "Where is the Bull among Men? means where is the supreme person.
24. "Above, below, across, and in the middle": here, "above" refers to the future time; "below" refers to the past time;
and "across and in the middle" refers to the present time. Regarding the phrase "having dispelled both delight and settling therein, consciousness":
in these [times] such as above and so forth, you must dispel craving, the settling of views, and the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*). Having dispelled them—
And it does not abide in existence; such being the case, it would not abide in either of the two kinds of existence.

Thus, first, in this interpretation of the meaning of the word *panudeti* as "drive away," the connection is as follows. However, in the interpretation of the meaning of *panuditvā*, the connection is simply:

"having driven away [these] consciousnesses which are the abode of delight, it does not abide in either of the two kinds of existence. These consciousnesses, which are the abodes of delight... having driven them away... in either of the two kinds of existence.
"One should not stand in existence" means:
by way of their respective locations, the world of the devas is above, the world of the states of misery is below, and the human world is in the middle.
In this context, "wholesome states" are called "above" because, having escaped the world of misery, they bestow rebirth in the higher realms.

Unwholesome states (*akusala-dhammā*) are called "below" because they grant rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the realms of misery (*apāya*). Because they are free from both of these, indeterminate states (*abyākata-dhammā*) are said to be "across" and also "in the middle.
By way of being entirely above, the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*) is "above. By way of being entirely below, the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) is "below.
By way of being between those two, the fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*) is "in the middle. [The term *khaṇa* is used] in the sense of piercing through afflictions of body and mind.
Pleasant feeling is "above. Painful feeling is "below" by way of its painful nature. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is "in the middle.
Showing the delimitation by way of the individual existence (attabhāva), he said: "Above means above the soles of the feet," and so forth.
Therein, "above the soles of the feet" means from the soles of the feet upwards. "Below the top of the head" means from the top of the head downwards. "In the middle" means between the two.
"Consciousness accompanied by the formation of merit" refers to kamma-consciousness associated with the thirteen kinds of formations of merit.
"Consciousness accompanied by the formation of demerit" refers to kamma-consciousness associated with the twelve kinds of formations of demerit.
"Consciousness accompanied by the formation of the imperturbable" refers to kamma-consciousness accompanied by the four kinds of formations of the imperturbable.
*Nujjāti* means "to cast away. *Panujjāti* means "to cast away excessively. *Nudāti* means "to pull out. *Panudāti* means "to pull out excessively.
*Pajahāti* means "abandon. *Vinodehī* means "make it distant.

*Kammabhavañca* refers specifically to the volition of meritorious formative action (*puññābhisaṅkhāra-cetanā*). *Paṭisandhikañca punabbhavaṃ* refers to renewed existence by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

And the renewed existence of form and so forth: abandoning it by means of the first path, dispelling it by means of the second path, bringing it to an end by means of the third path, and causing its non-existence by means of the fourth path.
"One would not stand in kamma-becoming" means one would not stand in the volitional formations of merit and so forth.

25. Having dispelled these and not standing in becoming, this one—thus dwelling—is the subject of the verse. Therein, "right here" means in this very teaching, or in this very personal existence. The explanation of this verse is plain in meaning.

26. Regarding the phrase "Well-expounded, O Gotama, is that which is without substrate (*anūpadhika*)," here "without substrate" refers to *nibbāna*. Addressing the Blessed One with reference to that, he said: "Well-expounded, O Gotama, is that which is without substrate.

In the *Niddesa*, it is stated that both the defilements (*kilesa*)—namely, lust and the rest—in the sense of burning (*upatāpana*), and the five aggregates consisting of result (*vipāka*) in the sense of a heap (*rāsa*), as well as wholesome and other formative volitions (*abhisankhāra-cetanā*), are called and spoken of as "substrates" (*upadhi*). The abandoning of the substrate...

By the abandoning of its factors, it is the subsiding of the acquisitions (*upadhi*) through suppression-abandoning; by the relinquishing of the acquisitions, it is the relinquishment of the acquisitions through eradication-abandoning;
and by the pacification of the acquisitions, it is the fruit. 27.
He did not abandon suffering alone—this is the verse beginning with "te cāpi. Therein, *aṭṭhitaṃ* means thoroughly.
"Or always. "I shall revere him"—therefore, I revere him. "Having approached" (*samecca*) means having gone near. "O Nāgas!"—this he said while addressing the Blessed One.

In the *Niddesa*, "having approached" (*samecca*) means having known, or having come together as one. "Having fully approached" (*abhisamecca*) means having penetrated [the truth]. "Having come together" (*samāgantvā*) means having come face to face.

"Having fully come together" (*abhisamāgantvā*) means having gone into his presence. "Face to face" (*sammukhā*) means in the presence of. "He does not commit sin" (*āguṃ na karoti*) means he does not perform evil.

28. Now, although the Blessed One was already known by that brahmin as one who had indeed abandoned suffering—since he had said, "Surely the Blessed One has abandoned suffering"—the Blessed One, without allowing himself to be identified [merely] by that, spoke the verse beginning with "O brahmin," in order to instruct a person who had abandoned suffering.

Its meaning is as follows: "That which one fully understands, because of having cast out evil, one is a *brāhmaṇa*; because of having gone by means of the Vedas, one is a *vedagū* (one who has reached the Vedas)."

One should know—that is, you should understand—that because of the absence of anything to cling to, he is "possessing nothing" (akiñcana); and because of his lack of attachment to sensual pleasures and states of existence, he is "unattached to sensual pleasures and existence.
Indeed, he has certainly crossed this flood; having crossed to the further shore, he is free from harshness and free from doubt.

In the *Niddesa*, "the clinging of lust" (*rāgakiñcana*) means the obstruction of lust. The same method applies to "the clinging of hatred" (*dosakiñcana*) and so forth. He has crossed the flood of sensual pleasures.
By the path of non-returning, he has crossed the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*). By the path of arahantship, he has crossed the flood of views (*diṭṭhi-ogha*).

By the path of stream-entry, he has crossed the flood of ignorance (*avijjā-ogha*). By the path of arahantship, he has crossed the flood of ignorance. He has crossed the path of saṃsāra by way of the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome kamma.
He has crossed over by the first path. He has fully crossed over by the second path. He has transcended by the third path. He has completely transcended...
He has transcended by means of the fourth path; he has attained the fruit. 29. And what more?
[It is explained] in the verse beginning with "The wise man who... Herein, "here" (*idha*) means in this teaching or in this personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"Having relinquished" (*visajja*) means having let go. In the detailed explanation (*niddesa*), "cling" (*sajjanti*) means releasing; "relinquish" (*visajjanti*) means letting go. The rest is clear everywhere. Thus...
The Blessed One taught this sutta also by means of the pinnacle of arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma exactly as described above.
Thus ends the commentary on the Cūḷaniddesa from the Saddhammappajjotikā.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Mettagū-māṇava-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Exposition of the *Dhotaka-māṇava-sutta* 30.

Regarding the fifth discourse, the *Dhotaka-sutta*: "I desire speech" (*vācābhikaṅkhāmīti*) means I desire speech.
