"One who desires nibbāna for oneself should train" (*sikkhe nibbānamattano*) means one should train in the higher virtue and so forth for the sake of the nibbāna of one's own lust and other defilements. In the detailed exposition (*niddesa*), there is nothing new.
"Thus" means from my own mouth. In the *Niddesa*:

"Ardor" (*ātappa*) is the burning away of the defilements. "Exertion" (*ussāha*) is the absence of shrinking back. "Strenuousness" (*ussoḷhi*) is powerful energy. "Firmness" (*thāma*) is being unslackened.
"Fortitude" (*dhiti*) is steadfastness. "Exert energy" means perform effort. "Generate desire" means produce a wish.
32. When this was said, Dhota, being pleased, spoke the verse beginning with "I see" (*passāmahaṃ*) while praising the Blessed One and requesting the resolution of his doubt.
Therein, "I see in the world of gods and men" (*passāmi ahaṃ devamanussaloke*) means: I see [it] in the world of gods and men.
"I shall revere that" (*taṃ taṃ namassāmi*) means: I shall revere such a one as that. "Release me" (*pamuñca*) means: set me free.
In the *Niddesa*, "paccekabuddhā" means those who have awakened by themselves (*sayameva buddhā*) to the Four Noble Truths individually (*pāṭiyekkaṃ*) regarding each respective object;
thus they are "paccekabuddhas. "Sīhasīho" means a lion among lions in the sense of being utterly fearless.

"Nāganāgo" means a naga among nagas in the sense of being free from defilements (*nikkilesa*), or in the sense of being exceedingly great (*mahanta*). "Gaṇigaṇī" means one who possesses a retinue more than those who possess retinues. "Munimuni" means...
"Among those possessing knowledge, you are exceedingly wise. 'Rājarāja' means the supreme king. 'Muñca maṃ' means release me.
'Pamuñca maṃ' means release me in various ways. 'Mocehi maṃ' means make me free. 'Pamocehi maṃ' means make me exceedingly free.
'Uddhara maṃ' means having lifted me up from the mire of *saṃsāra*, establish me on firm ground."
"Uplift me," he said, "having rightly lifted me up, establish me on dry land. "Deliver me" means:
having removed me from the dart of doubt, raise me up by way of separation.
Then the Blessed One, showing him that the resolution of his own doubts was dependent solely upon himself, by way of crossing the flood, said:
He spoke the verse beginning with “I will not. Therein, “I will not endure” means I will not endure; I am unable. “I will not strive” is what is meant.
“For the sake of release” means for the purpose of releasing. “How can I cross? means with doubt. “You would cross” means you might cross.
In the detailed explanation (niddesa), “I do not strive” means I do not make an effort. “I do not exert myself” means I do not make an excessive effort. [This applies to] those lacking faith.
"Persons" refers to persons devoid of faith in the Triple Gem. "Lacking desire" refers to those devoid of the aspiration for the path and its fruit.
"Lax" refers to those devoid of concentration. "Of inferior energy" refers to those who are weak in effort. "Not practicing" refers to those who do not engage in the practice.
When this was said, Dhota, being even more uplifted in mind, praised the Blessed One and requested his instruction.
He spoke the verse: “Instruct me, O Brahmā. In this context, “Brahmā” is a term for the supreme. Addressing the Blessed One with that, he said, “Instruct me, O Brahmā.
“The state of seclusion” refers to the state of Nibbāna, which is the seclusion from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
“Without falling into affliction” means without undergoing various kinds of suffering. “Being right here” means being present right here. “Unattached” means independent.
35–7. The two verses following this are exactly according to the method explained in the *Mettagū-sutta*.
The only difference is that where that [sutta] says "the Dhamma," here it says "peace" (*santi*). In the third verse as well, the first half is according to the same method as explained there.
In the second half, "clinging" (*saṅga*) means a place of attachment; "clinging" (*lagga*) is what is meant. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating specifically in Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma exactly as previously described.
The commentary on the exposition of the Dhotaka-māṇava Sutta in the *Saddhammappajjotikā*,
the sub-commentary to the *Cūḷaniddesa*, is completed.
6. Explanation of the Discourse to the Young Brahmin Upasīva (Upasīvamāṇavasuttaniddesavaṇṇanā) 38.

Regarding the sixth discourse, the *Upasīva-sutta*: "A great flood" (*mahantamogha*) means a vast deluge. "Unattached" (*anissito*) means not clinging to either a person (*puggala*) or a phenomenon (*dhamma*).
"I am unable" (*no visahāmi*) means I am not capable. "An object" (*ārammaṇa*) means a support (*nissaya*). "That which one is dependent upon" (*yaṃ nissito*)...
"Depending on which phenomenon (dhamma) or person (puggala). In the *Niddesa*, it says:

"By the path of non-returning, one would cross the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha); by the path of arahantship, the flood of existence (bhavogha); by the path of stream-entry, the flood of views (diṭṭhogha);
and by the path of arahantship, the flood of ignorance (avijjogha). 'One who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan' refers to the Blessed One."
This is stated by way of illustrating a high-born family. "Support" (*ālambana*) means a place that has been traversed; "basis" (*nissaya*) means that to which one clings;
"proximate cause" (*upanissaya*) means that which one leans upon. 39.
Now, because the brahmin is an attainer of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), yet he does not know even that peaceful basis.
Then the Blessed One, showing him that support as well as the further path to deliverance, spoke the verse beginning with “nothingness.

In this context, *pekkhamāno* means seeing that attainment of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-samāpatti*) by way of its impermanence and other characteristics, after having mindfully entered it and emerged from it.
*Natthīti nissāya* means relying on that attainment which occurs through the thought, “there is nothing whatsoever.”
"Making it the object": from that point onward, cross over the fourfold flood by means of insight (vipassanā) as it arises accordingly.
"With doubts": with hesitations. "Behold the destruction of craving day and night":
behold Nibbāna, having made it manifest throughout the day and night. By this, he described his dwelling in happiness in this very life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra).
In the Niddesa it says: "He brings that very consciousness to non-existence" means that, having made space the object, he brings the sublime consciousness that has arisen to non-existence;
he causes it to go to non-existence. "He makes it disappear" means he causes it to go to various kinds of non-existence. "He makes it vanish" means he causes it to go beyond the range of sight.
"He sees that 'there is nothing at all'" means he sees that there is not even so much as its mere dissolution.
40. Now, having heard the words “having abandoned sensual pleasures,” and perceiving the sensual pleasures he himself had abandoned by way of suppression, he spoke the verse beginning with “In all.
Therein, “having left behind” means having left behind the sixfold attainment that is inferior to that [state].
“He considers the supreme among the liberations of perception” means he dwells in the base of nothingness, which is the highest among the seven liberations of perception. He dwells...
"Would he not remain there, not departing?"—this asks whether that person might stand there in the Brahma-world of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) without passing away.

In the *Niddesa*, "not departing" (*aviccamāno*) means not being separated [from it]. "Not passing away" (*avigacchamāno*) means not undergoing separation. "Not disappearing" (*anantaradhāyamāno*) means not undergoing disappearance. "Not falling away" (*aparihāyamāno*) means not undergoing immediate falling away.
41-2. Then the Blessed One, granting him a lifespan of only sixty thousand kappas, spoke the fourth verse.
Having thus heard of his standing there, [the interlocutor] now asked about the nature of his eternity or annihilation, and spoke the verse beginning with "tiṭṭhe ce.
In that context, "pūgam-pi vassānam" means many, even innumerable, years; "gaṇanarāsim" means a heap of numbers.
The meaning is as follows. There is also a reading: “pūgampi vassāni. In that case, by changing the grammatical case, the genitive case should be made into the nominative;
or else, the meaning of “pūgam” should be stated as “many. They also read “pūgāni,” but the former reading alone is most excellent.
In that very place, he—meaning he might be liberated—that person, right there in the base of nothingness, [is freed] from various sufferings.
The intention is: "Would he be liberated, having attained a state of coolness, and remaining eternal once he has reached Nibbāna?
With the words "the consciousness of such a one would pass away," he asks about annihilation, implying: "Or rather, would the consciousness of such a one attain final Nibbāna without clinging?
He also asks him about rebirth-linking with the phrase "or it might [arise] for the purpose of grasping rebirth."
"His consciousness would perish" means that the consciousness of one who has arisen in the base of nothingness would undergo death.
"It would be annihilated" means it would come to an end. "It would be destroyed" means it would reach ruin. "It would not exist" means it would go to non-existence.
"Of one who has been reborn" means of one who has been reborn by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

43. Then the Blessed One, avoiding both annihilationism and eternalism, spoke the verse beginning with “Just as a flame” to show the final Nibbāna without clinging of a noble disciple who has been reborn there.
In that context, “it goes to its end” means it reaches its cessation.
“It does not enter into reckoning” means it does not enter into common usage such as “it has gone to such-and-such a direction. Thus is the sage [freed] from the mental body.
"Released": thus, the *sekha*-muni who has arisen therein was already naturally released from the form-body (*rūpakāya*) even previously;
having realized the fourth path therein, because the body of phenomena (*dhammakāya*) has been fully understood, he is further released from the name-body (*nāmakāya*) as well.

Being one released in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) and one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), he goes to the goal known as *anupādā-nibbāna* (Nirvana through non-clinging) and does not enter into reckoning as a "khattiya."
“...or a brahmin,” and so forth. In the *Niddesa*, it says: “*Khitta*” means moved;
“*Ukkhitta*” means excessively moved; “*Nunna*” means struck away; “*Paṇunna*” means driven far away; “*Khambhitā*” means made to retreat; “*Vikkhambhitā*” means not kept near.
Now, having heard the words “he has set out for his goal (*atthaṃ paleti*),” one who does not discern its meaning through wise reflection [thinks]: “He has gone to his end (*atthaṅgato so*).”
He spoke this verse. Its meaning is as follows: "Has he reached cessation, or does he not exist;
or rather, is he eternal, being healthy and of an unchanging nature? Thus, O Sage, please explain this well to me. For what reason?
Because this Dhamma is known to you in such a way.

In the *Niddesa*, "ceased" (*niruddha*) means having reached cessation. "Cut off" (*ucchinna*) means the continuity [of existence] has been severed. "Perished" (*vinaṭṭha*) means having reached destruction.
Then, the Blessed One, demonstrating that he cannot be described in such a way, spoke the verse beginning with "of one who has gone to rest" (*atthaṅgatassa*).

Therein, "of one who has gone to rest" means of one who has attained final nibbāna through non-clinging. "There is no measure" (*na pamāṇamatthi*) means there is no measure of form and so forth by which [he might be defined].

"By which they would call him" means by which passion (*rāga*) and so forth they would speak of him. "In all phenomena" (*sabbesu dhammesu*) means in all phenomena such as the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.

In the *Niddesa*, it says "and designations" (*adhivacanāni*): for terms such as "Sirivaḍḍhaka" (Fortune-increaser) or "Dhanavaḍḍhaka" (Wealth-increaser) are called "designations" (*adhivacanā*) because they proceed by making a mere verbal expression the primary focus. The "paths of designations" (*adhivacanapathā*) are the paths of those designations. "They form [volitional formations]" (*abhisaṅkharonti*).
“Monks, it is for this reason that they are called ‘formations’”—having thus determined and stated with their cause, such expressions are called *nirutti* (linguistic expression).

The paths of linguistic expressions are called *niruttipathā*. Because it makes known in various ways, such as “reasoning, directed thought, intention,” it is called *paññatti* (conceptualization). The paths of conceptualizations are called *paññattipathā*.
The remainder is clear in every respect.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta as well by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma exactly as previously described.
[End of] the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Cūḷaniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the Upasīva-māṇava-sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Nanda-māṇava-sutta: 46.

Regarding the seventh sutta, the Nanda-sutta—the meaning of the first verse: "In the world" refers to the various classes of people such as kṣatriyas and others; "among the Ājīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, and so forth" refers to the various ascetic sects.

Having intended this, they say, "There are sages in the world. How is this so? Do they call a sage one who has "attained through knowledge" because he is endowed with knowledge such as the knowledge of meditative attainments (*samāpatti-ñāṇa*), etc.? Or do they speak of such a one [in that way]?
Or rather, do they call him one who has "attained" by means of a life characterized by various kinds of coarse living?

In the *Niddesa*, "by the knowledge of the eight attainments" means by the knowledge associated with the eight attainments, beginning with the first jhāna; or "by the knowledge of the five higher knowledges" means by the knowledge that knows past lives and so forth. 47.
Then the Blessed One, having rejected both of those, spoke the verse beginning with "Not by view," showing [the true] sage.
48. Now, in order to remove doubt regarding the claims of those who say "purity comes through views and so forth," he asks: "Whosoever these... and so on.

In that context, "in various ways" means even by means of such things as superstitious omens and auspicious rites. In that context, "living restrained" means dwelling protected from the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
49. Then, demonstrating the absence of purity in them in that manner, the Blessed One spoke the fourth verse.

50. Having thus heard that "they did not cross over," he now asked, "Whoever these may be," desiring to hear about those who have crossed over. Then the Blessed One spoke the sixth verse, showing those who have crossed over birth and old age by way of the one who has crossed over the flood (*oghatiṇṇa*).

51. In this context, *nivutā* means covered, enveloped, or shrouded. *Ye sīdha*: "ye" means "those who," and "sīdha" (here) means "in this [world]"; furthermore, "su-" is merely a particle. *Taṇhaṃ pariññāya*:
having fully understood craving through the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*). The remainder is clear everywhere because it follows the method already explained previously. 52.
Thus the Blessed One brought the teaching to its conclusion precisely at the peak of Arahantship; however, at the conclusion of the teaching, Nanda—
Rejoicing in the Blessed One’s speech, he uttered this verse: “I rejoice in these. And here too, as previously stated, there was a realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya).
[End of] the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Cūḷaniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Nandamāṇavasutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the Exposition of the *Hemakamāṇavasutta* 53.
Regarding the eighth discourse, the *Hemakamāṇavasutta*: "Those who previously explained to me"—referring to Bāvarī and others who formerly explained their own [doctrine] to me.
They explained their own tenets. "Prior to the teaching of Gotama" means before the time of Gotama’s dispensation.

"All that increases discursive thought" means all that increases sensual thoughts and so forth. "And those other teachers of his" refers to those other teachers who instructed Bāvari in conduct. They...
"One's own view" (*sakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ*) means their own teacher’s view. "One's own preference" (*sakaṃ khantiṃ*) means what they themselves find acceptable.

"One's own liking" (*sakaṃ ruciṃ*) means what they themselves find pleasing. "Increasing discursive thought" (*vitakkavaḍḍhanaṃ*) means the arising and the repeated occurrence of discursive thoughts such as sensual desire-thoughts (*kāmavitakka*).

"Increasing intention" (*saṅkappavaḍḍhanaṃ*) means the increase of intentions such as sensual-intention (*kāmasaṅkappa*). These two terms are used in a comprehensive sense that includes all [such factors].

These have been stated. Now, in order to show sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) and the others according to their specific nature, he presented the nine types of thoughts by way of the method beginning with "increasing sensual thought" (*kāmavitakkavaḍḍhana*).
54. "The destruction of craving" (*taṇhānigghātana*) means the eradication of craving.
55–6. Then the Blessed One, explaining that Dhamma to him, spoke these two verses beginning with “Herein.

Therein, “Those who, having known this, are mindful”—this refers to those who, by means of such methods as “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,” have gradually come to know Nibbāna, the deathless state;

and who are mindful through the foundations of mindfulness such as the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā-sati*). “Completely extinguished in this very life” (*diṭṭhadhammābhinibbutā*) is because they have realized the Dhamma.
They have seen the Dhamma and are completely quenched by the extinction of lust and the other defilements. The rest is clear throughout.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta also by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma just as before.
From the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Cūḷaniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Hemaka-māṇava-sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the exposition of the *Todeyya-māṇava-sutta*:
Regarding the ninth sutta, the *Todeyya-sutta*, [the question] "What kind of liberation is desired for him? asks what kind of liberation should be sought for him.
58. Now, showing that there is no other liberation for him, the Blessed One spoke the second verse. Therein, "there is no other liberation for him" means that for him, no other liberation exists. 59.
Thus, although it has been stated that "the destruction of craving itself is liberation," one who does not perceive this meaning asks again: "Is he without aspiration, or is he still aspiring?
Therein, "or is he one who fashions with wisdom" means: or rather, by means of knowledge such as the knowledge of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)?
He constructs either a conceptualization based on craving (*taṇhākappa*) or a conceptualization based on views (*diṭṭhikappa*). 60.
Then the Blessed One, explaining this to him, spoke the fourth verse. Therein, "in sensual pleasure and existence" (*kāmabhava*) means in both sensual pleasures and in existence.

"He does not long for form" (*rūpe nāsīsati*) means he does not aspire, by way of desire and lust, toward the object of form arising from the fourfold origination. [The same applies] to faith and the other qualities as well.
The same method applies here. Lust itself is the "clinging" (kiñcana) in the sense of being an impediment; thus it is "lust-clinging. Or, it is so called in the sense of intoxication.
The same method applies to "hatred-clinging" and the rest. The remainder is clear throughout.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating in Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma just as before.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Todeyya-māṇava-sutta* in the *Cūḷaniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*, titled *Saddhammappajjotikā*, is completed. 10.
Commentary on the exposition of the *Kappa-māṇava-sutta*.

61. In the exposition of the sutta on the tenth aeon—“in the midst of existence” (majjhe bhavassa) means that it is said to be in the midst of saṃsāra because of the absence of the knowledge of the prior and subsequent limits.

“While it stands” (tiṭṭhantaṃ) refers to those who are standing [in saṃsāra]. “So that there may be no further beyond this” (yathāyidaṃ nāparaṃ siyā) means so that this suffering may not come to be again.
"Coming" (*āgamana*) means coming here from the past. "Going" (*gamana*) means going from here to the other world. "Coming and going" (*gamanāgamana*) is stated by way of both of these.
"Time" (*kāla*) means the time of death. "Destination" (*gati*) means rebirth. "From existence to existence" (*bhavābhava*) means from one state of becoming to another.
"And passing away" (*cuti ca*) means the falling away from existence. "And rebirth" (*upapatti ca*) means the rebirth of one who has passed away. "And arising" (*nibbatti ca*)...
"Manifestation" (pātubhāvo) and "dissolution" (bhedo) refer to the dissolution of the aggregates (khandhabhedo). "Birth" (jāti) refers to the act of being born. "Aging" (jarā) refers to decay.
"Death" (maraṇaṃ) refers to the relinquishing of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). "The prior limit is not discerned" means that there is no prior limit, it does not exist;
likewise for the subsequent limit.
“Ettakā jātiyo” means “births limited to this much. “Vaṭṭaṃ vatti” means the turning of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). “Tato paraṃ na vattati” means it does not proceed beyond that.
“Hevaṃ natthi” means “it is not thus”; it does not exist or is not found in such a way. “Hi” is a particle.
“Anamataggo” means this saṃsāra has an unknown beginning.
"Enshrouded by ignorance" means covered by ignorance. "Bound by the fetter of craving" means bound by the bond of craving known as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).
"Running on" means running again and again within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Wandering about" means wandering through the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and arūpadhātu*).
"Experienced suffering" means experienced and felt as bodily and mental suffering. "Intense" means thick or abundant.

"Calamity" (*byasana*) means decline or destruction. "The cemetery has increased" (*kaṭasī vaḍḍhitā*) means the charnel ground has expanded. "It is indeed sufficient" (*alam eva*) means it is truly appropriate.

"In all conditioned phenomena" (*sabba-saṅkhāresu*) refers to the conditioned phenomena of the three planes of existence. "To become disenchanted" (*nibbidituṃ*) means to become weary of them. "To become dispassionate" (*virajjituṃ*) means to generate dispassion. "To be liberated" (*vimuccituṃ*) means to be released.
"The round will proceed" (*vaṭṭaṃ vattissati*) refers to the turning of the cycle of existence, the round of the three planes of becoming.
"It will proceed in the future; beyond that, it will not proceed" means that from that point onward, the proceeding of *saṃsāra* in the future will not take place.
"Fear of birth" (*jātibhaya*) refers to the fear arising dependent upon birth. The same method applies to the fear of aging (*jarābhaya*) and so forth. 62–3.
Then the Blessed One, explaining that matter to him, spoke the subsequent verses. The meaning of the second verse has already been stated.
In the third verse, *akiñcanaṃ* means the opposite of *kiñcana*. *Anādānaṃ* means the opposite of *ādāna*;
thus, it is said to be the subsiding of both *kiñcana* and *ādāna*. *Anāparaṃ* means devoid of another counterpart or island; thus, it is said to be supreme (*seṭṭha*).
In the fourth verse, *na te mārassa paddhagū* means that they are not followers, attendants, or disciples who walk in the tracks of Māra.

He is called Māra because he binds and causes the death of great multitudes of people. He is Kaṇha (the Black One) because he is intent upon unwholesome deeds. He is Adhipati (the Lord) because he exercises sovereignty over the six celestial worlds.
He is Antagū (the Goer-to-the-End) because he has reached the end of unwholesome states. He is Namuci because he does not release sinful people.
He is Pamattabandhu (the Kinsman of the Negligent) because he is a relative to those individuals who are heedless due to the loss of mindfulness. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating specifically in Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma just as before.
The commentary on the exposition of the Kappamāṇava Sutta in the *Saddhammappajjotikā*,
the sub-commentary to the *Cūḷaniddesa*, is finished.
11. Commentary on the Exposition of the Jatukaṇṇi Māṇava Sutta 65.

Regarding the eleventh, the Jatukaṇṇi Sutta: “Having heard, O Hero, that I am one who does not desire sensual pleasures”—O Hero, having heard of the Buddha as one who does not desire sensual pleasures because he has no longing for them, according to the method beginning with “Thus indeed is the Blessed One,” and so forth; [I have come] to the Blessed One, who is free from desire and devoid of longing.
"I have come to ask. 'Sahajanetta' means the eye of co-arisen omniscient wisdom (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
'Yathātathaṃ' means according to reality. 'Brūhi me'—speaking thus, he entreats again. For one who entreats might speak even a thousand times, let alone twice.
The meaning of these phrases, 'Itipi so Bhagavā, Arahā, Sammāsambuddho,' has already been explained above. By means of the *vijjās*..."

Furthermore, because he is endowed with both clear knowledge (*vijjā*) and conduct (*caraṇa*), he is "one perfected in clear knowledge and conduct. In this context, "clear knowledge" refers to either the three clear knowledges or the eight clear knowledges.
The three clear knowledges are to be understood according to the method explained in the *Bhayabherava Sutta*, while the eight are [explained] in the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta*.

For there, having included the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) together with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and mind-made psychic power (*manomaya-iddhi*), they constitute the eight clear knowledges.

It has been stated. "Conduct" (*caraṇa*) should be understood as these fifteen factors: the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven true qualities (*saddhamma*), and the four fine-material-sphere jhānas.
Indeed, because by means of these fifteen factors the noble disciple conducts himself and proceeds toward the deathless state, they are therefore called "conduct."
It has been said. As it was stated: “Here, Mahānāma, the noble disciple is virtuous”—all this should be understood according to the method explained in the *Majjhima Paṇṇāsaka*.
The Blessed One is endowed with these true knowledges (*vijjā*) and with this conduct (*caraṇa*);
therefore, he is called "one perfected in true knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampanna*). In that regard, the Blessed One’s perfection of true knowledge fulfills omniscience.
He is established in the perfection of conduct, which consists in great compassion.

Having understood, through omniscience, what is beneficial and what is harmful for all beings, he avoids the harmful and directs them toward the beneficial by virtue of his great compassion, just as one endowed with true knowledge and conduct does.
Consequently, his disciples are well-practiced and not ill-practiced; for the disciples of those deficient in true knowledge and conduct—such as the "self-mortifiers" and others—are not so.

He is the Sugata because his going is beautiful (*sobhanagamanattā*), because he has gone to a beautiful place (*sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā*), because he has gone rightly (*sammā gatattā*), and because he has spoken rightly (*sammā ca gadattā*).
For "going" (*gamana*) is indeed called "gone" (*gata*). And that going of the Blessed One is beautiful, purified, and blameless.
But what is that? It is the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). For by means of that going, he has gone to the secure direction without being attached; thus, because his going is beautiful, he is the Sugata.
He has gone to the beautiful place, the deathless Nibbāna; thus, because he has gone to a beautiful place, he is the Sugata.
Furthermore, he has gone rightly, not returning again to the defilements abandoned by each respective path. For this has been said:
"Those defilements abandoned by the stream-entry path—he does not bring them back, does not go back to them, does not return to those defilements."

The Sugata... [as before] ...is called the Sugata because by means of the path of arahantship he does not bring back, does not return to, and does not go back to those defilements that have been abandoned.

Or else, he has gone rightly (sammā vā gato) from the foot of Dīpaṅkara onwards up to the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) through the right practice that fulfills the thirty perfections (pāramīs), bringing about only the welfare and happiness of the entire world, while avoiding eternalism (sassata), annihilationism (uccheda), and sensual pleasure (kāmasukha).
Not approaching these two extremes—the pursuit of self-mortification and the pursuit of sensual pleasure—he has "gone" (gata); thus, because he has gone rightly, he is the Sugata.
Furthermore, he speaks rightly; in appropriate circumstances, he utters only fitting speech; thus, because he speaks rightly, he is the Sugata.
On this point, there is this supporting sutta:
“Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and which is disagreeable and unpleasant to others—
that speech the Tathāgata does not utter. And whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true and correct,
yet unbeneficial, and which is disagreeable and unpleasant to others— that speech too the Tathāgata does not utter.”
And as for that speech which the Tathāgata knows to be true, real, and beneficial, yet which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others—
the Tathāgata knows the proper time for the explanation of such speech. And as for that speech which the Tathāgata knows to be untrue,
unreal, and unbeneficial, yet which is pleasant and agreeable to others— the Tathāgata does not [utter] that.
He utters speech. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true, real, and unbeneficial, even if it is pleasing and agreeable to others—that speech the Tathāgata does not utter.
But whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true, real, and beneficial, and which is pleasing and agreeable to others—in that case, the Tathāgata knows the proper time [to speak].
“...there is a resolution of that speech.
Thus, he should be understood as "Well-Gone" (*sugata*) because he has spoken rightly.

Furthermore, he is the "Knower of the World" (*lokavidū*) because he has known the world in every respect. For the Blessed One knew, understood, and penetrated the world in its entirety—by way of its intrinsic nature, its origin, its cessation, and the means to its cessation. As it is said:
“Where, friends, one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear—there I say that the end of the world cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling.
Yet, friends, I do not say that the ending of suffering is to be achieved without reaching the end of the world. Rather, friends, right here in this very world...”
“In this very body, a fathom in height, endowed with perception and mind, I proclaim the world, the origin of the world,
the cessation of the world, and the way leading to the cessation of the world.
‘The end of the world can never be reached by traveling.’”
"And there is no release from suffering without reaching the end of the world.
Therefore, the wise one who knows the world, having reached the end of the world and lived the holy life,
having understood the end of the world as one who has stilled himself, shall desire neither this world nor the next."
Furthermore, there are three worlds: the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), the world of beings (*sattaloka*), and the world of space (*okāsaloka*). Among these, in the passage, “One world:
all beings subsist by nutriment,” the world of formations is to be understood. In the passage, “Is the world eternal, or is the world not eternal? the world of beings is to be understood.

“As far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating the quarters with their radiance—so vast is the world-system of a thousand worlds wherein your power prevails. In this passage, the “world of space” is mentioned.
The Blessed One knew that as well in every respect. For instance, he said: “The world is one... [and so forth].
Beings subsist by nutriment. Two worlds are name and form. Three worlds are the three feelings. Four worlds are the four nutriments.
Five worlds are the five aggregates of clinging. Six worlds are the six internal sense bases.
Seven worlds are the seven stations of consciousness. Eight worlds are the eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds are the nine abodes of beings.
"Ten worlds, ten bases; twelve worlds, twelve bases; eighteen worlds, eighteen elements"—thus this world of formations is known in every way.
Furthermore, because he knows the disposition of all beings, he knows their underlying tendencies, and he knows their conduct.

He knows their inclinations; he knows beings who have little dust in their eyes and those who have much dust in their eyes, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those of good disposition and those of bad disposition, those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct, and those who are capable and those who are incapable.
Therefore, the world of beings is known to him in every respect. And as the world of beings is known, so too is the world of space. For instance, he [knows] a single world-system in its extent...
In width, it is one hundred and twelve thousand, three hundred and fifty yojanas. In circumference:
"Entirely round about, it is one hundred and thirty-six thousand, And ten thousand, and four hundred and fifty."
Therein—
two hundred thousand and forty nahutas;
so much, by its thickness, is this earth reckoned.
Its very support is as follows:
Four hundred thousand and eighty million—
so much in thickness is the water established upon the wind.
Its supporter as well—
nine hundred thousand and sixty thousand leagues— is the extent of the world's foundation, rising up into the sky by means of the wind.
And when it is established in this way, the measurement in yojanas is as follows:
Sineru, the supreme mountain, plunges eighty-four thousand [yojanas] down into the great ocean and rises up by exactly that same amount.
Then, in successive order, measuring half and half again,
there are divine peaks submerged and emerging, variegated with various jewels:
Yugandhara, Īsadharo, Karavīko, and Sudassano.
Nemindhara, Vinataka, Assakaṇṇa, and the vast mountain Brahā—
these are the seven great mountains surrounding Sineru;
they are the abodes of the Great Kings, frequented by devas and yakkhas.
The Himavat mountain is five hundred yojanas high;
it is three thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks.
The city called Nagavhayā has a circumference of five or six yojanas.
Its trunks and branches extend fifty yojanas on all sides;
it is one hundred yojanas wide and rises to that same height.
Jambu, by whose power Jambudīpa is illuminated;
and whatever is the measurement of this Jambu tree, that same is the measurement of the Cittapāṭali of the Asuras,
the Simbali tree of the Garuḍas, the Kadamba tree in Aparagoyāna, the Kappa tree in Uttarakuru, the Sirīsa tree in Pubbavideha, and [the Pārijāta] among the Tāvatiṃsas.
"Of the Pāricchattaka tree. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"The Pāṭalī, the Simbalī, the Jambū, the Pāricchattaka of the gods, the Kadamba, the Kappa-tree, and the Sirīsa is the seventh."
“Eighty-two thousand [yojanas] it plunges down into the great ocean;
It rises up just as high above;
The mountain range of the Cakkavāḷa stands encircling this entire world-system.”
Therein, the moon’s disk is forty-nine yojanas; the sun’s disk is fifty yojanas;
the realm of the Thirty-three is ten thousand yojanas, as are the realm of the Asuras, the great Avīci hell, and Jambudīpa.
Aparagoyāna is seven thousand yojanas; likewise Pubbavideha. Uttarakuru is eight thousand yojanas. And each of these—
The great island is surrounded by five hundred and five hundred minor islands. All of that together constitutes one world-sphere (*cakkavāḷa*), a single world-system (*lokadhātu*).

Between these are the Lokantara hells. Thus, with infinite Buddha-knowledge, the Blessed One knew, understood, and penetrated infinite world-spheres and infinite world-systems. In this way, his knowledge of the world of space was complete in every respect.
He has known [the world]. Thus, because he has known the world in every respect, he is the "Knower of the World" (*lokavidū*).
Furthermore, because there is no one superior to him in his own qualities, he is "without superior" (*anuttara*).

For in this way, he surpasses the entire world through the quality of virtue (*sīla*), and likewise through the qualities of concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*paññā*), liberation (*vimutti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*).
He is unequaled even in the quality of virtue, equal to the unequaled, peerless, matchless, and without rival... [and so on] ...even in the quality of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
As it is said in detail: "Indeed, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas... including gods and humans, who is more perfect in virtue than myself.
In this way, the *Aggapasāda-sutta* and other such texts, as well as the verses beginning with "I have no teacher," should be cited in detail.
"He trains those who are to be tamed by men" means he is a "charioteer of men to be tamed"; that is to say, he tames and disciplines them.
In this context, "men to be tamed" refers to untamed beings fit to be tamed, including animal-men, human-men, and non-human-men.
For instance, even among animal-men, the Blessed One tamed such as the Naga kings Apalāla, Cūḷodara, Mahodara, Aggisikha, and Dhūmasikha.
The Naga king Aravāḷa, the elephant Dhanapālaka, and others such as these were tamed and rendered free from venom;
they were established in the refuges and in the precepts. Among human beings, there were Saccaka the son of the Nigaṇṭhas, the young Brahmin Ambaṭṭha, Pokkharasāti, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, and others.
Among non-human beings, there were Āḷavaka, Sūciloma, Kharaloma, the Yakkhas, Sakka the King of the Devas, and others—all of whom were tamed and disciplined by various means.

"By means of disciplinary methods. "Kesi, I indeed discipline those to be tamed by men both gently, and I discipline them harshly, and I discipline them both gently and harshly"—this sutta should be cited here in detail.

Furthermore, the Blessed One, while explaining the first jhāna and so forth to those of purified virtue, and the higher path-practice to stream-enterers and others, disciplines even those who are already disciplined.
Alternatively, "the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed" is this single phrase of meaning.
For the Blessed One guides those men to be tamed in such a way that, while sitting in a single cross-legged posture, they run toward the eight directions without obstruction.
Therefore, he is called "the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed. "Monks, when an elephant to be tamed is guided by an elephant-tamer, it [runs] in only one direction..."
"...runs in all directions"—this sutta should be cited here in detail.

"Vīriyavā" means one who has desisted from all evils by means of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). "Pahū" means powerful. "Visavī" means one who arouses energy in the mental continuums of others. "Alamatto" means one whose mind is capable.
"Virato" means one who, through desisting by means of the Noble Path, will not undergo rebirth in the future. From all evils comes the suffering of hell.

"Having transcended" (*aticca*) means having transcended the suffering of hell by way of the non-relinking of future existence. "Abode of energy" (*vīriyāvāso*) means a dwelling place of energy. "He is energetic" (*so vīriyavā*):

he who has destroyed the outflows (*khīṇāsava*) is worthy of being called "energetic. Furthermore, these are words of praise for him: "He is one possessed of striving, a hero, such-like" (*padhānavā vīro tādī*).

For he is "possessed of striving" by virtue of the striving of the path and meditative absorption (*jhāna*); he is a "hero" because of his capacity to destroy the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*).
One such as that is called "thusness" (*tathattā*) because of being free from agitation; such a one is called "possessing energy.

"Those who desire their own desires" means those who long for the objects of desire, such as forms and so forth. "Passionate with passion" means colored by passion. "Perceiving with perception" means possessing the perception of passion.
"He does not desire desires" means he does not yearn for the objects of desire, such as forms and so forth. "Free from desire" means [free] from desires.
"Devoid of": "Free from desire" means one whose desire has been expelled.
"Omniscient knowledge" (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*): he is "all-knowing" (*sabbaññū*) because he knows the entire range of objects of knowledge throughout the three times;
the state of being all-knowing is "omniscience" (*sabbaññutā*), and that very omniscience is the "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*). It is the guide known as omniscient knowledge.
Having utterly defeated the defilements along with their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), he possesses the state of a Victor (*jinabhāva*) because of his victory;
and since this arose at one moment, at one time—without before or after, without prior or subsequent—it is "arisen" (*uppanna*), meaning it has descended from the past.

66. *Tejī tejasā*: "Possessing splendor by means of splendor," having overcome [all things] by means of splendor. *Yamahaṃ vijaññaṃ jātijarāya idha vippahānaṃ*: "That which I might know here as the abandoning of birth and aging"—that is, that Dhamma which constitutes the abandonment of birth and aging, may I know it right here.
“Jagatī” means the earth. “All that has gone into space” means everything spread out and occurring within space.
“Gone into darkness” means darkness itself; it is “gone into darkness” just as one says “gone into excrement” or “gone into urine. “Having struck down” means having destroyed.
“Having dispelled the darkness” means having driven away the darkness that obstructs the arising of visual consciousness. “Light...”
"Having shown" means having shown the light of the sun. "In the sky" means in the cloudless sky. "In the atmosphere" means in the empty space capable of containing the intermediate elements.
"On the path of the firmament" means he goes along the path of travel for the deities.

"The entire origin of volitional formations" means the whole of karma, which is the origin or arising; the meaning is that it is craving (*taṇhā*). "Having dispelled the darkness of defilements, the gloom of ignorance."
Having extracted and destroyed the darkness of ignorance, which is known as the gloom of defilements; having displayed the light of knowledge, the light of wisdom;
having fully understood sense-desires for objects—that is, having known the sense-desires for objects such as forms and so forth through the full understanding of knowing and scrutinizing;
and having abandoned sense-desires for defilements—that is, having relinquished the sense-desires for defilements characterized by burning through the full understanding of abandoning.
67. Then the Blessed One, explaining that Dhamma to him, spoke these successive verses.
Therein, "having seen renunciation as security" means having seen both Nibbāna and the path leading to Nibbāna as "security.
"Grasped" means grasped by way of craving and by way of views. "Or rejected" means it should be cast off, or rather, it should be relinquished.
"Let it not exist for you" means let it not be yours. "Possession" (*kiñcana*) refers to the possession of greed and so forth; let that also not exist for you.
"To be released from" means having released it, one should not take it up again. "To be abandoned" means to be cast off. "To be dispelled" means to be thrown out.
"To be brought to an end" means to be made to reach its limit of disappearance. "To be led to non-existence" means to be led step by step (*anu anu*) toward non-being.
68–9. "Past" refers to the defilements that have arisen with reference to past formations. "Brahmin," the Blessed One addresses Jaṭukaṇṇī. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta as well by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma exactly as before.
[End of] the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Cūḷaniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Jatukaṇṇi-māṇava-sutta* is finished.
12. Commentary on the Exposition of the *Bhadrāvudha-māṇava-sutta*:

70. In the twelfth discourse, the *Bhadrāvudha-sutta*: "Those who have abandoned the home" means those who have abandoned attachment (*ālaya*). "Those who have cut off craving" means those who have cut off the body of craving (*taṇhākāya*).
Unwavering amidst the worldly conditions, they abandon delight—that is, they abandon the longing for future forms and so forth. For craving is indeed one alone;
it is spoken of here in various ways by way of praise. They abandon conceptual construction—that is, they abandon the two kinds of conceptual construction.
"I entreat" means I beseech most fervently. Having heard [the teaching], they will turn away from this, O Nāga, from you, the Blessed One.
The intention [behind] the statement "having heard these words, many people will depart from this Pāsāṇaka Cetiya" is as follows:

"Those who have approached and grasped" means those who have approached and seized [them] by means of craving and views. "Mental fixations" means established in the mind. "Adherence and underlying tendencies" means having become established and having come to lie dormant.
71. "Assembled from various countries" means gathered here from countries such as Aṅga and others. "Explain" means teach the Dhamma.

“Saṅgatā” means these kṣatriyas and others have come together as one. “Samāgatā” means they have arrived from the aforementioned regions. “Samohitā” means they have formed a mass. “Sannipatitā” means they have assembled for the purpose of study. 72.
Then, teaching the Dhamma in accordance with his disposition, the Blessed One spoke the following successive verses.
Therein, “ādānataṇhā” means the craving for grasping, the craving that seizes upon form and so forth; it is what is called “craving as clinging. For whatever—
"In the world they cling" means that among these various types of clinging, such as grasping at form and so forth, they grasp whatever it may be.
"Therefore Māra follows the person" means that by way of the production of kamma-formations conditioned by that very clinging, the Māra of the rebirth-aggregates follows after that being.
73. Therefore they understand; therefore, one who understands these conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) by way of their impermanence and so forth understands this danger.

"Beholding beings attached to grasping" means: beholding this generation (*pajā*) clinging within the realm of death (*maccudheyya*) amidst the objects of grasping—form and so forth—in the sense that they are to be grasped;
or, beholding this generation stuck within the realm of death among all the world’s beings who are attached to grasping, or who are obsessed with grasping.

"Beholding this generation caught in the realm of death due to the cause of grasping and attachment, and being unable to transcend it, one should not take up anything whatsoever in the entire world. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating in Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma just as before.
The commentary on the exposition of the Bhadrāvudha Sutta within the *Cūḷaniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*, entitled *Saddhammappajjotikā*, is completed. 13.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Udaya Māṇava Sutta.

74. In the thirteenth discourse, the *Udayasutta*: "The liberation through final knowledge" (*aññāvimokkha*) refers to the meditation characterized by the power of wisdom; he asks about that liberation.

"One who meditates with the first jhāna" means one who meditates with the five-factored first jhāna associated with applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*). "With the second" means associated with rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind. "With the third" means...
"With pleasure and one-pointedness of mind. "With the fourth" means with that which is associated with equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.

"A meditator by means of jhāna accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought" means that, according to both the fourfold and fivefold systems, he is a meditator because he meditates by means of the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought.
"Without applied thought and with sustained thought only" refers to the second jhāna in the fivefold system. "Without applied thought and without sustained thought" refers to...
By the remaining jhānas, beginning with the second and third. "With rapture" means by the threefold jhāna associated with rapture.
"Without rapture" means by the remaining jhāna devoid of rapture. "Accompanied by pleasure" means by the threefold or fourfold jhāna accompanied by bliss.
"Accompanied by equanimity" means by the fourfold or fivefold [jhāna]. "Also as empty" means by that which is associated with the emptiness liberation.
"By the signless as well": one is a meditator (jhāyī) because one meditates with the signless jhāna obtained by removing the sign of impermanence, the sign of permanence, and the signless itself.

"By the desireless as well": this refers both to having purified and exhausted desire through the process of the path, and to the desireless state attained through the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti).
"By the mundane as well": this refers to the mundane first, second, third, and fourth jhānas.
"By the supramundane as well" means by that very [state] associated with the supramundane. "Delighting in jhāna" means being devoted to the jhānas.

"Devoted to solitude" means devoted to and intent upon solitude, which is the state of being alone (*ekībhāva*). "Valuing his own welfare" means valuing his own goal; here, the letter *ka* has been changed to *da*.
And "his own welfare" should be understood as Arahantship, for that is the self (*attā*) in the sense of being bound up with oneself.
It is called "one's own welfare" (*sakattha*) because it is one's own welfare in the sense of not abandoning [it] and in the sense of being one's own ultimate goal (*paramattha*).
By way of entering the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), one is "devoted to one's own welfare"; some say "devoted to Nibbāna. "Dustless" (*araja*) means free from defilements (*nikkilesa*).

"Stainless" (*viraja*) means with defilements removed. "Spotless" (*niraja*) means with defilements cast out; there is also the reading "free from dust" (*vitaraja*), which has the same meaning. "Devoid of dust" (*rajāpagata*) means having become distant from defilements.
“Abandoned of passion” means one who has abandoned the defilements (*kilesa*). “Dissociated from passion” means one who is freed from the defilements.

“At the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya” means at the site where the *Pārāyana Sutta* was taught on a stone surface. “Because all feverish agitation has been stilled” means because all the feverish agitations of the defilements have been calmed; he is seated because they have been destroyed.

“What is to be done and what is not to be done” refers to that which should be reflected upon by the mind thus: “This is to be done; this is not to be done. “What is to be performed and what is not to be performed” [is the same].
"By way of the body, this must necessarily be done and that must not be done"—thus [he knows] what is to be done and what is not to be done.
"Abandoned" means relinquished. "Attained to mastery" means having reached a state of proficiency. 75.
Then, because Udaya was an attainer of the fourth jhāna, the Blessed One, by way of the jhāna he had obtained, [addressed him as follows].
Showing the liberation through higher knowledge (*aññāvimokkha*) in its various aspects, he spoke the successive verses. Therein, regarding the phrase "the abandoning of sensual desire":
that which is the abandoning of sensual desire for one producing the first *jhāna*, that too I call "liberation through higher knowledge.
In this manner, all the phrases are to be applied.
"Unsoundness of mind" (*cittassa akalyatā*) is the state of illness of the mind; for one who is ill is called "unsound.
It is also said in the *Vinaya*: "Venerable sir, I am not sound. "Unwieldiness" (*akammaññatā*) is simply the mode of unwieldiness consisting of the sickness of the mind.
"Slackness" (*olīyanā*) is the mode of slackness; for the postural consciousness, being unable to sustain its posture, [clings] to a tree...
It clings like a bat or like a vessel of treacle stuck to a post; with reference to that mode of being, it is called "clinging" (*olīyanā*).
The second term is augmented by means of a prefix. "Stiffened" (*līnā*) means contracted due to a lack of expansion.
The other two are descriptions of its modes of manifestation. "Sloth" (*thinam*) is, like a lump of ghee, a state of non-expansion.

It stands in a state of density. *Thiya* is a designation for a mode; the state of being settled (*thiyitabhāva*) or the quality of being settled (*thiyitatta*), meaning stiffness by way of non-expansion.
76. *Upekkhāsatisaṃsuddhaṃ*: purified by the equanimity and mindfulness of the fourth jhāna. *Dhammatakkapurejavaṃ*:
by this [phrase], one refers to the liberation of Arahantship attained after standing in that liberation of the fourth jhāna and having practiced insight into the factors of that jhāna.
He says: For the preliminary impulse (*purejava*) for the liberation of arahantship consists of the investigation of phenomena (*dhammatakkā*), such as right intention associated with the path.
Therefore he said, "preceded by the investigation of phenomena. Regarding the phrase "the breaking up of ignorance":

we speak of this very liberation through final knowledge as "the breaking up of ignorance" by way of metaphorical designation (*kāraṇopacāra*), because it arises in dependence upon Nibbāna, which is known as the breaking up of ignorance.
Regarding the term *upekkhā* in the fourth jhāna: here, it is called *upekkhā* because it looks on (*ikkhati*) from a state of equanimity;
the meaning is that it sees evenly, seeing without falling into partiality. *Upekkhanā* is a description of its mode of activity.
*Ajjhupekkhanā* is the same word expanded by means of a prefix. *Cittasamatā* is the one-pointedness of mind. *Cittappassaddhatā* is the state of the mind being free from deficiency or excess.
“Equanimity” (*majjhattatā*) means the state of the mind abiding in the middle.
Having heard that Nibbāna was thus described by the statement on the classification of ignorance, he asks, “By the relinquishing of what is it called?

and recites the verse beginning with “What is its fetter? (*kiṃsu saṃyojano*). Therein, “What is its fetter? (*kiṃsu saṃyojano*) means “by what fetter does it have a fetter? (*kiṃsaṃyojano*). [The word] *vicāraṇaṃ* means investigation.
“Vicāraṇakāraṇaṃ”: *Kissassa vippahānenā* means by the complete abandoning of what—of which dhamma? 78.

Then the Blessed One, explaining that matter, spoke the verse beginning with “*Nandisaṃyojano*. Therein, *vitakkassa* refers to discursive thought such as sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth.
79. Now, asking for the path to that Nibbāna, he spoke the verse beginning with “*Kathaṃ satassā*. Therein, *viññāṇaṃ* refers to volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*).

Then, while explaining the path to him, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "Ajjhattañca" (Internally...). Therein, "evam satassa" means of one who is thus mindful and clearly comprehending. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta also by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma just as before.
[From] the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Cūḷaniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Udaya-māṇava-sutta* is finished.
14. Commentary on the Exposition of the *Posāla-māṇava-sutta*: 81.

Regarding the fourteenth sutta, the *Posāla-māṇava-sutta*: “He who points out the past” refers to the Blessed One, who points out for himself and for others the past, categorized as “even one birth,” and so forth.

"Even a single birth" (*ekampi jātiṃ*) refers to a continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) comprised within a single existence (*ekabhava*), beginning from the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and ending at the point of death (*cuti*).
This same method applies to "two births" (*dvepi jātiyo*) and so forth. However, regarding "many eons of dissolution" (*anekapi saṃvaṭṭakappe*) and so on:

an eon that is contracting is a "eon of dissolution" (*saṃvaṭṭakappa*), because at that time all beings gather together in the Brahma-world. An eon that is expanding is an "eon of evolution" (*vivaṭṭakappa*).

This is because at that time beings are expanding from the Brahma-world. Therein, by means of the contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa*), the period of subsistence after contraction is included, since it is rooted in that;
and by means of the expansion (*vivaṭṭa*), the period of subsistence after expansion is included. For it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these four incalculable periods of an eon (*kappa*). Which four?
The period of contraction, the period of subsistence after contraction, the period of expansion, and the period of subsistence after expansion."

These [terms] have been stated; they are thus determined. Regarding the phrases "during a period of dissolution" (*saṃvaṭṭakappe*) and "during a period of evolution" (*vivaṭṭakappe*), these are stated by taking half of a *kappa*.
Regarding the phrase "during a period of dissolution and evolution" (*saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe*), this is stated by taking the entire *kappa*.
If one asks, "How does he recollect? it is by way of the method beginning with, "I was there... (*amutrāsiṃ*). In that context, "I was there" means: in such-and-such a period of dissolution, I...
"In such a state of existence, or in such a womb, or in such a destiny, or in such a station of consciousness, or in such an abode of beings, or in such a class of beings, I existed.
"Of such a name" means Tissa or Phussa. "Of such a clan" means Kaccāna or Kassapa. This is stated by way of his recollection of his own name and clan in a past existence.
However, if at that time he [recalls] the excellence of his own complexion...
Or, if one wishes to recollect whether their mode of life was coarse or refined, whether it was full of pleasure or pain, or whether they were short-lived or long-lived, that too they recollect.
Therefore it is said: "Of such a complexion, with such a limit to their lifespan.
In this context, "of such a complexion" means either white or dark. "Of such food" means having rice and meat as food, or subsisting on wild fruits.
Or: "Thus experiencing pleasure and pain" means experiencing in many ways physical and mental pleasures and pains, distinguished as worldly (*sāmisa*) or unworldly (*nirāmisa*), and so forth.
"Thus having such a limit to his lifespan" means having a limit to his lifespan of at most one hundred years, or a limit to his lifespan of at most eighty-four thousand eons.

"Having passed away from there, I arose elsewhere": this means that having passed away from that particular existence, womb, destiny, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or class of beings, I was born again in such-and-such an existence, womb, destiny, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or class of beings.
"And there too... means: and then, in that existence, womb, or destiny...
"I existed again in a station of consciousness, an abode of beings, or a class of beings. The method for "having such a name," and so forth, is exactly as previously stated.
Furthermore, "I was there" refers to the recollection of one ascending step by step as far as desired;
"passing away from there" is the reviewing of one returning [from that point]. Therefore, "reborn here" refers to this present rebirth.
It should be understood that the statement "it arose there" refers specifically to his place of rebirth immediately following [the previous life].
However, the passage beginning with "there I was" is stated for the purpose of showing the recollection of his name, clan, and so forth, regarding the place of rebirth within this current existence.
The phrase "having passed away from there, I have arisen here" means: having passed away from that immediately preceding place of rebirth, I am now born here.
"Having passed away from there, he was reborn here in such-and-such a clan of kṣatriyas or a clan of brahmins.
Thus it is. "With its aspects and its particulars" means: with its particulars by way of name and clan, and with its aspects by way of complexion and so forth.
For a being is designated by name and clan as "Tissa Kassapa," while by way of complexion and so forth, they are distinguished from one another as "fair-skinned" or "dark-complexioned."
It is discerned. Therefore, name and clan are the "enumeration" (uddesa), while the others are the "modes" (ākāra). Regarding "past lives" (pubbenivāsa):

the aggregates (khandha) that have dwelt in previous, past births are "past lives. They are called "dwelt" (nivuṭṭha) because they were inhabited, experienced, having arisen and ceased within one's own continuum;
or alternatively, "dwelt" refers to the phenomena (dhamma) that have dwelt. They are "dwelt" by way of dwelling as their objective field (gocara), [perceived] by one's own consciousness.
"Known" means delimited; or alternatively, it is known by another's consciousness in cases such as the recollection of past existences (*chinnavaṭumaka-anussati*) and so forth.
These [powers] are found only in Buddhas. He "indicates" or "declares" that former existence (*pubbenivāsa*).
He "indicates" the past of others—that is, the former existences of other persons—in the manner beginning with "even a single birth," and so forth.
The *Mahāpadāniya-suttanta* is the *Mahāpadāna-sutta*, which is connected with the legends (*apadāna*) of the Great Beings.
The *Mahāsudassaniya-suttanta* is the *Mahāsudassana-sutta*, which is connected with the excellences of Mahāsudassana.

The *Mahāgovindiya-suttanta* is the *Mahāgovinda-sutta*, which is connected with the legend of the brahmin Mahāgovinda. The *Māghadeviya-suttanta* is [the discourse] connected with the legend of King Māghadeva.
The Maghadeva Sutta. "Knowledge that follows after the hundred" means knowledge associated with the recollection of past lives.
"As much as he wishes" means that he sends forth his knowledge with the thought, "I shall know as much as I desire to know.
Then his knowledge proceeds unimpeded and unobstructed, like a ball thrown into a hollow leaf-basket.
Therefore, he recollects as much as he desires. "Born at the foot of the Bodhi tree" means born at the root of the Bodhi tree.
"Knowledge arises" means the knowledge of the four paths arises. "This is the final birth": because the root of birth has been abandoned by that knowledge, another knowledge arises:
"This is the final birth; now there is no further becoming. "Knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties" (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa).
Here, having brought forward the word "of beings" (*sattānaṃ*) from above, it should be construed right here as:

"the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings" (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇaṃ*). Regarding the term *paropariyaṃ*: although one should say *parāparāni* (meaning "the further and the nearer"), by means of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), the letter *r* is inserted and it is called *paroparāni*.
The state of being *paropara* is *paropariyaṃ*; *paropariyaṃ* itself is *paropariyattaṃ*.

*Indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa* means the knowledge of the relative superiority and inferiority (*paropariyatta*) of the five faculties, such as faith and the rest, in those beings who are capable of being trained (*veneyya-sattā*).
It is the knowledge of the relative superiority and inferiority of the faculties; the meaning is the knowledge of the state of the faculties being superior or non-superior.
There is also a reading, *indriyavarovariyatta-ñāṇa*; here, "superior" (*vara*) and "inferior" (*avara*) together are called *varovariya*.
The state of being "higher and higher" (varovariya) should be understood as *varovariyatā*. Furthermore, *avariyāni* means "supreme" (*uttamāni*).
Alternatively, *parāni* and *oparāni* together form *paroparāni*; the state of these is *paropariyatā*, which should be so construed.
Here, *oparāni* is said to mean *orāni*, that is, "inferior," as in such passages as "having fully understood the phenomena of the high and the low" (*paroparāyassa samecca dhammā*).
...as it were. There is also a reading using a locative expression: “knowledge of the high and low degrees of the faculties” (*indriyaparopariyatte ñāṇaṃ*). “Of the Tathāgata”:
he who has come (āgata) in the same manner as the ancient seers such as Vipassī and others came;
and he who has gone (gata) in the same manner as they went. “The power of the Tathāgata” is the power belonging exclusively to the Tathāgata, not shared by others. Just as...
Or, it means the power that has come down through the accumulation of merit from previous Buddhas; thus, "power come down in such a manner" is the meaning.
In this regard, the Tathāgata’s power is twofold: bodily power and knowledge-power. Among these, the bodily power is to be understood according to the lineage of elephants.
For this was said by the ancients:
“Kāḷāvaka, Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tambapiṅgala, Gandha,
Maṅgala, Hema, Uposatha, and Chaddanta— these are the ten.
This refers to a thousand million elephants according to the count of ordinary elephants, or ten thousand million men according to the count of men.
There is physical strength; this, first of all, is the bodily power of the Tathāgata.

As for the power of knowledge, it consists of the knowledge of the ten powers as it appears in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence, the unshakable knowledge regarding the eight assemblies, the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth, and the knowledge that delimits the five destinations.
Furthermore, there are the seventy-three knowledges mentioned in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, making seventy-seven knowledges in total.
In this way, there are many thousands of other kinds of knowledge; this is called the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*).
Here too, it is specifically the power of knowledge that is intended, for knowledge is called "power" in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of providing support.

Regarding the phrase "knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies of beings": here, beings are so called because they are attached (*visatta*) to the aggregates, such as form and the rest, through desire and lust. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Rādha, it is because one is attached and clinging to whatever desire, lust, delight, and craving there is for form that one is called ‘a being.

It is because one is attached and clinging to whatever desire, lust, delight, and craving there is for feeling… for perception… for volitional formations… for consciousness that one is called ‘a being.’”
However, the grammarians, without investigating the meaning, maintain that "this is a mere name.
Even those who do investigate the meaning maintain that it is "a being" (satta) by virtue of its connection with existence (satva). For them, "abode" (āsaya) means that wherein beings dwell or rely;
this refers to the mental continuum of a being, which has been permeated by either wrong view or right view, or by sensual desire and so forth, or by renunciation and so forth.
It is a designation (*adhivacana*). They are called underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) because they lie latent (*anusenti*) and continue to flow along within the continuum of a being;

this is a designation for lust for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāga*) and so forth when they have become firmly rooted. "Latent disposition" (*āsaya-anusaya*) is a compound consisting of both "disposition" (*āsaya*) and "underlying tendency" (*anusaya*).

It should be understood as a singular form by virtue of the inclusion of the genus (*jāti*) and the nature of a copulative compound (*dvanda-samāsa*). Since the temperaments (*carita*) and inclinations (*adhimutti*) are included within latent dispositions, therefore, in the summary [list]...

The knowledges regarding conduct and inclinations are subsumed under the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*) alone; thus it is called "the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies.

Regarding "the knowledge of the Twin Miracle": herein, because the masses of fire, streams of water, and so forth, occur simultaneously and all at once without priority or sequence, it is "twin" (*yamaka*);
and because it carries away (*haraṇa*) the opposing states such as lack of faith and the like, it is a "miracle" (*pāṭihīra*). And the twin...
"And that miracle" refers to the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihīra*).

Regarding "knowledge of the attainment of great compassion" (*mahākaruṇāsamāpatti*): herein, it is called *karuṇā* because when there is suffering in others, it causes the hearts of the virtuous to tremble;

or, it is called *karuṇā* because it afflicts (*kināti*) or destroys (*hiṃsati*, *vināseti*) the suffering of others; or, it is so called because it is performed (*kirīyati*) by way of pervading those who are suffering.
It is called *karuṇā* because it extends (*pasārīyati*). It is "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) because it is great by virtue of its pervasive activity and its functional quality.
It is a "meditative attainment" (*samāpatti*) because those who possess great compassion enter into it; thus, it is both great compassion and an attainment, hence "the attainment of great compassion.
[The knowledge] is either that attainment itself or the knowledge associated with it.

"Omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). Here, one who has known all—that is, everything categorized under the five paths of the knowable—is "all-knowing" (sabbaññū).
The state of being all-knowing is "omniscience" (sabbaññutā); and while it should be called "omniscience-knowledge" (sabbaññutāñāṇa), it is stated as "omniscient knowledge" (sabbaññutaññāṇa).
For all phenomena, distinguished as conditioned and unconditioned and so forth, are indeed formations (saṅkhāra) and modifications (vikāra).

The characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), Nibbāna, and the conceptual designation (*paññatti*)—these five alone are the paths of the knowable (*neyyapatha*). Because it is dependent upon adverting (*āvajjana*), there is no obstruction to it;
therefore, that very [knowledge] is called "unobstructed knowledge" (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "unobstructed knowledge that is unattached and unimpeded in all respects": here, it refers to knowledge that proceeds being unattached—that is, free from attachment—and unimpeded—that is, free from adversaries—with respect to the past, future, and present, such that it is devoid of obstructions.
"He also prophesies the future, saying:
'In this auspicious aeon, there will be three leaders:
I am the Sambuddha now, and Metteyya shall also be [the Buddha] in the future.'"
“Monks, among humans with a lifespan of eighty thousand years, a Blessed One named Metteyya will arise in the world—an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct.

And: “Then, monks, King Saṅkha—who had caused that sacrificial pillar to be erected by King Mahāpanāda—having raised up that pillar, having lived there, and having given it away and released it, [he gave it] to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the beggars, and those who ask for alms.”

“Having given a gift, he will shave off his hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One Metteyya, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. And:
“In the future, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Aṭṭhissara,” and: “He will become a Paccekabuddha named Sumanissara.”
By this method, he declares the future of Devadatta and others. That he also declares the present is self-evident.

(82) "One whose perception of form has become resolved" means one who has transcended the perception of form. "One who abandons the entire body" means one who abandons the entire aggregate of form by way of specific abandonment (*tadaṅga*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana*);
the intention is that he has abandoned rebirth in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*). "There is nothing whatsoever" [refers to the base of nothingness].
"One who sees" means one who sees through the vision of the absence of consciousness, seeing that "there is nothing whatsoever";

thus it refers to one who has attained the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). "I ask about the knowledge of Sakka": addressing the Blessed One as "Sakka," he says, "I ask about the knowledge of that person;
what kind of knowledge should it be? "How is he to be led?": and how is he to be guided? How is his...
"Higher knowledge should be developed.

Regarding the phrase "What is the perception of form?": here, "perception of form" refers both to the fine-material-sphere jhāna spoken of by way of its characteristic of perception, and to its object.
For even the fine-material-sphere jhāna is called "form" in such passages as "possessing form, he sees forms," and so forth; and its object is likewise [called form].
In such passages as, “He sees external forms, beautiful and ugly,” it is used thus. Therefore, here, because perception is of form, it is called “perception of form” (*rūpasaññā*);
this is a designation for fine-material-sphere jhāna by way of its factor of perception. “Perception of form” means that form is its perception;
what is meant is that form is its name. Thus, this is also a designation for that which has the earth-kasiṇa and so forth as its object.

It should be understood as a designation (*adhivacana*). Here, however, only the perception of form (*rūpasaññā*)—comprising the fifteen jhānas by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional [consciousness]—is intended.
"Of one who has attained the attainment of the fine-material sphere" means of one who has attained the attainment of the wholesome jhāna of the fine-material sphere.
"Of one who has been reborn" means of one who has been reborn in that existence by way of the resultant jhāna. "Of one who dwells in happiness in this very life."
It occurs for one who, in this very life, enters into the meditative absorption of action (kiriyā-jhāna), gives rise to happiness, and dwells therein.
"Formless attainments" refers to the base of infinite space and so forth. "Of one who has acquired them" means of one who has produced and established them.
"Perceptions of form have become non-existent" means that perceptions of form have departed. "Disappeared" means destroyed. The reading "un-cultivated" (abhāvitā) is also found, which is excellent.
"By means of transcending through its factor" (*tadaṅgasamatikkama*) means by way of transcending through the abandoning of that factor.

"Abandoned by suppression" (*vikkhambhanappahāna*) means abandoned by the suppression [effected] through the attainment of the formless jhānas. "His material body" (*tassa rūpakāya*) refers to the fine-material-sphere body of that person who has attained the formless attainments.
"Sphere of Nothingness" (ākiñcaññāyatana): here, "nothing" (akiñcana) means that for this [state] there is nothing whatsoever;
it is said that not even a mere trace of attachment remains. The state of being nothing is "nothingness" (ākiñcañña);

this is a designation for the departure from the consciousness of the base of infinite space. That nothingness is the "sphere" (āyatana) of this perception in the sense of its foundation (adhiṭṭhāna), thus it is the "sphere of nothingness."
This is a designation for the jhāna whose object is the departure of consciousness that had been occurring in space.
"Having mindfully entered the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness" means having entered that base of infinite consciousness while practicing with mindfulness.
"Emerging from that" means emerging from that attainment while practicing with mindfulness. "That very same consciousness" refers to that consciousness which had occurred in space.
"Exalted consciousness. "He develops" means he causes it to perish. "He makes it disappear" means he causes it to perish in various ways. "He makes it vanish" means he causes it to go out of sight.

"How is he to be led? means in what manner is that person to be known? "He is to be disciplined" means he is to be known through various methods. "He is to be conciliated" means how he is to be guided by the mind again and again.
Then the Blessed One, having demonstrated his own unimpeded knowledge regarding such a person, in order to explain that knowledge—
He spoke this verse. Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgata, fully knowing all stations of consciousness":
by way of volitional formations there are four, and by way of rebirth-linking there are seven; thus, the Tathāgata is one who fully knows all stations of consciousness.
"He knows it as it stands" means he knows that person standing [in saṃsāra] by way of karmic volitional formations, thinking: "In the future..."
“This one will have such a destination. *Adhimuttaṃ* means intent upon the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) and so forth.
*Tapparāyaṇaṃ* means having that as its ultimate resort. *Viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo* refers to the stations of rebirth-consciousness; they are simply the aggregates accompanied by consciousness.

In this context, *seyyathāpi* is a particle used for the purpose of illustration, meaning “just as among humans. For even though world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) are immeasurable, there are immeasurable [beings] within them...
Among human beings, there are none who are exactly alike even in terms of their complexion, stature, and so forth.
