For even those who are twin brothers and may be identical in complexion or stature, they are nonetheless distinct in their ways of looking forward, looking around, and other such behaviors.
Therefore, they are described as "of diverse bodies. As for their rebirth-consciousness (*paṭisandhi-saññā*), however, it may be triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless.
Therefore, they are called "possessors of diverse perceptions. And some gods refers to the six classes of sense-sphere gods (*kāmāvacara-deva*).
For among them, the body of some is blue, while that of others is yellow or other colors. Their perception, moreover, may be triple-rooted or double-rooted, but it is never rootless.
And some beings in states of misery refers to the female *yakkha* Punabbasu-mātā, who is excluded from the four lower realms (*apāya*).
Piyaṅkaramātā, Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and others such as these, as well as other *vemānika* (intermediate) *peta*s.
For their bodies are diverse by way of being white, black, smooth-skinned, swarthy-colored, and so forth, and by way of being emaciated, stout, short, or tall;
and their perception is also like that of humans, according to whether it is triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless (*tihetuka*, *duhetuka*, *ahetuka*). However, they are not like the devas.
Those of great influence live like destitute people—of little power, with food and clothing difficult to obtain, and oppressed by suffering.

Some are miserable during the dark fortnight and happy during the bright fortnight; therefore, because they have fallen from the heights of happiness, they are called *vinipātika* (those fallen into ruin).
However, among those here, some who possess three roots of merit also experience the realization of the Dhamma, as was the case with Piyaṅkara’s mother and others.
"Brahmakāyikā" refers to the Brahmapārisajja, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā deities. "First-born" means that all of them are produced by the first jhāna.

However, among them, the Brahmapārisajja are produced by a limited degree [of the first jhāna], the Brahmapurohita by a middling degree, and their bodies are more expansive. The Mahābrahmā are produced by a sublime degree; however, their bodies—

It becomes even more expansive. Thus, due to the diversity of their bodies and the unity of their perception by way of the first jhāna, they are said to be "those with diverse bodies and unified perception.
And as it is for them, so it is for beings in the four woeful states;
for in the hells, the personal existence (attabhāva) of some is a quarter-league, of some half a league, and of some three-quarters of a league, such as that of Devadatta.
Furthermore, they are born reaching a hundred *yojanas* in size. Among animals, some are small and some are large.
In the realm of the *petas*, some are sixty cubits tall, some eighty cubits, and some are beautiful while others are ugly. The same applies to the *kālakañcika* asuras.
Moreover, among them there are those called the "long-backed *petas*" who even reach sixty *yojanas* in height. As for perception, however, it is the same for all of them.
It is exclusively the result of unwholesome kamma and is rootless (*ahetuka*). Thus, even those in the states of deprivation are designated as "those with diverse bodies and unified perception.
As for the *Ābhassara* (Radiant) devas: because light issues forth from their bodies and spreads out, falling away again and again like sparks from a firebrand, they are called *Ābhassara*.
Among them, according to the fivefold system, the second and third jhānas are limited (*paritta*).

Having developed [the first jhāna] to a limited degree, those reborn there are called the Parittābhas (Limited Radiance). Having developed it to a middling degree, those reborn there are called the Appamāṇābhas (Immeasurable Radiance).
Having developed it to a superior degree, those reborn there are called the Ābhassarā (Streaming Radiance). Here, however, all are included according to the highest limit.
For the bodies of all of them are of one and the same manifestation, while their perception is without initial application and consists of sustained application only.
And "without applied thought and without sustained thought" (avitakkavicāra) refers to their diversity.
"Subhakiṇha" means "interspersed with beauty"; the meaning is that they are a single mass of beauty due to the radiance and color of their bodies.
For in their case, unlike the Ābhassara devas, the radiance does not go forth by breaking off in fragments. This refers to the third [jhāna] in the fourfold system.
In the system of the fivefold jhāna, by way of the limited, medium, and sublime fourth jhāna, beings are reborn as the Limited Subha, Immeasurable Subha, and Subha-kiṇha devas respectively.
Thus, all of them should be understood as having a single body and possessing the perception of unity through the perception of the fourth jhāna.
The Vehapphala devas also belong to the fourth station of consciousness. The non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), however, are excluded due to the absence of consciousness.
They do not fall within this classification; they belong among the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
The Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) stand on the side of evolution (*vivaṭṭa*); they are not present at all times.

Even for a hundred thousand eons or an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeya*), they do not arise when the world is empty of Buddhas. Only within the interval of sixteen thousand eons, when Buddhas have actually arisen, do they appear.
They arise. They are like military encampments of the Blessed One who turns the Wheel of Dhamma.
Therefore, they do not belong to the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), nor to the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*). However, the Elder Mahāsīva said:
"But that dwelling, Sāriputta, is not easily found which has not been inhabited by me during this long period of time, except for the Suddhāvāsa devas."

When it is said that "by this sutta, even the Suddhāvāsa deities belong to the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings," that is accepted because the sutta does not contradict [the established doctrine].

Regarding the phrase "by completely transcending all perceptions of form" (*sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā*): here, "completely" (*sabbaso*) means either "in every way" (*sabbākārena*) or "all of them without remainder" (*sabbāsaṃ vā anavasesānaṃ*).
The meaning is as follows: "Of perceptions of form" refers both to the fine-material-sphere jhānas spoken of by way of their characteristic of perception and to their objects.

For even the fine-material-sphere jhāna is called "form" in such passages as "possessed of form, he sees forms," and its object is also called "form" in such passages as "he sees external forms, beautiful and ugly. Therefore, here "perception of form" means "perception of forms."
This is a designation for the fine-material-sphere jhāna spoken of by way of its perception. "Perception of form" (rūpasaññā) means that form is its perception;
what is meant is that form is its name. Thus, it should be understood as a designation for that which has the earth-kasiṇa and so forth as its object.
"Having surmounted" means by way of dispassion (*virāga*) and cessation (*nirodha*). What is meant?

It is by way of the complete and total dispassion and cessation of these fifteen perceptions of form—reckoned as jhānas by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional states—and of these eight perceptions of form reckoned as objects by way of the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
One enters and dwells in the base of infinite space for the sake of dispassion and for the sake of cessation.
For it is not possible to enter and dwell in this without having completely transcended the perception of form.

In this regard, since there is no transcending of perceptions for one who is not dispassionate toward the object, and since the object is indeed transcended when the perceptions have been transcended—
Therefore, without mentioning the transcendence of the object, it says:

"In this context, what are perceptions of form? The perception, perceiving, and state of having perceived belonging to one who has attained a fine-material-sphere attainment, or who has been reborn there, or who dwells in happiness in this very life—these are called perceptions of form. One has transcended these perceptions of form."
"He has transcended, he has completely surmounted it; therefore it is said: 'by completely surmounting perceptions of form.

Thus, in the *Vibhaṅga*, the surmounting of perceptions alone is mentioned. However, since these attainments are to be reached by surmounting the object, and not by remaining on a single object as is the case with the first jhāna and so forth, this [surmounting] is also to be understood by way of the surmounting of the object.
It should be understood that the explanation of the meaning has been given.

Regarding "the subsiding of perceptions of resistance" (*paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā*): perceptions arisen through the impact (*paṭighāta*) of the bases such as the eye and so forth with their objects such as visible forms and so forth are "perceptions of resistance";
this is a designation for the perception of visible form and the rest. As it is said: "In this regard, what are..."
“Perception of resistance? Perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of odors, perception of flavors, and perception of tangibles—these are called perceptions of resistance.

What is meant is that by the subsiding, the abandoning, and the non-arising of all ten perceptions of resistance—namely, the five wholesome-resultant and the five unwholesome-resultant—he brings about their non-occurrence.
Granted that these [bodily] pleasures and pains do not exist even for one who has attained the first jhāna and so forth—
for at that time the mind does not proceed by way of the five doors— nevertheless, just as pleasure and pain abandoned elsewhere [reappear] in the fourth jhāna,
and as the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth [reappear] in the third path, [the Blessed One spoke of them] in this very jhāna for the purpose of generating enthusiasm.
The mention of these [fetters] here should be understood by way of praising *jhāna*.
Alternatively, although these do not exist for one who has attained the fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) attainment, they do not fail to exist because they have been abandoned;

for the development of the fine-material sphere does not lead to dispassion toward the material, and their occurrence is dependent upon the material. This development, however, leads to dispassion toward the material.
Therefore, it is appropriate to say here that these [hindrances] have been abandoned. Not only is it appropriate to say so, but it is also appropriate to maintain this as an absolute certainty.
For it was precisely because they had not yet been abandoned prior to this stage that the Blessed One said, "For one who has attained the first jhāna, sound is a thorn.
And it is precisely because they have been abandoned here that the immovability and peaceful liberation of the formless attainments are established.
And it is said: “Āḷāra Kālāma, having attained the formless, did not see even five hundred carts passing by one after another, nor did he hear their sound.
“Non-attention to perceptions of diversity” means perceptions occurring with diversity as their object, or perceptions that are themselves diverse. For these—

“In this context, what are perceptions of diversity? The perception, perceiving, state of having perceived, of one who has not attained meditative absorption but possesses either the mind-element or the mind-consciousness-element—these are called perceptions of diversity.

Having been explained thus in the *Vibhaṅga*, it is these very perceptions intended here that, being comprised within the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element of one who has not attained absorption, occur with respect to a diverse object—that is, one of various natures and types such as visible forms, sounds, and so forth. And because these eight wholesome perceptions of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*)...
There are twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven wholesome-resultant perceptions of the sense sphere, two unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and eleven functional perceptions of the sense sphere.
Thus, these forty-four perceptions are diverse, of various natures, and dissimilar to one another;
therefore, they are called "diverse perceptions. By not attending to all those diverse perceptions—
It is non-orientation, non-attention, and non-reviewing; that is to say, because one does not orient toward them, does not attend to them, and does not review them.
Furthermore, because the aforementioned perception of form and perception of resistance do not exist even in the existence produced by this jhāna, [it is so called].

Even more so during the time of entering and dwelling in this jhāna within that very existence; therefore, their non-existence is stated in two ways as "with the surmounting" and "with the disappearance.

As for the perceptions of diversity, since twenty-seven perceptions arise with this jhāna—namely, eight wholesome perceptions of the sense sphere, nine functional perceptions, and ten unwholesome perceptions—[they are likewise absent].
They exist in the [sensuous] becoming; therefore, it should be understood that they are called "not attending to" (amanasikārā).
For even there, one who enters and dwells in this jhāna enters and dwells precisely by way of not attending to them;
whereas one who attends to them has not attained it. And here, in brief, by the phrase "with the surmounting of perceptions of form" (rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā), it is shown...

The abandoning of all fine-material-sphere phenomena has been stated. By the phrase, "With the disappearance of perceptions of resistance and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity," it should be understood that the abandoning and non-attention toward all sense-sphere consciousnesses and mental factors have also been stated.
Thus, through the surmounting of fifteen types of perceptions of form and the disappearance of ten types of perceptions of resistance, the Blessed One—
By the three phrases beginning with "by not attending to the forty-four kinds of perceptions of diversity," he spoke in praise of the attainment of the base of infinite space.
If one asks why, it was for the purpose of generating enthusiasm and for the purpose of enticing the listeners.
For if some who were unwise were to say, "The Teacher says, 'Attain the base of infinite space,'" [the listener would be inspired].
[He thought: "Who indeed would find purpose or benefit in producing this?
[Thinking,] "Let them not be permitted to speak thus," he spoke in praise of the attainment through these modes. For upon hearing this from him, they will think:
"If this attainment is indeed so sublime, we shall certainly produce it. Then, for the sake of its production...
“They will exert effort.
And for the sake of enticing them, he spoke in praise of her, just like a merchant of *visakaṇṭaka*. A merchant of *visakaṇṭaka* is said to be a sugar merchant.
It is said that he would take molasses, jaggery, candied sugar, white sugar, and so forth in a cart and go to a frontier village.
Having gone there, he proclaimed, “Seize the poison-thorn! Seize the poison-thorn! Hearing this, the villagers thought, “Poison is indeed harsh;
whoever eats it dies. The thorn also kills by piercing. Both of these are harsh; what benefit is there in this?
Thus they bolted the doors of their houses and sent their children away. Seeing this, [he said:]
The merchant thought, "These villagers are skilled at bargaining; come now, I shall make them pay by some stratagem. He then proclaimed, "Take it very sweet! Take it very delicious!
Sugar, molasses, and candied sugar are being sold at a low price; they can even be obtained for counterfeit māsakas and counterfeit kahāpaṇas!
Hearing this, the villagers went out with joyful hearts, and having paid much for the goods, they took them.
In this context, the Blessed One’s statement, “Attain the base of infinite space,” is like the merchant’s proclamation, “Take poison-thorns!
The villagers’ reflection, “Both of these are harsh; what benefit is there in this? is like [the thought]:
“The Blessed One said, ‘Attain the base of infinite space’; what indeed is the benefit here? There is none for him...”

The listeners’ thought was, “We know its quality. Then, the Blessed One’s exposition of the benefits—beginning with the surmounting of the perception of form—was like that merchant’s words, “Take it for a very high price,” and so forth.
Having heard this, their minds were enticed by these benefits; like those villagers who gave a large amount for the sugar, they exerted great effort.
He spoke thus for the purpose of generating enthusiasm and for the sake of encouragement, saying, "Having attained this meditative absorption (samāpatti), they will be reborn there.

Regarding the term *ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā*: here, that which has no end is "infinite" (*ananta*); infinite space is "infinite space" (*ākāsānanta*); that very infinite space is "space-infinity" (*ākāsānañca*);
and that space-infinity is the "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of a foundation for the associated mental states.
The base of infinite space is like a sanctuary for the deities of meditation; it is a designation for the space cleared by removing the kasiṇa.
Having produced jhāna therein and having entered existence in the base of infinite space by way of rebirth-linking, they are called "those who have reached the base of infinite space.
Hereafter, we shall describe only the distinctions between them.

Regarding the phrase "having completely transcended the base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma*): here, first of all, according to the method previously stated, the base of infinite space is so called in the sense of being its foundation;
thus, the jhāna itself is the "base of infinite space," and by the same method, the object is also so called.
Thus, having completely transcended both this jhāna and its object by means of non-occurrence and non-attention, [one enters the next stage].
Since one must enter upon and dwell in this base of infinite consciousness,
it should be understood that both of these have been stated together as "having completely transcended the base of infinite space.
Regarding the phrase "those who have reached the base of infinite consciousness," here "infinite" (ananta) means that which has no end (*anta*) because it is to be brought to mind as "infinite."

The infinite itself is the boundless (*ānañca*); although consciousness is boundless, it is not called "boundless consciousness" (*viññāṇānañca*), but is stated as "consciousness-boundless" (*viññāṇañca*). This is a conventional term (*ruḷhīsadda*) used here.
That very consciousness-boundless, in the sense of being a basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*), is the "base" (*āyatana*); thus it is the "base of consciousness-boundless" (*viññāṇañcāyatana*).
Having produced jhāna therein, those who have reached the existence of the base of consciousness-boundless are "those who have reached the base of consciousness-boundless" (*viññāṇañcāyatanūpagā*).
"Having completely surmounted the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*).
Here too, according to the method already stated, the "base of infinite consciousness" is the jhāna in the sense of its foundation, and by the same method, it is also the object.
Thus, having surmounted both this jhāna and its object through non-occurrence and non-attention—

Since one must enter upon and dwell in this base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), it should be understood that both [the base of consciousness and the base of nothingness] are combined together when it is said: "having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness.
Regarding the term *ākiñcaññāyatanūpaga*, here "nothing" (*akiñcana*) means that there is nothing whatsoever in it, even down to the mere moment of dissolution.
It means that for him there is nothing remaining. The state of having nothing is *ākiñcañña*; this is a designation for the departure from the consciousness of the base of infinite space.
That *ākiñcañña* is the "base" (*āyatana*) in the sense of a foundation; thus it is the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*).
Having produced jhāna therein and attained existence in the base of nothingness, they are "those who have reached the base of nothingness. This is the seventh station of consciousness.
He knows this as the seventh station of rebirth-consciousness. Because perception is so subtle in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, consciousness is likewise subtle;
thus, it is "neither consciousness nor non-consciousness," and for that reason it is not mentioned among the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

"That which has not been" refers to statements such as "form is the self," which have the sense of being non-existent. That is untrue because it is a state of perversion (*vipallāsa*), owing to its reliance on wrong view.
"Connected with what is harmful. Alternatively, "untrue" means non-existent or not found. It is like saying to one who is not a thief, "This was brought to you by theft;
this is not wealth in your house," and so forth. "Not so" means having a different form, existing otherwise.
"Connected with what is harmful" means not based on the welfare of this world or the welfare of the next world. The Tathāgata does not speak such [words].

"He explains" means that the Tathāgata does not speak that discourse which lacks liberation—namely, talk concerning kings and so forth, up to talk concerning spirits—which is real, true, but not conducive to the goal.
"Real, true, and conducive to the goal" refers to that which is based on the Noble Truths.
In this regard, the Tathāgata is one who knows the proper time; that is, for the purpose of explaining that question, he waits for the right occasion regarding that third type of explanation.

The Tathāgata knows the proper time. This means that, having understood the time for people to receive and the time for them to grasp [the teaching], he explains only at the appropriate and fitting time, providing the supporting reasons and causes.

He speaks at the appropriate and fitting time, thus he is a "speaker at the right time" (kālavādī). He speaks what is real and of its true nature, thus he is a "speaker of truth" (bhūtavādī). [He speaks] the ultimate meaning...
He speaks of Nibbāna, thus he is a speaker of the goal (*atthavādī*). He speaks of the Dhamma of the Path and its Fruits, thus he is a speaker of the Dhamma (*dhammavādī*).
He speaks of the Discipline of restraint and so forth, thus he is a speaker of the Discipline (*vinayavādī*).

In this context, "the seen" refers to the objective field of visible forms that comes into the range of the eye-doors of immeasurable beings within immeasurable world-systems; he knows that in all its aspects.

He sees. By thus knowing and seeing, he [analyzes] that form—whether by way of the desirable and undesirable, or by way of the terms available among the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—in various ways such as:

"What is that form which is the form-base (*rūpāyatana*)? It is that form derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which possesses visible appearance, is impinging, blue, yellow," and so forth.
When analyzed by means of thirteen names, eighteen phrases, and fifty-two methods, it remains exactly as it is; there is nothing false about it.

This same method applies to the door of the ear and the other sense doors as well. To demonstrate the various ways in which sounds and so forth appear when they come into the range of perception, he said:
"The seen, the heard. Therein, "the seen" refers to the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*); "the heard" refers to the sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*). "The sensed" (*muta*)...
The sense-sphere of odors (*gandhāyatana*), the sense-sphere of tastes (*rasāyatana*), and the sense-sphere of tangibles (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*) are so called because they are to be reached and grasped.
"Cognized" (*viññāta*) refers to phenomena such as pleasure and pain that serve as objects. "Attained" (*patta*) means attained either by seeking or without seeking.
"Sought after" (*pariyesita*) means sought after whether it has been attained or not attained. "Mentally explored" (*anuvicaritaṃ manasā*) means mentally traversed by the mind.
By the phrase "fully awakened to by the Tathāgata," this is shown:
for whatever objective form— blue, yellow, and so forth— arises within the range of the eye-door in these immeasurable world-systems of this world with its devas,
[the Tathāgata knows] that "at this very moment, having seen such an objective form, this being is glad, dejected, or neutral."

All this has been thus fully awakened to by the Tathāgata. Likewise, whatever sound-object—such as the sound of kettledrums or the sound of tabors—arises within the range of the ear-door in these immeasurable world-systems of this world including its devas;
or whatever odor-object—such as the scent of the heartwood or the scent of the bark—arises within the range of the nose-door; [all this has been thus fully awakened to by the Tathāgata].
Taste-objects such as "root-extract" or "piece-cake" come into the range of the tongue-door;
tangible objects classified as the earth-element, fire-element, and air-element—such as "hard" or "soft"—come into the range of the body-door.
[At that moment, one knows: "This being, at this very instant, having touched such a tangible object, is either glad or dejected."
or neutral”—all this has been thus fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.

Likewise, whatever object of a phenomenon—such as pleasure, pain, and so forth—arises within the range of the mind-door from among these immeasurable world-systems in this world with its devas, [he knows]:
"At this very moment, having cognized such an object of a phenomenon, this being is glad."
“...or whether he has become dejected or neutral”—all this has been thus fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
For, Cunda, regarding whatever has been seen, heard, sensed, or cognized by these beings, there is nothing therein that has not been seen, heard, sensed, or cognized by the Tathāgata;
yet, for this great multitude, even that which was not attained after searching—

There is that which exists without having been sought and without having been attained; there is that which exists having been sought and attained; and there is that which exists without having been sought and yet attained.
For the Tathāgata, there is nothing whatsoever that is not reached—that is, nothing not realized through his knowledge. Therefore he is called "Tathāgata.
Because he has gone (gata) in exactly the same way (tathā) as the world has gone, he is called "Tathāgata. Thus it is said in the Pāḷi.

However, it is said, “fully awakened” (*abhisambuddha*); that is synonymous with the word “gone. In this manner, the meaning of the term *tathāgata* as a conclusion should be understood in all instances.
“Cunda, on the night when the Tathāgata fully awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and on the night [when he passes away]...”

“He attains final Nibbāna by the element of Nibbāna without residue; whatever he speaks, utters, or explains during this interval, all that is exactly so and not otherwise; therefore he is called the Tathāgata.
Here, on the night when the Blessed One sat upon the invincible throne at the seat of enlightenment, having crushed the heads of the three Māras...
Having crushed [the defilements], he awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
and from the night he attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue between the twin sāla trees, throughout this intervening period of forty-five years—

whether during the first, middle, or last enlightenment— whatever discourse (sutta), song (geyya), and so forth, up to the analytical exposition (vedalla) was spoken by the Blessed One, [all that is included].

All of that is, both in meaning and in phrasing, irreproachable, neither deficient nor redundant, complete in every aspect, and a crusher of the intoxication of lust, hatred, and delusion; therein there is not even a hair’s breadth of error.
All of it is as if marked with a single seal, measured with a single reed, and weighed with a single scale.
And it is exactly so; there is nothing false. Therefore he said: “Cunda, on whatever night the Tathāgata...
[all that] is exactly so, not otherwise; therefore he is called the ‘Tathāgata’. For here the word *gata* has the sense of *gada*, meaning speech.

Furthermore, *āgada* means speaking; thus, the meaning is: “He whose speech (*āgada*) is true (*tatho*), that is, unerring. By changing the letter *da* to *ta*, the derivation of the word should be understood in this sense as *gata*.
Regarding the passage, “Cunda, as he speaks... [etc. ...he is so called,” here the body conforms to the Blessed One’s speech, and his speech conforms to his body;
therefore, the Blessed One is one who acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts.
The meaning is that for one who has become such, just as his speech is, so too does his body proceed accordingly; and just as his body is, so too is his speech.
"Thus-gone" (*tathāgata*) should be understood here as a compound meaning "one who has gone [to the goal] and returned.

"The Conqueror, unconquered" (*abhibhū anabhibhūto*): from the peak of existence above down to the Avīci hell below, throughout immeasurable world-systems, he conquers all beings by means of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation; there is no equal to him.
Or there is no measure [for him]. He is incomparable, immeasurable, unsurpassed; the king of kings, the god of gods, the supreme among the Sakkas, the supreme among the Brahmas.
*Aññadatthu* is a particle used in the sense of certainty (*ekamsatthe*). *Dakkhati* (he sees) thus he is *dasa*. *Vasaṃ vatteti* (he exercises mastery) thus he is *vasavattī*.

Herein, this derivation of the words should be understood: like a medicine (*agada*), it is a "medicine" (*agada*); but what is this? It is both the splendor of his teaching and the accumulation of his merit.
For by means of that, this one of great majesty, like a physician with a divine antidote, overcomes all proponents of other doctrines as well as the world with its devas. Thus,
because he possesses an antidote (*agada*) consisting of the splendor of his teaching and the accumulation of merit— which is true (*tatha*) and unerring in overcoming the entire world—
one should understand him as the *Tathāgata*, the letter *da* having been changed to the letter *ta*.
"He knows only for this world by way of the formation of kamma" means that he knows only for this world by way of the formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*).
"With the breakup of the body, after death" means after death, following the dissolution of the acquired aggregates (*upādinnakkhandha*).

Regarding terms such as "the plane of misery" (*apāya*): it is called a "plane of misery" because it has departed from the bliss consisting of growth. It is called a "bad destination" (*duggati*) because it is a resort or refuge for suffering.
"Vinipāta" means they fall down into this state because they have performed difficult deeds. "Niraya" means a place devoid of joy (*niratiaṭṭha*) or devoid of essence (*nirassādaṭṭha*).
That *apāya*... [etc. ...is the niraya. "Upapajjissati" means he will arise by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

"Tiracchānayoni": they move horizontally (*tiriyaṃ*), thus they are *tiracchānā*; their birthplace is the *tiracchānayoni*; that is the *tiracchānayoni*. "Pettivisaya" means... [etc. ...the realm of the departed.

The realm of those who have reached the state of being *peta* (departed) is the *pettivisaya*; that is, the *pettivisaya*. Humans (*manussa*) are so called because of the abundance of mind (*manasa-ussannatā*); among them, "among humans.
Hereafter, regarding the phrase "by way of the formation of kamma" (*kammābhisaṅkhāra-vasena*), the meaning should be understood as "by way of the formation of merit" (*puññābhisaṅkhāra-vasena*).

"With the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khaya*) means by the vanishing of the taints. "Taintless liberation of mind" (*anāsavaṃ cetovimutti*) refers to the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship, which is devoid of taints.

"Released by wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship. It should be understood that the concentration of the fruit of arahantship is the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust, while the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship is the release by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance.

Alternatively, the fruit of arahantship attained by one of craving-temperament after suppressing defilements through the power of absorption-jhāna is the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust; [the same applies for one of] view-temperament.
The fruit of arahantship attained by developing mere access concentration and practicing insight is liberation through wisdom (paññāvimutti) due to the fading away of ignorance (avijjāvirāga).
Alternatively, the fruit of non-returning, with reference to sensual lust (kāmarāga), is liberation of mind (cetovimutti) due to the fading away of lust (rāgavirāga);
the fruit of arahantship is liberation through wisdom due to the fading away of ignorance in every respect.
Regarding the phrase "the base of nothingness is resolved upon" as "by way of liberation": in what sense should liberation be understood?
It is in the sense of being resolved upon (*adhimuccana*). What is this so-called sense of being resolved upon?

It is the sense of being thoroughly liberated from opposing states, and the sense of being thoroughly liberated by way of delighting in the object, like a child whose limbs and members are relaxed in his father’s lap.
It is said that [the mind] occurs toward the object with non-attachment, by way of being unobstructed like a bed.
"Resolved through such liberation" means: having been released from the base of infinite consciousness, it is resolved—that is, attached—toward the base of nothingness by way of non-attachment.
"Resolved therein" means attached to that concentration. "Resolute therein" means toward that...

"Devoted to jhāna": "That as the dominant factor" means that jhāna is the preeminent [condition]. "Devoted to forms," etc., are stated by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure being held in high esteem.
"Devoted to clans," etc., three [terms], are stated by way of the Kṣatriya and other clans being held in high esteem.
"Devoted to gains," etc., eight [terms], are stated by way of the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*). "Devoted to fishermen," etc., [the remaining terms]...
The four [types] are stated by way of conditions (*paccaya*). "One intent upon the Suttantas," and so forth, are stated by way of the Three Piṭakas.

"One intent upon the forest-dwelling factor," and so forth, are stated by way of undertaking the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). "One intent upon the first jhāna," and so forth, are stated by way of attainment (*paṭilābha*).

“Devoted to kamma” means by way of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*). “Devoted to fruition” means by way of the course of existence (*pavatti*). “Heavy with kamma” means heavy with volition (*cetanā*). “Heavy with rebirth-linking” means heavy with the state of rebirth (*upapatti*).

84. “Having known the non-arising of the base of nothingness” means: having emerged from the attainment of the base of nothingness and understood the volitional formation of kamma that produces the base of nothingness, [one thinks], “How is this an impediment?
“The fetter of delight” refers to that which is termed attachment to the fourth immaterial realm.

Nandi, having understood that fetter, then sees it through insight (*vipassati*). This means that after emerging from the attainment of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-samāpatti*), he sees that attainment by way of its impermanence and so forth.

"This knowledge is true for him" means that this knowledge of Arahatship, which arises gradually for that person who is thus practicing insight, is unerring. "Of one who has lived the holy life" (*vusīmato*)...
"Of one who has lived [the holy life]. The remainder is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta also by way of the pinnacle of Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma just as before.
From the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Cūḷaniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the *Posāla-māṇava-sutta* is finished.
15. Commentary on the exposition of the *Mogharāja-māṇava-sutta*.
85. Regarding the fifteenth discourse, the *Mogharāja-sutta*: "Twice" means two times. For previously, after the *Ajita-sutta*, [he spoke].
At the conclusion of both the Tissametteyya Sutta and the next discourse, he questioned the Blessed One twice;
however, the Blessed One, awaiting the ripening of his faculties, did not answer him. Therefore he said: "Twice, Sakka, I asked.

And as for the statement, "Up to three times, O Goddess, he answered me—so have I heard," this means that when questioned up to three times in accordance with the Dhamma, he who had become a pure deity...
"The Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, explains"—thus have I heard. It is said that he heard this very thing while at the banks of the Godhāvarī River.
Therefore he said: "I have heard that he explains. Whatever needs to be said regarding the exposition of this verse follows the same method as stated previously.
86. "This world" refers to the human world. "The other world" refers to everything remaining after setting that aside.

"Together with the devas" refers to all remaining [worlds] associated with both devas by birth and by convention, excluding the Brahmā-world. Alternatively, the phrase "the Brahmā-world together with the devas" is merely an illustration of the method for the expression "the world together with the devas," and so forth;
by this, the entire world described in such ways should be understood.

87. “Thus one of excellent vision” means thus one of supreme vision; it shows that he is capable of seeing the inclinations, dispositions, destinations, and final goals of the world together with its devas.

88. “Behold the world as empty”: behold the world as empty in two ways—either by way of discerning the occurrence of what has been determined [as non-existent], or by way of contemplating conditioned phenomena as hollow.
“Having uprooted the view of self” means having eradicated the personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).

"It breaks" (*lujjati*) means it disintegrates. "It sees" (*cakkhati*) means it is the eye (*cakkhu*). This [eye] exists within the black circle (*kaṇhamaṇḍala*), which is surrounded by a white circle (*setamaṇḍala*), of the composite eye;

situated in the middle of the visible circle (*diṭṭhamaṇḍala*)—the location where the shape of the body arises for those standing directly in front—it remains effecting the status of being respectively the basis (*vatthu*) and the door (*dvāra*) for eye-consciousness and the other [mental states]. "They give form" (*rūpayanti*)...
The meaning is that visible forms, undergoing a change in color, manifest the state of being present in the heart.
Consciousness that arises from the eye, or consciousness that belongs to the eye or is dependent upon the eye, is "eye-consciousness" (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
Contact that arises from the eye is "eye-contact" (*cakkhusamphassa*). "Conditioned by eye-contact" means conditioned by contact associated with eye-consciousness.
"Vedayitaṃ" means finding; the meaning is "feeling" (*vedanā*). That very thing causes one to be happy, thus it is "pleasure" (*sukha*);
the meaning is that it makes that to which it arises happy. Or, it thoroughly consumes (*suṭṭhu khādati*) and digs away (*khanati*) bodily and mental afflictions, thus it is "pleasure.
It causes suffering, thus it is "pain" (*dukkha*); the meaning is that it makes that to which it arises suffer. Not pain... [not pleasure]...
"Sukha" refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukha*). The letter "m" is used here according to the rules of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).

Furthermore, that [feeling] acts as a condition in eight ways toward the feeling associated with itself in visual contact (*cakkhusamphassa*): by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, result, nutriment, association, presence, and non-disappearance; and toward the feeling associated with the [mental] reception (*sampaṭicchana*), it acts as a condition by way of proximity, contiguity, decisive support, absence, and disappearance.
In five ways, it acts as a condition by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) for those states associated with investigation (*santīraṇa*) and so forth.

It is called "ear" (*sota*) because it hears; that [ear] exists within the ear-canal together with its constituent parts, in a location shaped like a finger-stall (*aṅgulivedhaka*), covered with fine brown hair, performing the function of being the appropriate physical basis (*vatthu*) and door (*dvāra*) for ear-consciousness and the rest. They are "heard" (*saddīyanti*)...
"Sounds" (*saddā*) means they are uttered. "It smells" (*ghāyati*), thus it is the nose (*ghāna*);

that [nose] stands within the nostril-cavity—which together with its constituent parts—is shaped like a goat's hoof, performing the function of being the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the door (*dvāra*) for nose-consciousness and the rest as appropriate.
"Odors" (*gandhā*) means they are smelled; the meaning is that they manifest their own physical basis. "It invites life" (*avhāyati*), thus it is the tongue (*jivhā*), in the sense of tasting.

Or the tongue: excluding the very tip, the root, and the sides of that tongue together with its constituent parts, it remains in the middle of the upper surface in a location shaped like the point of a split lotus petal, establishing itself as the appropriate basis (vatthu) and door (dvāra) for tongue-consciousness and the rest.
They are called *rasa* because beings taste them; the meaning is that they provide relish (*assādentīti*).
"Body" (*kāya*) is the accumulation (*āya*) of loathsome defilements (*āsava*). "Accumulation" (*āya*) means the place of arising.

To the extent that there is the occurrence of what is clung-to (*upādinnapavatti*) in this body, therein the bodily sensitivity (*kāyappasāda*) mostly remains, establishing itself as the basis (*vatthu*) and door (*dvāra*) for body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa*) and the rest, as appropriate.
They are "touched" (*phusanti*), thus they are "tangibles" (*phoṭṭhabba*). It "thinks" (*manati*), thus it is "mind" (*mano*); it "cognizes" (*vijānāti*), thus...

Meaning: They are called *dhammas* because they bear their own characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*). "Mind" (*mano*) refers to the mind together with the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

"Dhammas" refers to all remaining objects of consciousness (*dhammārammaṇa*), excluding Nibbāna. "Mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*) refers to the impulsion-mind-consciousness (*javana-manoviññāṇa*).

"Mind-contact" (*manosamphassa*) is the contact associated with that [consciousness]; it [serves as a condition] for the associated feeling, except for the condition of kamma-result (*vipāka-paccaya*).

It is a condition by means of the remaining seven conditions. Immediately after [the preceding], it is a condition for the remaining ones by those same [seven] and by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) alone.
"By way of observing the occurrence that takes place involuntarily" means by way of looking at, that is, seeing, the formations that occur without one's own will.
"No mastery is obtained over form" means that in regard to form, the state of mastery—the state of being a lord—is not obtained. The same method applies to feeling and the others as well.
“Monks, this body is not yours. When there is a self, there is what belongs to a self; yet the self itself does not exist.
Therefore he said, “Monks, this body is not yours. Nor is it “of others”; for “another” refers to the self of others.
If that existed, it would belong to others; but that too does not exist. Therefore he said, “Nor is it of others. This is ancient...
“Monks, ‘kamma’—this does not refer to past kamma alone; rather, this body is produced by past kamma.

Therefore, it is spoken of in this way by way of conventional usage regarding conditions (*paccaya-vohāra*). The passage beginning with ‘volitionally produced’ (*abhisaṅkhata*) is stated by way of the conventional usage of ‘kamma’ itself, because it possesses the essential characteristics of the former [the kamma].
This, however, is the meaning here: ‘volitionally produced’ should be understood as ‘made by conditions. ‘Volitionally intended’ (*abhisañcetayita*)...”
It should be understood as having volition as its basis and volition as its root. "To be felt" (vedanīya) should be understood as the basis for feeling.
"No core is found in form" means that no core such as permanence, etc., is found in form. The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates.
"Form is coreless and devoid of core" means that form is without essence and bereft of a core. "Devoid of a core" means departed from a core.

"By means of the essence of permanence" means either by means of a permanent essence that exists having transcended disintegration, or by means of a permanent essence; since there is no such thing as a permanent essence for anything, there is no essence by way of a permanent essence.

"By means of the essence of happiness" means either by means of the essence of happiness; since there is no such thing as an essence of happiness for anything that exists having transcended the happiness of stability, there is no essence by way of the essence of happiness.
"By means of the essence of self" means by means of the essence of a self or what belongs to a self.
Or "by the permanent" (*nicca*): because there is nothing whatsoever that exists permanently by transcending dissolution;
thus, it is "or by the permanent. Or "by the stable" (*dhuva*): because even during the time of its existence, there is nothing whatsoever that is stable due to its dependence on conditions;
thus, it is "or by the stable. Or "by the eternal" (*sassata*): because there is nothing whatsoever that exists at all times without interruption; thus, [it is not by the eternal].

"Or by way of eternalism. "Or by way of a nature that does not change" means: because there is nothing whatsoever whose intrinsic nature (*pakati*) is non-changing in terms of aging and dissolution, it is said "or by way of a nature that does not change.
"The eye is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self" means: [empty] of that which is imagined as "an agent, an experiencer, one who is independent."

It is empty because of the absence of a self, and because of the absence of anything belonging to a self among one's own requisites. The meaning is that all mundane phenomena, such as the eye and so forth, are called "empty" because herein there is neither a self nor anything belonging to a self.
Supramundane phenomena are likewise empty of self and what belongs to a self; it is said that there are no phenomena apart from emptiness.
It exists. It is stated that within that phenomenon there is an absence of any essence consisting of self or what belongs to a self.

In the world, when one says "an empty house" or "an empty pot," it is not that the house or the pot itself is absent; rather, it is stated that there is an absence of something else within that house or pot.
And by the Blessed One it was said: "Whatever is not present therein, by that it is empty."
But as for that which remains there, he understands it, being present, as "this exists"—this is the meaning stated.
This same meaning is found likewise in the *Ñāyagantha* and the *Saddagantha*. Thus, in this sutta, only the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) is explained.
"By way of lack of mastery" means because one does not exercise power over oneself. "By way of being made to act against one's will" means [acting] against one's own will.

By way of causing lack of relish. "Unreachable" means because there is no standing place or foundation for it to remain. "Not subject to one's own will" means because it does not function according to one's own power.
"From the other side" means by way of impermanence and because its occurrence is dependent upon conditions. "Secluded" means by way of escape.
"Pure" means exclusively, without being produced by a Lord, time, or primordial nature, but occurring solely by way of dependence on conditions.
"Pure" means being devoid of anything belonging to a self; it is a mere heap of pure phenomena (*dhamma*).

For one who sees and knows the pure arising of phenomena, the pure continuity of formations—that is, the uninterrupted continuity of formations—just so, for one who sees the formations and so forth as pure, these have been stated with care two or three times as having a single meaning.
For one who sees in this way, there is no fear at the mouth of death. "Gāmaṇī" is a form of address.
"The world as like grass and sticks": this refers to the world comprised of the aggregates of clinging (*upādinnakkhandha*).

When one sees with wisdom that it is like grass and sticks—just as when grass, sticks, and so forth are being taken in the forest, one does not think, "They are taking me," or "They are taking what belongs to me"—so too [with these aggregates].
Even when grass, wood, and so forth perish or go to ruin of their own accord, it does not occur [to him] that "the self perishes" or "that which belongs to the self perishes.

Thus, regarding this body as well, when it perishes or goes to ruin, one who does not perceive that a self or anything belonging to a self is destroyed, but perceives it through wisdom as being equal to grass and wood, is said to be such. He desires nothing else whatsoever, other than non-relinking.
Except for Nibbāna, which is devoid of rebirth-linking, he does not long for any other existence or personal identity (*attabhāva*).
"He investigates form" means he seeks the essence of form. "As 'I'" is by way of views;
"as 'mine'" is by way of craving; "as 'I am'" is by way of conceit. "That too does not exist for him" means that these three kinds [of notions] do not exist for that person.
*Idha* is a particle used for the designation of a place; this refers in some instances to the world, as it is said:
"Here, the Tathāgata arises in the world. In some instances, it refers to the Teaching, as it is said: "Right here, monks, is the ascetic; right here is the second ascetic.
In some instances, it refers to a location, as it is said: [and so forth].
“While remaining right here, having become a deity, I have obtained life once again; know this, O worthy ones.
In some instances, it serves merely to fill out the meter, as it is said: “In this case, monks, I would have been one who has eaten and is invited.”
Furthermore, it should be understood that this is stated with reference to the world. Regarding the term "the uninstructed worldling" (*assutavā puthujjana*):

here, one is to be known as "uninstructed" due to the absence of both scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*). For one who lacks both the scripture that prevents wrong views—because they are devoid of study, inquiry, and discernment concerning the aggregates, elements, bases, the mode of conditions, the foundations of mindfulness, and so forth—and the realization that is to be attained through practice because it has not been attained; [such a person is the uninstructed worldling].
He exists, but due to the absence of both scriptural learning (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*), he is to be known as "one who has not heard" (*assutavā*).

Furthermore, he is a worldling (*puthujjana*) for these reasons: because he is born among many (*puthu*), because of various causes such as birth and so forth, because he is included within the class of worldlings (*puthujjana-antogadhattā*), and because this person is manifold (*puthu*) in his nature.
For he is called a *puthujjana* because he generates various kinds of defilements and so forth through causes such as their production; as it is said:

"They are *puthujjanas* because they generate various defilements (*puthu kilese janenti*); they are *puthujjanas* because they have not abandoned the various views of identity (*puthu avihatasaṅkhāyadiṭṭhikā*);

they are *puthujjanas* because they look toward the faces of various teachers (*puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikā*); they are *puthujjanas* because they have not emerged from the various realms of existence (*puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitā*)."

They are called *puthujjana* because they perform various and manifold volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*); they are called *puthujjana* because they are carried away by various and manifold floods (*ogha*);

they are called *puthujjana* because they are tormented by various and manifold fevers (*santāpa*); they are called *puthujjana* because they are consumed by various and manifold burning pains (*pariḷāha*);
they are called *puthujjana* because they are attached, greedy, infatuated, muddled, obsessed, and stuck to the five various strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).

"Ordinary persons" (*puthujjana*) means those who are attached and obstructed; they are called "ordinary persons" because they are individually enveloped, covered, enclosed, shut off, concealed, and closed in by the five hindrances.

Alternatively, they are called "ordinary persons" because they are included among the multitude of people who have passed beyond the path of calculation, who are averse to the noble Dhamma, and whose conduct consists of lowly things. Or, this [category] is a distinct enumeration in itself, separate from others.
A worldling (*puthujjana*) is one who has gone away from and is dissociated from noble persons (*ariya*) endowed with qualities such as virtue and learning.
Thus, by these two terms, "the uninstructed worldling," those [who have been described] are referred to:
"Two kinds of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun."
“The blind worldling alone, and the noble worldling alone”—thus two types of worldlings are mentioned;
it should be understood that among them, the blind worldling is the one being discussed here.

Regarding the phrases “one who does not see the Noble Ones,” and so forth: “Noble Ones” (*ariya*) refers to those who are far removed from defilements (*kilesa*), because they do not proceed in what is not the right way (*anaya*), but proceed in the right way (*aya*).
Because they are to be honored by the world together with its devas, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha are called "Noble Ones" (*ariya*);
or rather, here it is the Buddhas alone who are the Noble Ones. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, in the world together with its devas... the Tathāgata is called the Noble One.
However, in this context, Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Tathāgata should be understood as "True Persons" (*sappurisa*).
For they are "true persons" (*sappurisa*) because they are beautiful men by virtue of their possession of supramundane qualities. Or rather, all these [categories] are stated in two ways:
for both Buddhas and Noble Ones (*ariya*) are true persons, as are Pacceka-buddhas and disciples of the Buddha. As it is said:
"He who is grateful and mindful of benefits, wise, a good friend, and firm in devotion..."
“They perform their duties with care for one who is suffering; such a person they call a true man.
By the words “he is a friend of the virtuous and firm in devotion,” the disciple of the Buddha is thus described.

It is by means of gratitude and other such qualities that Paccekabuddhas and Buddhas are defined. One who is habitually indifferent toward these Noble Ones and does not take pleasure in seeing them [is described as follows].
Thus, he should be understood as one who does not see the Noble Ones (*ariya*). He is twofold: one who does not see with the eye, and one who does not see with wisdom (*ñāṇa*);

of these two, it is the latter who does not see with wisdom that is intended here. For even if the Noble Ones are seen with the fleshly eye or the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), they remain as if unseen;
for by means of those eyes, only their physical appearance is grasped, not their state as Noble Ones or their sphere of experience. This is also the case with dogs, jackals, and the like.
They see with the noble eye, yet they are not seers of the noble ones.

Here is an illustration: it is said that one day, an attendant who had gone forth in old age, while walking for alms with an elder whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava) at Cittala Mountain, took the elder’s bowl and robe and followed behind him.
As he was approaching, he asked the Elder, "Venerable sir, what are those called 'Noble Ones' (ariya) like?

The Elder said, "In this world, there is a certain elderly man who, though he carries the bowl and robes of the Noble Ones and performs his duties while traveling with them, does not recognize a Noble One at all;
thus, friend, the Noble Ones are difficult to recognize. Even when this was said, he still did not understand. Therefore, by means of his eye—
Seeing is not seeing; only that which is seen by means of knowledge is true seeing. As it is said: "Enough of you, Vakkali!
What is the use of seeing this putrid body? He who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, he sees me.
Therefore, even one who sees with the eye, if he does not see with knowledge the characteristics of impermanence and so forth as seen by the Noble Ones, [is not seeing the Noble Ones].

One who has not attained the Dhamma already attained, and because he has not seen the qualities that make one noble and the state of nobility itself, should be understood as "one who has not seen the Noble Ones.
"Unskilled in the Noble Dhamma" means unproficient in the Noble Dhamma distinguished by the foundations of mindfulness and so forth. Regarding the phrase "undisciplined in the Noble Dhamma": here—
"Discipline (vinaya) is twofold, and each of these is fivefold here;
because of the absence of that [discipline], one is called 'undisciplined' (avinīta).

For this discipline is twofold: the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) and the discipline of abandonment (pahāna-vinaya). And herein, within each of these two types of discipline, each one is fivefold.

The Vinaya is fivefold. For the Vinaya of restraint is fivefold: the restraint of virtue, the restraint of mindfulness, the restraint of knowledge, the restraint of patience, and the restraint of energy.
The Vinaya of abandoning is also fivefold: abandoning by substitution of opposites, abandoning by suppression, abandoning by eradication, abandoning by subsiding, and abandoning by escape.

In this context, “He is endowed with, fully endowed with, this restraint of the Pātimokkha” refers to the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*). “He guards the faculty of the eye; he attains restraint over the faculty of the eye” refers to the restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*).
“Whatever streams there are in the world, O Ajita,” said the Blessed One, “mindfulness is their dam.”
“I declare the restraint of the taints; by means of wisdom they are closed off.

This is restraint through knowledge. “He is patient with cold and heat”—this is restraint through patience. “He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire”—this is restraint through energy.
And all this restraint is, according to its respective objects, that which ought to be restrained.
It is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because it restrains bodily misconduct and so forth, and it is called "discipline" (*vinaya*) because it disciplines them.
Thus, first of all, it should be understood that discipline as restraint is fivefold.
Likewise, among the insights (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) such as the discernment of name-and-form, it is the opposite of [ignorance], just as light is the opposite of darkness.
By each respective knowledge of insight comes the abandoning of its corresponding disadvantage. That is to say: by the definition of name-and-form, the abandoning of the personality-belief;
by the discernment of conditions, the abandoning of the views of no-cause and wrong-cause; subsequently, by the overcoming of doubt, the abandoning of perplexity;
by the comprehension of groups, the abandoning of the grip of "I" and "mine"; and by the definition of the path and the non-path...
By the perception of a path where there is no path; by the view of annihilation through the vision of arising;

by the view of eternalism through the vision of passing away; by the perception of safety in what is fearful through the vision of fear; by the perception of gratification through the vision of danger;

by the perception of delight through the contemplation of disenchantment; by the desire not to be released through the knowledge of the desire for release; and by equanimity through the knowledge of equanimity.

By means of the conformity [knowledge] regarding the stability of phenomena and Nibbāna, there occurs through the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) the abandoning of the grasping at the sign of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*).
This is called "abandoning by way of its own factor" (*tadaṅgappahāna*).
Furthermore, by means of concentration—distinguished as access and absorption—there is the warding off of the state of occurrence, just as the surface of water is cleared by the removal of a jar.
The abandoning of those various states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is called "abandoning by suppression" (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).
That which, through the cultivation of the four noble paths, occurs within the continuum of one who possesses each respective path—

by way of the absolute non-arising of the mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination, as described in the formula beginning with "for the abandoning of views" (*diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāya*)— is [the abandonment by eradication].

This is what is called abandonment by cutting off (*samucchedappahāna*). Furthermore, that state of the defilements being subsided at the moment of the fruition (*phalakkhaṇa*) is what is called abandonment by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*).

And Nibbāna, which has abandoned all conditioned things because it has escaped from all conditioned things, is what is called abandonment by escape (*nissaraṇappahāna*). And all this abandonment is abandonment in the sense of relinquishment (*cāga*).

In the sense of disciplining, it is the Vinaya; therefore, it is called "the Vinaya of abandoning. Alternatively, because each respective Vinaya arises for one who possesses that particular abandonment, it is also called "the Vinaya of abandoning.
Thus, it should be understood that the Vinaya of abandoning is likewise divided fivefold.

Thus, this discipline (*vinaya*), which is twofold in brief and tenfold in detail, does not exist for this uninstructed worldling because his restraint has been broken and because what is to be abandoned has not been abandoned. Therefore, due to its absence in him, he is called "undisciplined" (*avinīta*).
The same method applies to one who does not see true persons (*sappurisa*) and is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons.
Regarding the phrase "untrained in the Dhamma of the true person" (*sappurisadhamme avinīto*), there is no difference in meaning here [from the previous term]. As it has been said:
"Those who are noble (*ariya*) are the same as those who are true persons (*sappurisa*). Those who are true persons are the same as those who are noble.
Whatever is the Dhamma of the noble ones is the same as the Dhamma of the true persons. Whatever is the Dhamma of the true persons is the same as the Dhamma of the noble ones."
The Dhamma is indeed their noble discipline; what is their noble discipline is indeed their discipline of the true person.

What is their discipline of the true person is indeed their noble discipline. Whether one says "noble" or "true person," "noble Dhamma" or "Dhamma of the true person," "noble discipline" or "discipline of the true person"—these are identical, one, of the same meaning, equal, of the same portion, of the same kind, and the very same thing.
"One regards form as self" means that here someone regards form as self, regarding form and self as non-dual, thinking: "Whatever is form, that am I; whatever I am, that is form.
It is just as when an oil lamp is burning, one regards the flame and the color as non-dual, thinking: "Whatever is the flame, that is the color; whatever is the color, that is the flame."
In the same way, here someone regards form as self... [as before]... thus he sees form through the vision of the view, "This is self. Or, regarding the self as possessing form:
having grasped the formless as "self," he regards that [self] as possessing form, like a tree possessing shade.
Or, regarding form as being in the self: having grasped the formless itself as "self," [he regards it as such].
One regards form as being in the self, just as one perceives fragrance in a flower.

Or, regarding the self as being in form—that is, having grasped the formless itself as "self"—one regards that self as being in form, like a gem within a casket. The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates.
In this context, when it is said, "one regards form as self," it is pure form alone that is spoken of as "self. When it is said, "possessing form..."
Or [he regards] the self as form, form as being in the self, or the self as being in form. He regards feeling as self...
perception... volitional formations... consciousness as self. In these seven instances, the formless is spoken of as "self.
Likewise, regarding the four aggregates: "or the self as possessing feeling, or feeling as being in the self, or the self as being in feeling," and so forth.

By way of each of the three [aggregates] across twelve positions, a self consisting of a mixture of form and formless [aggregates] is described. Among these, the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is described in five positions:
"one regards form as self," and likewise "one regards feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as self.
In the remaining positions, the view of eternalism (*sassatadṛṣṭi*) is described. Thus, there are fifteen [positions] here.

The five views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) are views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*). All of them should be understood as obstacles to the Path (*magga-āvaraṇa*), not as obstacles to heaven (*sagga-āvaraṇa*), and as being eradicated by the First Path (*paṭhama-magga-vajjha*).
"A forest-dweller" (*āraññiko*) means one who dwells in the forest. "In the woods" (*pavane*) means in a great, deep forest. "Wandering" (*caramāno*) means here and there.
"Wandering about": he goes with confidence, meaning he moves about fearless and free from apprehension. "Having come out of the range of the hunter":
having gone beyond the sight of the deer-hunter. "He brought Māra to an end": he brought either the Māra of the defilements (*kleśamāra*) or the Māra of the son of a god (*devaputramāra*) to an end.
"Having struck down the trackless": having slain and destroyed the track of the defilements. "The eye of Māra was rendered invisible."
"Gone" means he has reached a state beyond the range of Māra's sight. "Gone out of reach" means he has come before Māra's face.
The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta with the pinnacle of Arahantship itself, and at the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma exactly as described.
The explanation of the exposition on the Discourse to the Young Brahmin Mogharāja in the Sub-Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) to the *Cūḷaniddesa* of the *Saddhammappajjotikā* is completed. 16.
Explanation of the Exposition on the Discourse to the Young Brahmin Piṅgiya.

89. Regarding the exposition of the Piṅgiya Sutta in the sixteenth [chapter]: “I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded”—it is said that this brahmin was overcome by old age, being one hundred and twenty years from birth, and he was weak such that when he intended, “I will place my foot here,” he would place it elsewhere;
and his former skin-color had perished. Therefore he said: “I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded. May I not...
"May I not perish, deluded in the interval"—let it not be that I, having failed to realize your Dhamma, should perish in the interim through ignorance.

"The complete abandoning of birth and aging right here"—may I come to know the flavor of the Dhamma, Nibbāna, which is the complete abandoning of birth and aging right here at your feet, either at Pāsāṇaka or at the Cetiya; explain that to me.
"Powerless" means devoid of strength. "Weak" means having feeble strength. "Of little strength" means having limited strength. "Of little vigor" means having limited energy.
"Deprived of color" means one whose skin-color has changed. "Free from color" means one whose skin-color has departed.
"Color vanished" means one whose skin-color has become distant. "That former beautiful appearance" refers to that which was beautiful.
That beauty which existed in former times has now disappeared and vanished;
the danger has become manifest, meaning that calamity has appeared. Having established the reading "that former beautiful appearance," some explain it as "whatever beauty there was."
"Unclean" means unclean due to cataracts and the like. "Impure" means impure due to darkness (timira) and the like.
"Not thoroughly pure" means not thoroughly pure because it is completely enveloped by films, cataracts, and so forth. "Not bright" means it is not clear, though it resembles something clear.
"I do not see forms with the eye in such a way" means that I do not see or look at the object of form with the eye as I did with my former eye.
"In that same way, I do not see [it] now. The same method applies to the phrases "the ear is impure," and so forth. "May I not perish" means "may I not be destroyed.

90. Now, because Piṅgiya spoke thus—"I am old"—out of attachment to the body, the Blessed One uttered the verse beginning with "Having seen forms being afflicted," in order to cause him to abandon his affection for the body. Therein, "forms" (*rūpesu*)...
"By way of form as cause, by way of form as condition. "Being afflicted" means being oppressed by punishments such as those meted out for criminal acts.
"They are struck in forms" means that people are struck and tormented by eye diseases and so forth, due to form itself as the cause.
"They are slain" means they are executed. "They are afflicted" means they are harassed. "They are intensely afflicted" refers to [punishments] such as the cutting off of hands and feet.
They obtain [it]. "They afflict" means they undergo death. "They become disturbed" means they turn over.
"They oppress" means they fall into distress. "They strike" means they reach the state of being struck. "Afflicted by disease" means terrified.
"Dejected" means having fallen into mental distress. "Diverse" means perishing.

91. Having heard the practice taught by the Blessed One in this way, up to the stage of Arahantship, Piṅgiya, because he was weakened by old age and had not yet attained any distinction, again praised the Blessed One with the verse beginning, "The four directions," and requested further instruction. 92.
Then the Blessed One, once more showing him the path leading up to Arahantship, spoke the verse beginning, "Those overcome by craving."

*Taṇhādhipanna*: those who have been overcome by craving; those who stand having been liberated from craving. *Taṇhānugeta*: those who go along with craving. *Taṇhānugata*: those who follow after craving.
*Taṇhānusaṭa*: those who run together with craving. *Taṇhāya panne*: those submerged in craving. *Paṭipanna*:
those obstructed by craving. *Abhibhūta*: those who are crushed. *Pariyādinnacitta*: those whose wholesome minds have been exhausted and seized by craving.

"Santāpajātā" means one in whom mental anguish has arisen. "Ītijātā" means one in whom disease has appeared. "Upaddavajātā" means one in whom misfortune has arisen. "Upasaggajātā" means one in whom suffering has emerged. Regarding the phrase "virajaṃ vītamalaṃ":
here, "virajaṃ" means free from the dust of passion and so forth; "vītamalaṃ" means free from the stains of passion and so forth.
For passion and the like are called "dust" (rajo) in the sense of overwhelming, and "stain" (malaṃ) in the sense of defiling. "Dhammacakkhu" means the eye of the Dhamma.
In some cases it is the knowledge of the first path; in some cases, the first three path-knowledges; and in some cases, even the fourth path-knowledge.
Here, however, it is the fourth path-knowledge for the thousand jaṭilas, while for Piṅgiya it is only the third path-knowledge.
This refers to the state of one who proceeds by way of insight thus: "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease."
The meaning is that the Dhamma-eye arose. The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating specifically in Arahantship, and at the conclusion of the teaching, Piṅgiya was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala).
It is said that from time to time he thought: "Such wonderful eloquence indeed..."
“My maternal uncle Bāvari does not receive an opportunity to hear my teaching. Because of that distraction caused by affection, he was unable to attain *arahantship*.
However, his one thousand disciples, the matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭila*), attained *arahantship*;
they all became “come-hither” monks (*ehibhikkhu*), wearing robes and bowls produced through supernormal power (*iddhimaya*).
The commentary on the exposition of the *Piṅgiyamāṇavasutta* in the *Cūḷaniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*, titled *Saddhammappajjotikā*, is completed. 17.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Verses in Praise of the *Pārāyana*.
93. From this point on, the compilers of the collection, praising the teaching, said: "This the Blessed One spoke," and so forth.
Therein, "this he spoke" means he spoke this *Pārāyana*. "Of the sixteen attendants" means of the sixteen together with Piṅgiya, who was an attendant of Bāvari;
or, it refers to the sixteen attendants of the Buddha, the Blessed One—thus, "of the sixteen attendants."

And those very brahmins were seated there in the sixteen directions—six yojanas in front, six behind, six on the left side, and six on the right side—so that in a straight line they formed a distance of twelve yojanas. "Requested" (*ajjhiṭṭho*) means entreated.

94–97. "Having understood the meaning" (*atthamaññāya*) means having understood the meaning of the text (*pāḷiattha*). "Having understood the Dhamma" (*dhammamaññāya*) means having understood the text (*pāḷi*). "The Pārāyana" (*pārāyanaṃ*).
Having thus applied this designation to this discourse on the Dhamma, they spoke, enumerating the names of those brahmins:

"Ajita... [and so forth] ...approached the Best of Buddhas. In that context, "one whose conduct is perfected" means one who is endowed with the Pātimokkha virtue and so forth, which serve as the foundation for the state of Nibbāna.
"Isi" means a Great Sage (mahesi).

In the *Niddesa*, "they approached" (*upāgamiṃsu*) means they went near. "They came to" (*upasaṅkamiṃsu*) means they went to a place not far away. "They waited upon" (*payirupāsiṃsu*) means they sat down nearby.
"They questioned thoroughly" (*paripucchiṃsu*) means they brought forward thorough questions. "They grasped" (*parigaṇhiṃsu*) means they weighed [it]. Some say, "They reproached" (*codayiṃsu*).
"The accomplishment of virtue and conduct" (*sīlācāra-nibbatti*) means the accomplishment of supreme virtue and conduct; the meaning is the virtue produced by the Path (*magga*).
"Profound" (*gambhīra*) is a term that excludes the state of being shallow.

"Hard to see" (*duddasa*) means because it is profound, it is difficult to see; it must be seen with difficulty and cannot be seen easily. Precisely because it is hard to see, it is "hard to awaken to" (*duranubodha*);

it must be understood with difficulty and cannot be understood easily. "Peaceful" (*santa*) means extinguished (*nibbuta*). "Sublime" (*paṇīta*) means unsurpassed (*atappaka*). These two [terms] refer exclusively to the supramundane (*lokuttara*).

This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). "Beyond the reach of reasoning" (*atakkāvacara*) means that which is not to be traversed or fathomed by reasoning, but only to be traversed by direct knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
"Subtle" (*nipuṇa*) means delicate. "To be experienced by the wise" (*paṇḍitavedanīya*) means to be realized by the wise who have practiced correctly.
98. "He satisfied" (*tosesi*) means he brought them to a state of contentment. "He gladdened" (*vitosesi*) means he produced various kinds of joy in them. "He inspired confidence" (*pasādesi*)...

He caused their minds to become clear. "He won them over" (*ārādhesi*) means he won them over; he led them to attainment (*siddhi*). "He made them contented" (*attamane akāsi*) means he made them well-disposed by way of gladness (*somanassa*). 99.
"Thereafter they practiced the holy life" (*brahmacariyam acariṃsu*) means they practiced the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*). 101.
"Therefore it is called the *Pārāyana*"—it is said that this is the "going" (*āyana*) to that which has reached the further shore (*pāra*), namely, Nibbāna.
The commentary on the exposition of the verses of praise for the *Pārāyana* in the *Cūḷaniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*, titled *Saddhammappajjotikā*, is finished. 18.
Exposition of the verses of the *Pārāyanānugīti*.

102. This is the connection for those who will recite the *Pārāyana*: when the Blessed One had taught the *Pārāyana*, sixteen thousand matted-hair ascetics attained arahantship, and there was a penetration of the Dhamma by the remaining fourteen crores of gods and humans.
For this has been said by the ancients:
“Then, at the delightful Pāsāṇaka, during the assembly at Pārāyana,
the Buddha caused fourteen koṭis of living beings to attain the Deathless.
When the teaching of the Dhamma was concluded, the people who had come from here and there, through the power of the Blessed One, [attained their respective goals].

They appeared only in their own villages, towns, and so forth. The Blessed One also went to Sāvatthī, surrounded by many thousands of bhikkhus, including sixteen personal attendants. There, Piṅgiya paid homage to the Blessed One and said:
"Venerable sir, I shall go to announce the appearance of the Buddha to Bāvari; for it was to him that I promised. Then, by the Blessed One—
Having been permitted, he went to the banks of the Godhāvarī by means of his supernormal knowledge alone, and then proceeded on foot toward the hermitage.
As the brahmin Bāvarī sat watching the path, he saw him from afar approaching in the guise of a monk, free from his matted hair and carrying-pole;
seeing this, he reached the conclusion: "A Buddha has appeared in the world. And when [the Buddha] had arrived—
He asked him: “What, Piṅgiya, has a Buddha appeared in the world? “Yes, brahmin, he has appeared;
sitting at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine, he is teaching us the Dhamma, and I shall teach it to you.
