Then Bāvari, together with his assembly, honored him with great respect and prepared a seat. Having sat down there, Piṅgiya said: “I shall sing the *Pārāyana*,” and so forth.

In that regard, they will sing along with the Blessed One’s song; I too shall sing along. "As he saw" (*yathāddakkhi*) means as he himself saw through his own perfect awakening and his unique knowledge.
"Free from desire" (*nikkāmo*) means one who has abandoned desire. There is also a reading, "one who exerts effort" (*nikkamo*), which means one who possesses vigor.

Or, "one who has gone forth" (*nikkhanto*) from the side of the unwholesome. "One who is free from the forest" (*nibbano*) means one who is devoid of the forest of defilements, that is, one who is indeed free from craving.
Or: for what reason does he speak falsely? He shows that those defilements by which one might speak falsely have been abandoned by him.
By this, he generates enthusiasm in the brahmin for listening.
"Amala" means free from the stain of defilement (*kilesamala*). "Vimala" means the stain of defilement has departed. "Nimmaḷa" means purified of the stain of defilement.
"Free from stain" means he moves about having become distant from the stains of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Having abandoned stain" means he has abandoned the stains of the defilements.
"Released from stain" means released from the defilements. "Transcended all stains" means he has gone beyond all stains of the defilements, such as the residual impressions (*vāsanā*).
"Those forests" refers to these aforementioned types of defilements.
103. “Endowed with beauty” means endowed with virtue. 104. “He who is called by the name Truth”:
for the Buddha is indeed possessed of the name “Truth. “Brahmā”—with this he addresses that brahmin. In this context, “the world” (*loka*) is so called in the sense of breaking up (*lujjana*).
One world is the “world of existence” (*bhavaloka*), which is the kamma-result of the three planes. For it is said: “It comes to be (*bhavati*).”
"Bhava" (existence) means the world of existence, *bhavaloka*. Regarding the phrase "the world of existence and the world of origination," each of these consists of two types.

For the world of existence (*bhavaloka*) is twofold, by way of the existence of prosperity (*sampattibhava*) and the existence of adversity (*vipattibhava*). The world of origination (*sambhavaloka*) is also twofold, by way of the origination of prosperity and the origination of adversity.
Therein, the world of existence as prosperity is the world of happy destinies (*sugati*). For that is called a "beautiful world" because it consists of desirable fruits.

"Becoming" (*bhava*) means "existence"; excellence itself is becoming, thus "becoming of excellence" (*sampattibhava*). That very thing is the world, hence "the world of the becoming of excellence" (*sampattibhavaloka*).

"The world of the origin of excellence" (*sampattisambhavaloka*) refers to the karma that leads to the state of a Sugata. For that [karma] is the "origin" (*sambhava*) because the fruit arises from it;
the origin of excellence is "the origin of excellence," and that very origin of excellence is the world, thus "the world of the origin of excellence."

The "world of the state of misfortune" (*vipattibhavaloka*) is the world of the lower realms (*apāyaloka*). For that is called "misfortune" (*vipatti*) because it is a world of undesirable results and is deformed;

it is called "state" (*bhava*) because it comes into being (*bhavati*); thus, "misfortune itself as a state" is *vipattibhava*. "The world of the state of misfortune" is simply the world of that state of misfortune.

The "world of the origin of misfortune" (*vipattisambhavaloka*) refers to the karma leading to the lower realms. For that is called "origin" (*sambhava*) because the fruit originates (*sambhavati*) from it; it is the origin of misfortune.
The arising of misfortune; indeed, the world is the arising of misfortune, hence it is called "the world as the arising of misfortune.
"Three feelings" refers to pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—all of which are mundane. "Nutriments" means conditions.
For conditions are called "nutriments" (āhāra) because they bring about their own fruit. They are: edible food, contact as nutriment, mental volition as nutriment, and consciousness as nutriment.
There are four [nutriments]. It is called *kabaḷīkāra* because it is to be made into mouthfuls by way of its substance;

it is called *āhāra* because it is to be swallowed. This is the name for the nutritive essence (*ojā*) that has rice, boiled milk-rice, and so forth as its substance. For that [essence] brings in the eight types of material form consisting of nutritive essence, thus it is "nutriment" (*āhāra*).

The sixfold contact, beginning with visual contact, is called "nutriment" because it brings in the three kinds of feeling. Mental volition is "mental volition" (*manosañcetanā*) because it belongs to the mind, not to a being.

Just as one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*), or volition associated with the mind (*manosañcetanā*)—as in the expression "chariot of a thoroughbred horse"—refers to wholesome and unwholesome volitions belonging to the three planes of existence;
for that indeed brings about the three realms of existence (*bhava*), and thus it is nutriment (*āhāra*).

"Consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) refers to the nineteenfold rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*); for that brings about the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) of rebirth-linking, and thus it is nutriment.

“Aggregates of clinging” (*upādānakkhandhā*): aggregates that have clinging as their domain are “aggregates of clinging”; here, one should see the middle word omitted [as in *rāja-puriso*, “king’s man,” becoming *puriso*].
Alternatively, aggregates produced from clinging are “aggregates of clinging,” just as there is grass-fire or chaff-fire.
Or, aggregates subject to clinging are “aggregates of clinging,” just as there is a king’s man. Or, aggregates originating from clinging are “aggregates of clinging.”

Just as there are flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees, so too there are four types of clinging (*upādāna*): clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), and clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*).
In terms of meaning, however, clinging is "grasping intensely" (*bhusam ādānam*).

These are the aggregate of form subject to clinging (*rūpupādānakkhandha*), the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging (*vedanupādānakkhandha*), the aggregate of perception subject to clinging (*saññupādānakkhandha*), the aggregate of mental formations subject to clinging (*saṅkhārupādānakkhandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging (*viññāṇupādānakkhandha*).
Five. The six internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāni āyatanāni*) are: the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
The seven stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*) are exactly as previously described. Likewise, there are the eight worldly conditions (*lokadhammā*).
Moreover, these eight are: gain, loss, fame, disrepute, blame, praise, pleasure, and pain.
Because the world is subject to constant change while worldly activity persists, these are called "worldly conditions" (*lokadhammā*).
There is no being whatsoever that is free from them; they affect even the Buddhas. As it is said:
"Monks, these eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions."
“What eight? Gain and loss... pleasure and pain.
These, monks, are the eight worldly conditions that revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions.
In this context, “revolve around” means they follow along, they are not abandoned; the meaning is that they do not turn away from the world.
"Gain" (*lābha*) refers to the acquisition of robes and so forth for one who has gone forth, and the acquisition of wealth, grain, and so forth for a householder.
When that very gain is not obtained, it is called "loss" (*alābha*), meaning "not-gain. It is not, however, to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*) as having become a non-self (*attābhāva*).
"Fame" (*yasa*) refers to a retinue or following. When that very fame is not obtained, it is "infamy" (*ayasa*). "Censure" (*nindā*) is the speaking of dispraise. "Praise" (*pasaṃsā*) is—
The description of the colors. "Pleasure" refers to the bodily and mental [feeling] pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

"Pain" refers to the bodily and mental [feeling] of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*); for non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and arahants, it is only the bodily [feeling]. "Abodes of beings" (*sattāvāsa*) means the dwellings or places of residence of beings;
however, these are simply the aggregates (*khandha*) manifested in such a way. Among the seven stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), by means of the non-percipient being (*asaññasatta*)...
Together with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are nine abodes of beings. "Ten bases" refers to these ten:
the eye base, the form base, the ear base, the sound base, the nose base, the odor base, the tongue base, the taste base, the body base, and the tangible-object base.
"Twelve bases" refers to [the above] together with the mind base and the mental-phenomena base.
Together, there are thus twelve. Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*): the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element...
[and so on] ...the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element—by taking three for each [of the six bases], there are eighteen elements.

"Having a similar name" means having a name that expresses a single quality. "Called by a similar name" means being addressed by a name expressing a single quality. "Truly called by a similar name" means being addressed by a name expressing a single quality that is non-false and non-erroneous.
"Āsita" means approached. "Upāsita" means having approached, one has served [him]. "Payirupāsita" means having served him excessively by way of devotion.
(105) "Kubbanaka" means a small grove. "One might dwell in a forest with much fruit" means one might come and live in a forest filled with various kinds of many fruits and so forth.
"Appadassa" refers to those of limited wisdom, such as Bāvari and others. "Mahodadhi" refers to [lakes] such as Anotatta.
"A great mass of water.
"Of little vision" means those of dull vision. "Of limited vision" means those of extremely dull vision. "Of scant vision" means those who see even less than the limited.
"Of inferior vision" means those whose vision is base. "Of wretched vision" means those whose vision is insignificant.
*Chatukkadassā* means those who do not see the supreme. *Appamāṇadassā* means those who see the immeasurable, having transcended all measure, seeing Nibbāna.
*Aggadassā* means those who see the foremost, in the manner of the verse beginning, "Truly, those who have faith in the Foremost One... and so forth, seeing the foremost Dhamma.
*Seṭṭhadassā* means those who see the best, [thinking] "The Fully Enlightened One is the best among bipeds. *Viseṭṭhadassā* and the following four [terms] are likewise explained.
These [terms] are augmented by prefixes. *Asama* means "unequal" (*na samaṃ*), that is, the Omniscient One. *Asamasama* means equal to those who are unequal—the Buddhas of the past;
thus, he is "equal to the unequaled. *Appaṭisama* means devoid of anyone similar to himself. *Appaṭibhāga* means devoid of any counterpart or reflection of himself.
*Appaṭipuggala* means devoid of any rival person. *Devātideva* means the god beyond even the purified gods.
He is a bull (*usabha*) in the sense of being esteemed as supremely auspicious; a lion among men (*purisa-sīha*) in the sense of being fearless;
an elephant among men (*purisa-nāga*) in the sense of being faultless; a thoroughbred man (*purisa-ājāñña*) in the sense of being supreme;

a leader of men (*purisa-nisabha*) in the sense of standing in an unshakable position, unmoved by any adversary or enemy in the world with its devas, having trampled upon the earth of the eight assemblies; and a draft-ox among men (*purisa-dhorayha*) in the sense of bearing the yoke of teaching the Dhamma.
Or they remember it as "Mānasa," having thought of it with the mind and made it so, or simply by name.
Or they burn [it], for the moon and sun, while moving southward or northward, illuminate it through the gap between the mountains;
when moving directly [overhead], they do not illuminate it. For that very reason, the designation "Anotatta" arose for it. Such is Anotatta.
"Or a burning [fire]. "Unshakeable, immeasurable water": a mass of immeasurable water that cannot be moved.
"Even so" is the application of the simile: the Buddha, the Blessed One, is unshakeable and like a bull, impossible to move from his position.
"Immeasurable splendor": immeasurable splendor of knowledge. "Penetrating knowledge": by way of the ten powers of knowledge and so forth.
Knowledge of distinctions. "One with open eyes" means one with the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*).

"Skilled in the analysis of wisdom" means dexterous in knowing the divisions of wisdom according to the method beginning with, "What is wisdom? It is understanding, investigation, thorough investigation," and so forth.
"One who has attained the analytical knowledges" means one who has acquired the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). "One who has reached the four grounds of self-confidence."

“He has attained confidence regarding the four grounds stated in the manner beginning with: ‘For you who claim to be a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddha*), these things have not been fully realized’.
“Devoted to faith” means being intent upon and entered into the utterly pure consciousness of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
“The white individuality” refers to the perfectly pure, unique personal existence resulting from the complete abandonment of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
"Advayabhāṇin" means devoid of dual speech because its utterance is non-discriminative. "Tādin" means such-like, or one who is unshakable amidst the desirable and the undesirable.
"Tathāpaṭiñño" means one whose recognition is thus; that [one]. "Aparitta" means not small.
"Mahanta" means having attained greatness by transcending the three realms (the triple world).
"Profound" means difficult for others to enter. "Immeasurable" means immeasurable in the sense of being incomparable.

"Difficult to fathom" means difficult to penetrate. "Abounding in jewels" means abounding in the jewels of faith and so forth. "Equal to the ocean" means similar to the sea because it is a mine of jewels.
"Endowed with the sixfold equanimity" [means]: "Having seen a form with the eye..."
It is fulfilled by the sixfold equanimity according to the method stated: "He is neither elated nor dejected.
"Incomparable" (*atulam*) means devoid of measure, that which is impossible to weigh. "Vast" (*vipulam*) means exceedingly great. "Immeasurable" (*appameyyam*) means impossible to measure.
"Such as he is" (*taṃ tādīsam*) refers to the Blessed One, who is endowed with such qualities. "To those speaking ill, who speak of the path" (*pavadataṃ maggavādinam*).
The syntactical connection is: "among those who speak, those who discourse, and those who utter the highest discourse, they find him.
"Like Meru among mountains" means like Sineru among the peaks. "Like Garuḍa among birds" means like the Supaṇṇa among those born of the feathered race.
"Like a lion among beasts" means like the lion among quadrupeds. "Like the ocean among seas" means...
I reached the Supreme Victor, the Best of Buddhas, like one crossing the ocean in the midst of a vast sea.
(106) "Those who were before" means those who were in the past.

(107) "The dispeller of darkness, seated" means the dispeller of darkness who is seated. "Of abundant wisdom" means the banner of knowledge. "Of vast intellect" means one possessed of expansive wisdom.
In the *Niddesa*, "light-maker" (*pabhaṅkara*) means one who produces heat. "Luminosity-maker" (*ālokakara*) means one who produces the absence of darkness.
"Radiance-maker" (*obhāsakara*) means one who produces radiance, that is, light; thus, he is a radiance-maker. "Lamp-maker" (*dīpaṅkara*) means one who produces a light similar to a lamp.

"Torch-maker" (*padīpakara*) means one who produces a light similar to a torch. "Illumination-maker" (*ujjotakara*) means one who produces brilliance. "Splendor-maker" (*pajjotakara*) means one who produces brilliance throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions.
"Bhūripaññāṇo" means one whose knowledge is broad. "Ñāṇapaññāṇo" means one who is made manifest by knowledge. "Paññādhajo":
since wisdom is his banner in the sense of being raised high, he is "one whose banner is wisdom," just as in expressions such as "the banner is the mark of the chariot.

"Vibhūtavihārī" means one whose dwelling is manifest. (108) "Sandiṭṭhikaṃ akālikaṃ" means the fruit is to be seen by oneself; it is not a fruit to be attained at some other time. "Anītikaṃ" means free from the calamities of the defilements and so forth.

"Visible here and now" (*sanditthika*): the supramundane Dhamma which has been realized by one is "visible here and now" because it is to be seen by oneself through the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*), having abandoned the need to proceed on the strength of another's faith; that which is thus visible is *sanditthika*.
With reference to its giving of its own fruit, there is no [fixed] time for it, thus it is "timeless" (*akālika*); being timeless, it is *akālika*. That which is the noble path-dhamma herein—
The meaning is that it gives its fruit immediately after itself; thus, it is "timeless" (*akālika*).
It is "inviting one to come and see" (*ehi-passika*) because it deserves the method of "come and see" (*ehi-passa*) expressed as "Come, see this Dhamma.
It is "leading onward" (*opanayika*) because it deserves to be brought into one's own heart even by disregarding a burning garment or head; thus, it is "leading onward" (*opanayika*).

By all those—beginning with the one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement—it should be personally realized within each individual that "the path has been developed by me, the fruit has been attained, and cessation has been realized"; thus it is "to be personally realized by the wise.
(109) Then Bāvarī said to him: "What indeed from that... with two verses.

“Even for a moment” (*muhuttam-pi*) means even for a short while. “Even for an instant” (*khaṇam-pi*) means not for a long time. “Even for a second” (*layam-pi*) means even for a minute. “Even for a fraction” (*vayam-pi*) means even for a portion.
“Even for a duration” (*addham-pi*) means even for a day. 111–113. Then Piṅgiya, demonstrating that he would never be separated from the Blessed One, said:
“I do not [leave] him,” and so forth. “I do not... see him with mind or with eye” means that I see that Buddha with the mind, just as one might see with the physical eye (*maṃsa-cakkhu*).
"I see. "Worshipping, I spend the night"—I pass the night while indeed worshipping. 114.

"In that very direction I am bowed"—this shows that in whichever direction the Buddha is, in that very direction I too am bowed; it indicates that I am inclined toward him and leaning toward him. 115.

"Of one who is weak and lacking strength"—meaning of one who has little strength. Alternatively, it means of one who is weak and of poor constitution, or even of one who is deficient in power and energy.
This is what is meant. "Therefore the body does not flee" means that because of that very weakness and lack of strength, the body does not go;
it does not go toward where the Buddha is. There is also the reading "na pareti," which has the same meaning.
"Therein" means in the presence of the Buddha. "By way of intention" means by the movement of intention. "Joined with that" means joined with that [direction] toward where the Buddha is.
This shows that he is devoted and intent upon it.
"In the direction where the Buddha is": he does not go away in the direction from which the Buddha is to be approached;
or rather, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative. He does not go, he does not depart, to where the Buddha is. Not...
"He goes" means he does not go forward. "He does not walk" means he does not turn back. "He does not overstep" means he does not approach. 116.
"Lying in the mire" means lying in the mud of sensual desire (*kāma*). "Island after island they leap" means that from one teacher I went to another teacher.
Then I saw the Perfectly Enlightened One; thus, having adopted such a wrong view and wandering about, I—
Then, at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, I beheld the Buddha.
Therein, *semāno* means sitting; *sayamāno* means lying down; *āvasamāno* means dwelling; *parivasamāno* means dwelling constantly.
*Pallaviṃ* means I emerged; *upallaviṃ* means I went further; *sampallaviṃ* is a word expanded by a prefix.
They saw the introductory verse of the exposition. They saw means they perceived. They beheld means they looked upon.
They saw means they sought. They penetrated means they pierced through.
At the conclusion of this verse, the Blessed One, having understood the ripening of the faculties of both Piṅgiya and Bāvari, [spoke].

While remaining right there in Sāvatthī, he emitted a golden radiance. Piṅgiya, who was sitting and extolling the Buddha’s qualities to Bāvari, saw that radiance and, wondering "What is this?", looked around;
seeing the Blessed One standing as if before him, he announced to the brahmin Bāvari, "The Buddha has arrived. The brahmin rose from his seat and, with palms joined—

Having taken hold [of the branch], he stood there. The Blessed One, having radiated light and revealed himself to the brahmin, and perceiving what was suitable for both of them, addressed Piṅgiya alone and spoke this verse: “Just as it was with Vakkali.
Its meaning is as follows: just as the Elder Vakkali was devoted to faith, and reached Arahantship by means of faith alone as his primary vehicle.
Just as among the sixteen there was one named Bhadrāvudha, and just as there was Āḷavika-Gotama, even so you too should release your faith; then,

resolving through that faith and undertaking insight meditation by way of the method beginning with "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent," you will go to the further shore of the realm of death, which is Nibbāna— thus the teaching concludes with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

He brought it to completion. At the conclusion of the teaching, Piṅgiya was established in Arahatship, Bāvarī was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala), and five hundred disciples of the brahmin Bāvarī became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna).
In this context, *muñcassu* means "you should release"; *pamuñcassu* means "you should cause to release"; and *adhimuñcassu* refers to "resolute confidence" (*adhimokkha*) therein.
"Practice! Have conviction! means: "Arouse great respect. "All conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) are impermanent" is in the sense of their non-existence after having come to be.
"All conditioned phenomena are suffering" is in the sense of the nature of suffering. "All phenomena (*dhammā*) are non-self" is in the sense of being devoid of mastery.

118. Now, Piṅgiya, announcing his own confidence, said: "This is even more... and so forth. In that context, "possessed of eloquence" means endowed with the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).
“More and more” (*bhiyyo bhiyyo*) means higher and higher.
“Having directly known the supreme deities” (*adhideve abhiññāya*) means having understood the qualities that make one a supreme deity. “High and low” (*paroparaṃ*) means inferior and superior;

what is meant is that he knew all classes of phenomena that make for the state of a supreme deity, both for himself and for others. “Of those who profess themselves to be doubters” (*kaṅkhīnaṃ paṭijānataṃ*).
Of those who are still doubting, yet claim "we are free from doubt.

In the *Niddesa*, "of the questions of the Pārāyanika [Brahmins]" means of the inquiries of the Brahmins of the *Pārāyana*. "He makes an end" (*avasānaṃ karoti*) means he is the one who brings it to its conclusion.

"He makes a limit" (*koṭiṃ karoti*) means he is the one who establishes its boundary. "He makes a demarcation" (*sīmaṃ mariyādaṃ karoti*) means he is the one who defines its limits. "He makes a settlement" (*nigamaṃ karoti*) means...

"Parivaṭumakaro": he brought to completion. By saying "of the questions of Sabhiya," etc., it is shown that he brings to an end not only the questions of the brāhmaṇas of the *Pārāyanavagga*, but also the questions of the wanderer Sabhiya and others.
(120) "Asaṃhīraṃ": unshakable by lust and the other [defilements]. "Asaṅkuppaṃ": unshakeable, having the nature of being non-subject to change.

He speaks of Nibbāna with two phrases: "I shall certainly go" means that I will go with absolute certainty to that element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*); "I have no doubt in this" means that I have no doubt regarding this Nibbāna.

"Thus hold me as one whose mind is resolute"—by these words, Piṅgiya [expressed] his faith in himself through this exhortation of the Blessed One: "In this very way, you too shall release your faith."
Having thus aroused [faith] and being liberated by means of faith alone, he declared that very resolution of faith to the Blessed One, saying:
"Hold me as one whose mind is resolved. This is the intended meaning here:
"Just as you have spoken of me, so indeed hold me as one whose mind is resolved."
"Is not withdrawn" means that once grasped, it cannot be withdrawn. "A definitive statement" means a logical statement.
"A statement of establishment" means a statement of certainty. Whatever has not been stated here and there within this *Pārāyana-vagga* should be understood according to the method explained below.
The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the explanation of the verses of the *Pārāyanānugīti* in the *Cūḷaniddesa-aṭṭhakathā*,
titled *Saddhammappajjotikā*, is finished. The commentary on the *Pārāyanavagga* is finished.
The Exposition of the Rhinoceros Horn Sutta:
A Commentary on the Exposition of the Rhinoceros Horn Sutta.
1. Commentary on the First Chapter.
121. Following this, the opportunity has arrived for the commentary on the exposition of the *Khaggavisāṇasutta*.
Therein, we shall explain only the remaining portion of the verse beginning with “Having laid aside the rod toward all beings. Regarding that, “toward all” (*sabbesu*) means without exception.

“Beings” (*bhūtesu*) means sentient beings (*sattesu*). Here, although the word *bhūta* appears in the phrase “an offense of expiation regarding a being” (*bhūtasmiṃ pācittiyan*), [it refers here to sentient beings].
In such cases as these, where it exists: in the pentad of aggregates in passages such as, "Sāriputta, do you perceive this as 'it has come to be' (bhūta)?";
in the fourfold form consisting of the earth element and so forth, in passages such as, "Bhikkhu, the four great elements are the causes";

in those who have destroyed the taints, in passages such as, "And he who has become one who devours time (kālaghasa-bhūta)"; and in the passage, "All beings (bhūtā) in the world shall surely lay [the burden] down."
In such passages as “samussaya,” it refers to all sentient beings; in such passages as “bhūtagāmapātabyatāya,” it refers to trees and so forth;
and in such passages as “bhūtaṃ bhūtato pajānāti,” it applies to the category of beings starting from those below the Cātumahārājika realm.
However, here, without distinction, the beings born upon the earth, mountains, and so forth, should be understood as “beings” (bhūta). Among these:
"Among beings": *nidhāya* means having laid down.
"Staff" (*daṇḍa*) refers to the staff of body, speech, and mind; it is a designation for bodily misconduct and so forth.
For bodily misconduct is a "staff" because it punishes (*daṇḍati*); what is meant is that it afflicts and brings about ruin and calamity. The same applies to verbal misconduct.
And misconduct of the mind. Or rather, "the stick" refers specifically to the weapon; thus it is also said, "having laid aside that. "They do not harm" means not harming.
"Even one or another" means any single one whatsoever. "Of them too" means of all those beings.

"One should not desire as a son" means any one among these four types of sons: the son born of one's own womb (*atraja*), the son born of the field (*khetta-ja*), the son given (*dinna-ka*), and the pupil (*antevāsika*).
He would not desire a son; how much less a companion? For how could he even desire a companion?

He is "one" (eko) in the sense of being one through what is called renunciation, one in the sense of being without a second, one in the sense of having abandoned craving, one because his defilements have been entirely removed, and one because he has awakened to solitary enlightenment (paccekabodhi). For even if he were living in the midst of a thousand ascetics...
He is "one" because the fetters of household life have been severed; likewise, he is "one" by way of what is called the going-forth.

He is "one" because he stands alone, goes alone, sits alone, lies down alone, and conducts himself and carries out his duties alone. Thus, he is "one" in the sense of being without a second. As it is said:
"A person with craving as a companion wanders through the long journey."
“From this state to another state, one does not transcend saṃsāra.
Having understood such danger— that craving is the origin of suffering—
a bhikkhu should wander mindfully, free from craving and without grasping.”

Thus, in the sense of having abandoned craving, he is one. All his defilements have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future;

thus, in the sense of being entirely free from defilements, he is one. Having become teacherless, self-become, and awakened by himself to Pacceka-enlightenment, thus, in the sense of having awakened to Pacceka-enlightenment by himself, he is one.
One should practice these eight modes of conduct. Namely: the conduct of postures in the four postures for those endowed with aspiration;
the conduct of the sense bases in the internal sense bases for those who guard the doors of the senses;
the conduct of mindfulness in the four foundations of mindfulness for those dwelling in heedfulness; and the conduct of concentration in the four jhānas for those devoted to higher consciousness.
The conduct of knowledge regarding the four noble truths for those endowed with wisdom; the conduct of the path regarding the four noble paths for those who have practiced rightly;
the conduct of practice regarding the four fruits of recluseship for those who have attained the fruits;
and the conduct for the welfare of the world toward all beings by the three types of Buddhas, whereas for the Paccekabuddhas and disciples it is only partial. As it has been said:
“Conduct (*cariyā*)” means the eight modes of conduct, which are the modes of deportment (*iriyāpathacariyā*); this is the detailed explanation. The meaning is:

one should be endowed with those modes of conduct. Alternatively, regarding these [faculties]: “while resolving, one conducts oneself through faith; while exerting, one conducts oneself through energy;
while establishing, one conducts oneself through mindfulness; while being undistracted, one conducts oneself through concentration; while understanding, one conducts oneself through wisdom.”

“He practices; practicing with consciousness, he practices while cognizing. For one who has practiced thus, wholesome states flow toward him, so he practices by way of the practice of flowing (*āyatanacariyā*).
One who has practiced thus attains distinction, so he practices by way of the practice of distinction (*visesacariyā*)”—thus eight further modes of practice are stated.
The meaning is: “May he be endowed with these. “Like the rhinoceros horn” (*khaggavisāṇakappo*): the rhinoceros horn...
The name is *khaggamigasiṅga* (the horn of the rhinoceros deer).
Furthermore, this word *kappa* has many meanings, such as: conviction, conventional usage, time, designation, cutting off, alternative, trace, entirety, similarity, and so forth.
For instance, it is used in the passage: "This is to be accepted from Master Gotama, as it is for one who is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One."

In such instances as these, it has the sense of "firm conviction. In such passages as, "Monks, I allow you to consume fruit according to the five ascetic conventions," it has the sense of "convention" (*vohāra*).
In such passages as, "By which indeed I dwell for the entire duration of my life (*niccakappa*)," it has the sense of "time" (*kāla*).

In such passages as, "Thus spoke the Venerable Kappa," it has the sense of "designation" (*paññatti*). In such passages as, "Adorned, with hair and beard trimmed," it has the sense of... [the sense of "adornment"].
*Chedanaṃ* means cutting off. In such expressions as “the two-finger-breadth allowance is permitted,” it means an adaptation.
In such expressions as “there is the possibility of lying down,” it means a slight degree. In such expressions as “having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana grove,” it means pervasiveness on all sides.
In such expressions as “Indeed, sir, while consulting with a disciple who was like the Teacher himself, we did not realize [it],” it means a likeness or a counterpart.
This is the meaning. Here, however, the meaning should be understood as "its counterpart is similar," which is to say it is like the horn of a rhinoceros.
This, then, is the commentary on the meaning according to the words.
According to the underlying intention and the connection of the text, however, it should be understood as follows: this aforementioned kind of punishment, when being inflicted upon living beings...
He becomes one who is well-disposed; since those [unwholesome states] do not arise in him, and because he has laid aside the rod toward all beings by bestowing benefit through loving-kindness—
the very opposite of those states— and because he has laid aside the rod,
he does not harm beings with a rod, a sword, a hand, or a clod of earth, unlike those beings who, having not laid aside the rod, afflict other beings with rods, swords, hands, or clods.
"By resorting to this meditation subject of loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*) from among those [three], and having practiced insight (*vipassanā*) into whatever there was pertaining to feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as other formations following that very sequence, I have attained this Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*).
This, first of all, is the intended meaning.
This is the connection [of the narrative]: When this had been said, those ministers asked, "Now, venerable sir, where are you going?
Then, having reflected and understood—[asking himself], "Where do the former Paccekabuddhas dwell?"—and having replied, "On Mount Gandhamādana," they spoke again:
"Venerable sir, now leave us; we do not wish for you to go. Then the Paccekabuddha...
He said: "One should not desire a son," and so forth. Herein, this is the intended meaning:
"I do not now desire even any kind of son among my own offspring and the like; how much less a companion such as you?
Therefore, even among you, whoever wishes to go with me or desires to be like me, let him wander alone like the rhinoceros horn. Or alternatively:
When they said, "Venerable sir, please abandon us now; we do not wish [to stay]," that Paccekabuddha, saying, "One should not desire a son,
much less a companion," saw the virtue of the solitary life in the sense already described,
and being gladdened and filled with joy and happiness, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna).
In this context, "those" refers to those with clear vision (*vipassaka*). "The steadfast" refers to those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
"Terrors and horrors" refers to minor and trivial mental anxieties. "Having laid aside" means having discarded. "Having set down" means having placed.

"Having lowered" means having brought down. "Having fully lowered" means having released what had gone downward. "Having put away" means having removed from that place. "Having calmed" means having caused to settle.

"Addressing" (*ālapanam*) means speaking at the beginning. "Conversing" (*sallapanam*) means speaking properly. "Exalting" (*ullapanam*) means speaking by way of exaltation. "Exalting together" (*samullapanam*) means speaking repeatedly by way of exaltation.
"The conduct of the postures" (*iriyāpathacariyā*) means the conduct of the postures; the meaning is their manifestation. The same method applies to the others as well.

However, "conduct regarding the sense bases" (*āyatanacariyā*) is the conduct of mindfulness and clear comprehension with respect to the sense bases. "Attainments" (*pattiyo*) means fruits; for these are what are attained.

“Patti” (attainment) has been stated. The distinction is that the worldly aims of the world of sentient beings—both pertaining to the present life and the future life—are called “lokattha” (worldly aims).
Now, showing the ground for those types of conduct, he said, “In the four postures,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “in the foundations of mindfulness” (*satipaṭṭhānesu*):

although they are spoken of even as the foundations of mindfulness as objects (*ārammaṇa-satipaṭṭhāna*), they are not other than mindfulness; yet, by way of conventional usage, they appear as if they were other.

This was said having made [this distinction]. "In regard to the Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccesu*) is said by way of grasping each truth individually through mundane knowledge of the truths during the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).
"In regard to the Noble Paths and the Fruits of Asceticism" (*ariyamaggesu sāmaññaphalesu*) is also said merely by way of conventional designation (*vohāra*).

"From a partial standpoint" (*padesato*) means from one part of the conduct for the welfare of the world (*lokatthacariyā*); for only Buddhas perform the conduct for the welfare of the world in its entirety (*nippadesato*). Again, those same modes of conduct...
Showing [the distinction] by way of the individual as the agent, he said, "Those endowed with aspiration," and so forth.

In that context, "endowed with aspiration" means being endowed with the very postures for the sake of stability because of the composure of their postures; they possess unshakable postures, being endowed with peaceful postures befitting the state of a bhikkhu.

"Guardians of the doors of the sense-faculties" (*indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ*): among the six sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth, those for whom each individual door is guarded against the arising [of unwholesome states] when it functions toward its respective object, by way of each single door, are "guardians of the doors"; [the phrase refers to] those guardians of the doors. And here, "doors" refers specifically to the eye and so forth, by way of being the doors for the arising [of consciousness].
"Dwelling in heedfulness" (*appamādavihārīnaṃ*): those who possess the practice of dwelling in heedfulness regarding virtue (*sīla*) and the other [bases of training].
"To those devoted to higher consciousness" means to those devoted to concentration, which is termed "higher consciousness," by way of being the foundation for insight (vipassanā).
"To those endowed with wisdom" means to those endowed with the knowledge that proceeds from the discernment of name-and-form up to the stage of the lineage (gotrabhu).
"To those who have practiced rightly" refers to the moment of the four paths. "To those who have attained the fruit" refers to the moment of the four fruits.
"Tathāgatānaṃ" means "of those who have come thus. "Arahantānaṃ" means "of those whose defilements are far removed.
"Sammāsambuddhānaṃ" means "of those who have perfectly and individually awakened to all phenomena. The meaning of these terms has already been explained above.
"Padesato paccekabuddhānaṃ" means "of the Paccekabuddhas in part," that is, from one perspective. "Sāvakānaṃ" means "of the disciples as well."
"In part. "Resolving" means exercising resolve. "Proceeding by way of faith" means occurring through the influence of faith.
"Exerting" means striving with the energy of the four right efforts. "Establishing" means establishing the object of mindfulness through mindfulness.
"Bringing about non-distraction" means not allowing distraction to occur through the power of concentration. "Understanding" means...
"Knowing in the manner of the wisdom that knows the Four Truths.

"Discerning" means discerning the object by means of the advertence-consciousness (*āvajjana-viññāṇa*) preceded by the impulsion (*javana*) associated with the faculties. "By the course of consciousness" means by way of the course of the advertence-consciousness.
"Of one who has thus practiced" means of one who has practiced by way of the course of the faculties together with the advertence. "Wholesome states bring [him] forth" means...
Wholesome states occurring by way of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) "sustain" (yāpenti) intensely; the meaning is that they proceed.
"By the practice of the bases" (āyatanacariyāya) means by the intense practice of the bases of wholesome states;

what is meant is "by the practice of their occurrence. "He attains distinction" means by way of suppression (vikkhambhana), substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), eradication (samuccheda), and tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi).
One attains distinction.

Regarding the phrases "the practice of seeing" (*dassanacariyā*) and "right view" (*sammādiṭṭhi*), it is called right view because one sees rightly, or because one sees rightly by means of it, or because it is a praised and beautiful view. The "practice of seeing" consists in making that right view directly manifest as *nibbāna*.
It is *sammā-saṅkappa* because one intends rightly, or they intend rightly by means of it, or it is a commendable and beautiful intention;
it is the mental activity of directing the mind toward its object. It is *sammā-vācā* because one speaks rightly, or they speak rightly by means of it, or speech is commendable and beautiful;
this is the name for the abstention from wrong speech. Its activity consists in being embraced by the fourfold restraint of speech.

One acts rightly, or they act rightly by means of it, or it is a praiseworthy and beautiful action; thus it is right action (*sammākamma*). Right action itself is the "right course of action" (*sammākammanta*);
this is the name for the abstention from wrong courses of action. Its conduct arises from the threefold restraint of the body.

One lives rightly, or they live rightly by means of it, or it is a praiseworthy and beautiful livelihood; thus it is right livelihood (*sammāājīva*). [This is the name for] the abstention from wrong livelihood.
This is the name. Its practice of purification is the practice of purity. One exerts oneself rightly, or they exert themselves rightly by means of that;
it is a lauded or beautiful exertion, thus it is right effort (*sammāvāyāma*); its practice is the practice of exertion. One remembers rightly, or they remember rightly by means of that;
it is lauded or beautiful mindfulness, thus it is right mindfulness (*sammāsati*); its practice is the practice of establishment. Rightly...
It is "right concentration" (*sammāsamādhi*) because one becomes concentrated by means of it, or because they are rightly concentrated by it, or because it is praised or beautiful as a concentration;
its function is non-distraction.

It is called "reasoning" (*takka*) because it is fashioned (*kappa*) by that [reasoning]; the meaning is "of such a kind. It is "like that" (*tassadisa*) because it resembles that; or alternatively, it is "of that sort" (*tassadika*).
The reading is *tappaṭibhāgo*. "Its counterpart" (*tappaṭibhāgo*) means that which has a counterpart to it; the sense is "of such a kind.

"Excessively salty" (*atiloṇaṃ*) is salt that has transcended [the limit of] sweetness. "Salt-like" (*loṇakappo*) is said to be similar to salt. "Excessively bitter" (*atitittakaṃ*) is that which has transcended bitterness;

"bitter-like" (*tittakakappo*) is said to be similar to the bitter [pungent] substances such as *pucimanda* (nimba). "Excessively sweet" (*atimadhuraṃ*) refers to things such as milk-rice (*khīrapāyāsa*). "Snow-like" (*himakappo*)...
"Like water mixed with milk. "Equal to the Teacher" means equal to the Buddha, the Teacher. "In this very way" is the application of the simile.
In this regard, having shown the method for explaining the insight (*vipassanā*) of this Paccekabuddha in brief, we shall proceed.
Therein, desiring to perform the discernment of mind-and-body (*nāmarūpa-pariggaha*), the Paccekabodhisatta—among the eight attainments of the fine-material and immaterial realms—whatever...

Having entered a certain jhāna and emerged from it, he delimits the jhāna factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth, as well as the states associated with them such as contact (*phassa*) and the rest, by way of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), functions (*rasa*), manifestations (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), and proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*).

He then defines them thus: "All this is called 'mentality' (*nāma*) in the sense of bending, because it bends toward the object. Then, while seeking its condition, [he sees] the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).
He sees that [consciousness] occurs dependent [on them]. Then, having seen both the bases as conditions and the derived material forms, he discerns:
"All this is 'form' (rūpa) because of its susceptibility to change (ruppana).

Then, he defines name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in brief thus: "Name has the characteristic of bending; form has the characteristic of change. This is according to the method for those whose vehicle is serenity (samatha-yānika).
It has been said. However, one who takes insight (vipassanā) as his vehicle, having delimited the primary and derived material phenomena by means of the analysis of the four elements, sees:
"All this is material form (rūpa) because of its capacity to be affected (ruppana).

Consequently, the immaterial states (arūpadhammā) that arise in dependence upon the eye and so forth—which have thus been delimited as material form—come into range. Then, all those immaterial states [are seen] by way of the characteristic of bending (namana).
Having grouped them together, one sees, "This is such-and-such," and thus defines them in two ways: "This is name, this is form.
Having defined them in this way, one sees: "Apart from name and form, there is no other being, person, deva, or Brahmā.
For just as when the collection of parts exists, there is the designation "chariot";
Thus, while the aggregates exist, there is the conventional designation "a being.
In the same way, while the five aggregates of clinging exist, there is the mere worldly usage of "a being" or "a person.
By means of such a method, through the knowledge that constitutes purification of view—defined as seeing name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as it truly is—one [discerns] name-and-form.
Having discerned [the aggregates], and further discerning their conditions, he discerns name-and-form according to the method already stated.
Then, searching with the thought, "What indeed is the cause of this?", and seeing the fault in theories of no-cause and irregular causes,
he— like a physician who, upon seeing a disease, searches for its primary cause and origin— discerns its cause and condition.

Searching [for the conditions], he sees that ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma—these four phenomena—are called "causes" because they are the conditions for the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);
and he sees nutriment as a "condition" because it is a condition for its support.
For these three phenomena beginning with ignorance are the supporting bases for this body like a mother to a child, while kamma is like a father to a son.
The producer; nutriment is like a nurse who sustains a child.

Having thus analyzed the conditions for the material body, he further analyzes the conditions for the mental body (nāmakāya) according to the method beginning with: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.
Analyzing in this way, he understands: "Past and future phenomena also proceed in exactly this same manner."
He makes a definitive conclusion.
Regarding that, the fivefold doubt concerning the past which was stated—namely, "Did I exist in the past?
Did I not exist? What was I? How was I? Having been what, did I become what in the past?"—is [abandoned].

Furthermore, regarding the future, the fivefold doubt has been stated as: "Shall I exist in the future? Or shall I not exist? What shall I become? How shall I become? Having been what, what shall I become in the future?"
Furthermore, whatever sixfold doubt regarding the present time has been stated—such as being perplexed about the present, thinking:
"Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? From where has this being come?
Where will he go?"—all that is abandoned by means of the discernment of conditions. Thus, through the discernment of conditions...

The knowledge that stands having overcome doubt regarding the three periods of time is called "purity by overcoming doubt," "knowledge of the stability of phenomena," "knowledge of things as they really are," and "right vision.
In this context, there are indeed three mundane thorough knowledges: thorough knowledge as the known, thorough knowledge as investigation, and thorough knowledge as abandoning. Therein—

“Wisdom that proceeds by way of discerning the individual characteristics of various phenomena— such as ‘matter has the characteristic of being afflicted (ruppana), feeling has the characteristic of being experienced (vedayita)’—

is called full understanding through knowledge (ñātapariññā). However, wisdom consisting of insight (vipassanā) that takes characteristics as its object proceeds by attributing the general characteristics to those very same phenomena according to such methods as ‘matter is impermanent, feeling is impermanent.’”

This is called full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*). Furthermore, the wisdom that consists in insight (*vipassanā*) having the characteristics [of phenomena] as its object, which occurs by way of abandoning the perception of permanence and so forth regarding those very same phenomena, is called full understanding by abandoning (*pahānapariññā*).

Among these, the stage beginning from the delimitation of formations (*saṅkhārapariccheda*) up to the discernment of conditions (*paccayapariggaha*) belongs to full understanding by knowing (*ñātapariññā*). For in this...
In the interval [between these], there is the predominance of the penetration of the individual characteristics (*paccatta-lakkhaṇa*) of phenomena alone.

From the stage of comprehension by groups (*kalāpa-sammasana*) up to the contemplation of rise and fall (*udaya-bbaya-anupassanā*), this is the plane of full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*). For in this interval, there is the predominance of the penetration of the general characteristics (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*) alone.
From the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅga-anupassanā*) onwards, it is the plane of full understanding through abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*). And beyond that...
For starting from that point, one who contemplates as impermanent abandons the perception of permanence; contemplating as suffering, the perception of pleasure;
contemplating as non-self, the perception of self; becoming disenchanted, delight; becoming dispassionate, lust; causing cessation, origination;
and relinquishing, grasping—one thus abandons these seven [fetters], which are the means for abandoning the perception of permanence and so forth.

the predominance of the contemplations. Thus, because the delimitation of formations and the discernment of conditions have been accomplished within these three kinds of full understanding, this practitioner has attained the full understanding by knowing (*ñāta-pariññā*).
Furthermore: "Whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external... [etc. ...whether far..."
Or near—at hand—every form is impermanent because of its non-existence after having come to be;
it is suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away; it is non-self because it is not subject to one's control. Whatever feeling... whatever perception... whatever formations...
whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or...
"Whether refined or coarse, far or near, all consciousness, having come to be, is impermanent because of its non-existence;
it is suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away; it is non-self because it is not subject to one's control. In such a manner he performs the comprehension of aggregates.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "having applied the three characteristics."
Having thus performed the comprehension of the aggregates by way of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, he again sees only the arising and passing away of formations. How?
"With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form; with the arising of craving, karma, and nutriment, there is the arising of form.
Thus, by seeing the dependence of the aggregate of form upon conditions, he sees the arising of the aggregate of form—its characteristic of production.
Even while passing by, one sees the arising of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). Thus, in five ways, one sees the arising of the aggregate of form.

By seeing the cessation of conditions—thinking, "With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of form; with the cessation of craving, karma, and nutriment comes the cessation of form"—one sees the passing away of the aggregate of form.
Furthermore, even while seeing its characteristic of change, one sees the passing away of the aggregate of form.
"He sees" means that he thus sees the fall of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) in five ways.
Likewise, by seeing its dependence on conditions—namely, "with the arising of ignorance there is the arising of feeling;

with the arising of craving, karma, and contact, there is the arising of feeling"—he sees the rise of the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha); and even when seeing its characteristic of production, [he sees it].
One sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling. By seeing the cessation of conditions—thinking, "With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of feeling;
with the cessation of craving, karma, and contact comes the cessation of feeling"—one sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling.
One also sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling by seeing its characteristic of change. The same applies to the aggregate of perception and the others.
But this is the distinction: in the place of contact for the consciousness aggregate, one should apply the phrases "with the arising of name-and-form" and "with the cessation of name-and-form.

Thus, for each aggregate, there are ten [contemplations] by way of seeing the rise and fall through the condition's arising, the characteristic of production, the condition's cessation, and the characteristic of change.

Having performed the ten [tasks], fifty characteristics have been stated. By means of these, one attends to the matter in detail according to both conditionality and momentariness, thinking: "In this way too there is the arising of form; in this way too there is the passing away of form.
As he attends in this manner, his knowledge becomes clear: "Indeed, it seems that these phenomena, having not been, come to be; having been, they vanish."
It occurs thus: "In this way, indeed, these phenomena that have not yet arisen come into being, and having arisen, they cease. Thus, formations appear as ever-new.

Not only are they ever-new, but like a dewdrop at sunrise, like a bubble on water, like a line drawn with a stick on water, like a mustard seed on the point of an awl, and like a flash of lightning, they endure for only a brief moment.
They appear as being without core and devoid of substance, like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a circle of fire, a city of Gandharvas, a bubble, a plantain trunk, and so forth.

At this point, by means of the wisdom of comprehension (*sammasanapaññā*), he has penetrated the characteristics [of formations] in the manner of: "Only that which is subject to fall arises, and what has arisen passes away"; thus he stands in the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*).
First, the knowledge of insight that is still immature is attained. Through the attainment of which, one comes to be reckoned as "one who has commenced insight.

Then, in that clansman who has commenced insight, ten imperfections of insight arise: illumination, knowledge, rapture, tranquility, bliss, resolve, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and attachment. Herein, illumination...
At the moment of insight (vipassanā), because of the strength of knowledge, the blood settles; by that, a mental effulgence (cittobhāsa) is produced.
Seeing this, an unskilled practitioner thinks, "The Path has been attained by me," and relishes that very effulgence. The knowledge is also just insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa).
As one comprehends (sammasati) formations, that knowledge proceeds having become pure and serene. Seeing that, as before—
“He relishes it as ‘the path. The rapture (*pīti*) is indeed the rapture of insight (*vipassanā-pīti*).
For at that moment, fivefold rapture arises for him. “Tranquility” (*passaddhi*) is the tranquility of insight.
At that time, there is no distress, no heaviness, no rigidity, no unwieldiness, no sickness, and no crookedness of body or mind. There is also bliss (*sukha*).
It is indeed the bliss of insight (vipassanā-sukha). It is said that at that time, an exceedingly refined bliss arises, permeating his entire body.
Resolve (adhimokkha) is the faith (saddhā) active at the moment of insight; for at that moment, there arises a powerful faith that is an extreme state of clarity within the mind and mental factors.
Exertion (paggaha) is the energy (vīriya) associated with insight.
For at that moment, energy arises that is neither lax nor over-exerted, but well-sustained.
"Establishment" refers to mindfulness associated with insight; for at that moment, mindfulness arises well-established. Equanimity is twofold by way of insight-attention (*vipassanā-āvajjana*);
for at that moment, there arises that which is called equanimity of insight, being neutral toward the grasping of all conditioned formations.
Knowledge arises with strength, as does the equanimity of adverting at the mind-door. And that [equanimity] flows forth, becoming keen and sharp, for one who adverts to this or that object.
"Attachment" refers to attachment to insight (*vipassanā-nikanti*).

For when one forms an attachment toward the illumination and so forth, a subtle and peaceful form of attachment arises. Herein, the illumination and so forth, by virtue of being the basis for defilements—
They are called "defilements" (upakkilesa) not because they are unwholesome (akusala). However, attachment (nikanti) is both a defilement and a basis for defilement.
But a wise bhikkhu, when the illumination (obhāsa) and other signs arise, does not fall into distraction; rather, he recognizes: "The states such as illumination are not the Path;
rather, the insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that has entered the right course and is free from defilements is the Path. Thus, [he discerns] the Path...
And he defines what is not the path. The knowledge established by him in this way—having understood, "This is the path;
this is not the path"—is called purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.

From here on, the knowledge of insight that has reached its culmination by means of the eight knowledges of insight, and the ninth, the knowledge in conformity with the truths, is this purification by knowledge and vision of the way.

These eight knowledges are as follows: knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall, knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, knowledge of appearance as terror, knowledge of contemplation of danger, knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment, knowledge of desire for deliverance, knowledge of reflective contemplation, and knowledge of equanimity towards formations.
The ninth is called "knowledge in conformity with the truths," which is the name for *anuloma* (conformity).
Therefore, one who desires to accomplish that should apply himself to these knowledges, beginning with the knowledge of rise and fall which is free from defilements.
For when one sees rise and fall, the characteristic of impermanence becomes manifest as it truly is;
and for one who sees the oppression by rise and fall, the characteristic of suffering [becomes manifest], according to the words: "Only suffering comes to be; suffering..."
And one perceives the characteristic of non-self in the thought, "It stands" or "it moves.
Herein, this distinction should be understood: the impermanent has the characteristic of impermanence, the painful has the characteristic of pain, and the non-self has the characteristic of non-self.
In that context, "the impermanent" refers to the five aggregates. Why? Because they possess the nature of arising, passing away, and change.

Or [it is impermanence] because of its non-existence after having existed. "Change" (*aññathatta*) is indeed aging (*jarā*). The characteristic of impermanence (*aniccalakkhaṇa*) consists in arising, passing away, and change;

or it is a transformation of mode characterized by non-existence after having existed. Because of the statement, "That which is impermanent is suffering," that same pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) is suffering.
Why? Because of constant oppression. The mode of constant oppression is the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇa*). "That which..."
Because of the statement, "It is suffering; it is non-self," that very pentad of aggregates is non-self. Why? Because of the lack of mastery over them.
The mode of lacking mastery is the characteristic of non-self. These three characteristics become the objects of one who sees rise and fall.
Furthermore, he contemplates material and immaterial phenomena as "impermanent" and so forth; for him, formations [arise] very rapidly.
When they come into range, then—without making arising, stability, occurrence, the sign, or the object a basis—the mind remains established in the very cessation of their exhaustion and passing away;
this is called the knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅga-ñāṇa*). From the moment of arising onwards, this practitioner [reflects]:
"Just as these conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) break up and cease, so too was the state of conditioned phenomena in the past."
"It has broken up in the past and it will break up in the future"—thus he stands contemplating cessation alone.

As he cultivates and develops this knowledge of contemplation of dissolution, formations that differentiate all states of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations, and abodes of beings appear as a great terror, like a pit of glowing embers and the like. This is called the knowledge of the appearance of terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*).

As he cultivates that knowledge of the appearance as terror, all states of existence and so forth appear to him like glowing embers, like an uplifted sword, like an enemy, providing no refuge and fraught with danger. This is called the knowledge of contemplation of danger.
As he thus sees formations as dangerous, because of the danger inherent in formations even within the realms of existence and so forth...
The arising of weariness and lack of delight toward volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) is called the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā-ñāṇa*).
For one who is disenchanted with and weary of all volitional formations, there arises from that state a desire to be freed from and a desire to escape from those formations;
this is called the knowledge of the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*). Furthermore, in order to be freed from those very formations...
The knowledge that investigates by applying the three characteristics to formations through the knowledge of contemplation of reflection is called the knowledge of contemplation of reflection.

Having thus applied the three characteristics and comprehended formations, because he has clearly seen the characteristic of non-self in them, he does not grasp at them as "self" or "belonging to self.
Abandoning both fear and delight toward formations, he [contemplates] within formations...

He is indifferent and neutral; he does not grasp at "I" or "mine," and is equanimous toward the three realms of existence—this is called the knowledge of equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*).
Furthermore, if he perceives the state of peace, Nibbāna, as peaceful, he relinquishes the entire process of conditioned formations.

It leaps forward, inclining toward Nibbāna. If it does not see Nibbāna as peace, it continues to proceed with formations as its object alone, by way of the threefold contemplation—either as "impermanence," "suffering," or "non-self.
And while persisting in this way, it remains having attained the state of being the gateway to the threefold liberation.
For the three contemplations are called "the three gateways to liberation. Thus, one who attends to things as impermanent and is abundant in resolution attains the signless liberation;
one who attends to them as suffering and is abundant in tranquility attains the desireless liberation;
and one who attends to them as non-self and is abundant in wisdom attains the void liberation.
And here, "the signless liberation" refers to the Noble Path that proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object in its aspect of signlessness.
For it is "signless" because it has arisen in the signless element, and it is "liberation" because it is freed from the defilements.
By this same method, that which proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object in its aspect of desirelessness is "desireless," and [that which proceeds] in its aspect of emptiness...
It should be understood as "emptiness" (suññatā) when it occurs having Nibbāna as its object.
For a clansman who has thus attained equanimity regarding formations, insight has reached its culmination. This very [insight] is called "insight leading to emergence.
As he cultivates that knowledge of equanimity toward formations, an even sharper equanimity toward formations arises.
Thinking, "Now the path will arise," he comprehends formations as "impermanent," "suffering," or "non-self" and enters the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

Immediately after the life-continuum, mind-door adverting consciousness arises by attending to them in the aspect of impermanence and so forth, according to the method already described for equanimity regarding formations. For one who attends in that very way, first—
The impulsion consciousness arises. That which is called "preliminary work" (parikamma) is followed immediately by that same second impulsion consciousness arising.
That which is called "access" (upacāra) is likewise followed immediately by that same third impulsion consciousness arising.
That which is called "adaptation" (anuloma) is distinct from these.
In general, however, all three of these—namely, repetition, preparation, access, and conformity—are called "repetition," "preparation," "access," and "conformity.
This knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), moreover, is the conclusion of insight (*vipassanā*) that leads to emergence and has formations as its object;
but in the ultimate sense, it is only the change-of-lineage knowledge (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) that is called the conclusion of insight. From that...

Taking supreme Nibbāna as its object, transcending the lineage of the worldling, and entering the lineage of the noble ones, the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhu-ñāṇa) arises; it is the first act of attention directed toward the object of Nibbāna and is irreversible.

However, this knowledge does not belong either to the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi) or to the purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).

In the interval, it is simply beyond description. Because it has fallen within the stream of insight (*vipassanā*), it is designated as either "purification by knowledge and vision of the way" (*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi*) or simply "insight" (*vipassanā*).

When the change-of-lineage knowledge (*gotrabhuñāṇa*)—which takes Nibbāna as its object—has ceased, one takes Nibbāna as the object through the perception provided by that [knowledge], thereby abandoning the fetter of views (*diṭṭhisaṃyojana*) and the fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojana*).
Regarding the fetter of doubt (*vicikicchā-saṃyojana*): the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) arises, shattering the three fetters.
Immediately thereafter, two or three fruition-consciousnesses (*phala-citta*), which are the results of that very path, arise because supramundane wholesome states have immediate fruition.

At the conclusion of the fruition, having interrupted the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) that has arisen, there occurs mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*) for the purpose of reviewing.
It arises. For he reviews the path, thinking, "By this very path indeed have I come.
Then he reviews the fruit, thinking, "This benefit has been obtained by me. Then he reviews the defilements abandoned, thinking, "These specific defilements have been abandoned.
Then he reviews the defilements remaining, thinking, "These specific defilements still remain," namely those to be abandoned by the three higher paths.
And at the conclusion [of each fruit], one reviews the deathless Nibbāna, thinking: "This Dhamma has been realized by me.
Thus, there are five reviews for a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer. Likewise at the conclusion of the fruits of once-returning and non-returning.
At the conclusion of the fruit of arahantship, there is no review of remaining defilements. In this way, there are nineteen reviews in total.

Having reflected in this way, that practitioner of yoga, seated on that very seat, having practiced insight (vipassanā) according to the method described, attains the second path while thinning out sensual lust and ill will; immediately thereafter, he likewise attains the fruit according to the method described.
Then, having practiced insight according to the method described, he brings about the complete abandonment of sensual lust and ill will without remainder.

He attains the third path and, in the manner described, the fruit thereof. Then, having practiced insight in that very same sitting in the manner described, he attains the fourth path by abandoning attachment to the fine-material realm, attachment to the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance without remainder, and he attains the fruit thereof in the manner described.
At this point, he becomes an Arahant, one whose great taints are destroyed, a Paccekabuddha. Thus, among these—
Knowledge regarding the four paths is called purification by knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*).

Up to this point, there has been purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*), because through the passage "having laid aside the rod toward all beings, not harming even one of them," the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha and so forth was described.
Through the passage "one should desire neither a son, much less a companion," by way of avoiding aversion and attachment...

Because loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the other [immeasurables] are mentioned, there is purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*). However, because the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpapariggaha*) and so forth are mentioned by the verse, “One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn,” the seven purifications are thereby stated:

purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*), purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*), purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (*maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi*), purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi*), and purification by knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*).
This is merely an indication of the beginning here.
However, one who desires a detailed account should consult the *Visuddhimagga* and learn from it. Up to this point, this Paccekabuddha has fulfilled the verse:
“He is impartial toward the four quarters and free from resentment; content with whatever comes his way;
undaunted and enduring all dangers; he should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.”
"Having attained a state worthy of praise and so forth, he dwelt adorning Mount Gandhamādana"—thus it is in all instances.
This concludes the commentary on the explanation of the first verse. 122.

In the second [verse], "of one born into association" (*saṃsaggajāta*) means of one who has come into association. Therein, by way of seeing, hearing, conversing with the body, and sharing enjoyments—

There are five kinds of association (*saṃsagga*). Among these, "association by seeing" (*dassana-saṃsagga*) refers to lust arising through the process of the eye-consciousness continuum upon seeing one another.

In this regard, there was the daughter of a householder in the village of Kāḷadīghavāpī on the island of Siṃhala who, having seen a young bhikkhu residing at Kalyāṇavihāra while he was wandering for alms, became infatuated with him; yet, failing to obtain him by any means, she passed away.
Seeing a fragment of her lower garment, he thought, "He did not obtain cohabitation with one who wears such clothing," and having his heart torn asunder, he died; that very youth is the illustration.

Furthermore, upon hearing the excellence of form and so forth being described by others, or the sounds of laughter, talk, singing, or music produced by oneself, by way of the cognitive process of auditory consciousness—

The arising of lust is what is called "association with hearing. In that regard, the dweller of the Five-Door Cave, while traveling through the air, heard the sound of a smith’s daughter living in a mountain village who, having gone to a lotus pond with five young women, bathed, placed a garland upon her head, and was singing loudly;
through lust for sensual pleasure, he fell away from his meditative absorption and met with ruin and disaster.
The young monk Tissadaha is the illustration.
Sexual contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*) refers to the arising of lust through the mutual touching of limbs;
here, the young bhikkhu Dhammagāyana is the illustration. It is said that while a young bhikkhu was preaching the Dhamma at the Mahāvihāra, there was a great crowd of people present.
When he arrived, the king also went there together with his harem.

Then, upon perceiving the prince’s form and voice, a powerful passion arose in the king’s daughter and in that youth as well. Seeing this, the king took notice and had them enclosed by a curtain-screen;
they touched one another and embraced. Again, having removed the curtain-screen, they looked at each other.
"I saw both of them already dead.
However, when passion arises during mutual conversation and discourse, it is called "contact through conversation.
When passion arises while using things in common with monks and nuns, it is called "contact through communal enjoyment. And in both of these cases, [it occurred] at the Maricavaṭṭi Monastery.
The monk and the nun serve as the illustration. It is said that during the festival of the Maricavaṭṭi Mahāvihāra, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya, having prepared a great almsgiving, served both Saṅghas.
There, when hot rice gruel was being distributed, a nine-year-old novice nun gave a tooth-bracelet to a nine-year-old novice monk who had no supporter and engaged him in conversation.
Having both received full ordination (*upasampadā*), they became sixty years old and went to the opposite shore. Through conversation with one another, they regained their former recognition;
immediately thereafter, having developed affection for each other, they transgressed the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) and became those who have committed a defeat (*pārājika*).
Thus, among the five kinds of association (*saṃsagga*), through whichever association one has become associated, affection arises due to the condition of prior passion.
Strong lust arises. Then, following upon that affection, this suffering comes into being;

as one pursues that very affection, this suffering—which consists of various forms such as sorrow and lamentation pertaining to both the present life and the future—comes forth, is produced, comes into existence, and is born.
Others, however, say that "attachment" (saṃsagga) is the fixing of the mind upon an object. From that, affection and the suffering of affection arise.
Having spoken this half-verse concerning the classification of the self (*atthappabheda*), that Paccekabuddha said:
"Indeed, by digging out the root of that suffering—this suffering consisting of affection and arising from sorrow and the like—I have attained Paccekabuddhahood.
When this was said, those ministers asked: "Venerable sir, what must we do now?"
Then he said: “Whether you or others, whoever desires to be freed from this suffering, let him, seeing the danger born of affection, wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
And here, it is with reference to that which was stated as “this suffering arises from affection” that [the verse] says, “seeing the danger born of affection.”
It should be understood as "it was said. Alternatively, one may connect it thus: "From such association as has been described, affection arises for one who has become associated;
from affection, this suffering comes into being. Seeing the danger born of affection as it truly is, [the Blessed One thought], "I have attained [this state].
In this way, the fourth quarter-verse was spoken as an inspired utterance (udāna) according to the method previously explained.
This is to be understood. Beyond this, everything is exactly as stated in the preceding verse. In the *Niddesa*:
"He produces" means that having seen a secondary mark (*anubyañjana*) in a form, he clings to it.
"He pursues" means that he binds himself to a form through affection (*sneha*). "They come to be" means they exist. "They are born" means they arise. "They are produced" means they proceed.
"Manifesting" means they become evident. "Arising," "being born," and "coming into existence" are three terms augmented by prefixes.
From here on, it should be understood according to the method stated in the Aṭṭhakavagga.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the second verse.
123. In the third [verse], they are "friends" (*mitta*) by way of loving-kindness (*mettāyaṇa*); they are "companions" (*suhajja*) by virtue of being well-disposed toward one another.
