For some are friends indeed because of their desire for absolute welfare, but not companions; some are companions indeed because they produce happiness in the heart through walking, coming, standing, sitting, conversation, and so forth, but not friends;
and some are both companions and friends by virtue of both those qualities. These are of two kinds.

There are both householders and those who have gone forth from the household life. Among them, householders are of three kinds: benefactors, those who share in pleasure and pain, and the compassionate.
Those who have gone forth are preeminently exponents of the goal. Thus they are endowed with four factors each, as it has been said:
“Householder’s son, a helpful friend who is well-disposed should be recognized by four grounds: he protects one when one is negligent;
he protects one’s property when one is negligent; he becomes a refuge when one is afraid;
and when there are duties or tasks to be performed, he provides twice as much wealth.
Likewise:
“Householder’s son, a friend who is easy to please should be known by four grounds as one who shares in both pleasure and pain:
he reveals his secrets to him, he guards his secrets, he does not abandon him in times of misfortune, and even his own life is surrendered for his sake.”
Likewise:

"Householder’s son, a compassionate friend who wishes you well is to be known by four grounds: he does not rejoice in your misfortune, he rejoices in your prosperity, he restrains you when you speak dispraise [of others], and he commends you when you speak praise.
Likewise—"

“Householder’s son, a friend who speaks for one’s welfare and is well-disposed should be known by four grounds: he restrains one from evil, establishes one in what is wholesome, makes one hear what has not been heard, and points out the path to heaven.

Here, those who are householders are intended; however, in terms of meaning, all [types of friends] are applicable. These are friends and well-wishers. “Feeling compassion” means feeling sympathy, desiring to bestow happiness upon them and desiring to remove their suffering.

“He ruins his welfare” means that he ruins or destroys welfare in two ways: by losing what has already been gained and by failing to produce what has not yet been gained. Welfare is threefold according to the categories of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*); likewise, it is also threefold according to one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both.
“With a dependent mind” means having placed oneself in a low position, thinking: “I cannot live without this person; he is my refuge, he is my final resort.”

Even when placing himself in a subordinate position, he is one whose mind is bound [to others]. Even when placing himself in a high position, thinking, "These cannot live without me; I am their refuge, I am their final resort," he is one whose mind is bound.
However, it is this latter kind of one whose mind is bound who is intended here.
"This fear" refers to the fear of losing one's goal; he speaks with reference to the loss of one's own meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

"Familiarity" (*santhava*) is threefold, by way of familiarity through craving (*taṇhā*), views (*diṭṭhi*), and friends (*mitta*). In this context, craving, which is divided into eight hundred types, is familiarity through craving;
views, which are divided into sixty-two types, are familiarity through views; and compassion for friends due to a bound mind is familiarity through friends.
"Intimacy with friends": this is what is intended here. For by means of that, his meditative attainment has been lost. Therefore he said: "Perceiving this danger in intimacy.
The remainder should be understood as being exactly as before; there is nothing further to be said in the commentary.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the third verse.
124. *Vaṃsa* means bamboo. *Visāla* means broad. The letter *va* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), or this is the particle *eva*.
Here, by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), the letter *e* has been dropped. Its connection is with the following word; we shall join it later.
*Yathā* means in the counterpart-image (*paṭibhāga*). *Visatta* means clinging, entangled, or woven together. *Puttesu dāresu ca* means among sons, daughters, and wives.
"Whatever longing" means whatever craving or affection. "Like a bamboo shoot, unattached" means not clinging like a bamboo shoot.

What is meant? Just as a bamboo is broad and attached, so too, whatever longing there is for children and wives—that longing is indeed "attached" because it stands by interweaving those very objects. Thus, I was possessed of that longing.

"Like a broad bamboo, he is 'entangled' (visatta)"—thus, having seen the danger in such attachment through insight, and cutting that attachment with the knowledge of the Path, he does not cling by way of craving, conceit, or views to form and so forth, or to the seen and so forth, or to gain and so forth, or to sense-desire existence and so forth;
like this bamboo shoot, he has attained Pratyekabuddhahood. The rest is exactly as explained in the previous method.
This should be understood. There is nothing additional even in this exposition.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the fourth verse. 125.
Regarding the fifth [verse], "deer" (*miga*) is a designation for all four-footed wild animals; however, here—
A deer is intended [here]. "In the forest" means the remainder of the area excluding the village and its precincts;
however, in this context, a pleasure grove is intended, which is why it is said "in a pleasure grove. "As he pleases" means according to his own inclination.
"Unbound" means not bound by any means such as ropes or ties; by this, he indicates a state of unrestrained movement. "Wherever he wishes."
"He goes for his range" means that he goes to whatever direction he wishes to go for the sake of his range;
therefore, it is illustrated that he goes as far as he wishes to go there, and eats whatever he wishes to eat.
"A wise man" refers to a learned person. "At will" refers to living according to one's own desire and being independent of others.
"Pekkhamāno" means looking with the eye of wisdom. Alternatively, it refers to the "serita" (freedom) of both the Dhamma and the person.
For supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhammā*) are "free" (*serina*) because they do not fall under the power of the defilements (*kilesa*), and the persons endowed with them are likewise free;
thus, "pekkhamāno" means looking at the description of their nature. What is meant? Just as a deer, unbound in the forest, goes wherever it wishes—

"For the sake of going about. [Thinking: "When indeed shall I too, having severed the bond of craving, go in this manner?"—thus, seeing the disadvantage in being unable to go wherever one wishes because you stood surrounding me from here and there, binding me so that I could not go as I desired, and seeing the benefit in going wherever one wishes, [I attained] the gradual fulfillment of serenity and insight.
I went [there]. Thereafter, I attained the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. Therefore, another wise man, desiring the state of solitude (*serita*), should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the fifth verse.

126. This is the summary of the sixth [chapter]: For one standing in the midst of companions, there is an addressing in various ways—such as “Listen to this from me,” “Give this to me,” and so forth—in regard to the dwelling known as daytime rest, the place known as the great assembly, the journey known as going to the park, and the wandering known as traveling through the countryside; therefore, I [have spoken] therein.
Having become disillusioned with that, he saw that although the going forth— cultivated by noble persons, possessing manifold benefits, and exclusively blissful— is thus,
it is nonetheless uncraved and unsought by all base men who are overcome by greed; and observing that this state, being uncraved,
is available only to capable individuals through their lack of subjection to others, he applied himself to insight and gradually attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
"Attained": the remainder is exactly as described by the method already stated.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the sixth verse. 127.
Regarding the seventh [verse], "play" (*khiḍḍā*) means sporting. It is twofold: bodily and vocal. Therein, the bodily...

"Playing with elephants," "with horses," "with chariots," "with bows," "with spears," and so forth. "Vocal [pleasures]" refers to singing, the recitation of verses (*siloka*), the *mukhabherika* (mouth-drum), and so forth.
"Delight" (*rati*) refers to the delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*).

"Extensive" (*vipula*) means reaching as far as the marrow of the bones, pervading the entire physical existence. The rest is self-evident. The connection of the sequence (*anusandhiyojanā*) is also [self-evident].
And here, this should be understood according to the method stated in the verse on association (*saṃsaggagāthā*).
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the seventh verse. 128.
Regarding the eighth [verse], *cātuddiso* means one who dwells at ease in the four directions, as expressed in such passages as, "He dwells having pervaded one direction," and so forth.
Alternatively, it is "four-directional" (*cātuddisa*) because the four directions have been suffused by the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) according to this method.
It is "non-reactive" (*appaṭigha*) because one does not strike against any beings or conditioned phenomena within those directions out of fear.
"Contented" means being satisfied by way of the twelve kinds of contentment. "With this or that" refers to requisites that are high or low.

Regarding the phrase "enduring dangers, undaunted": here, they are called *parissaya* because they afflict the body and mind, or because they cause their excellence to decline, or because they lie in wait depending upon them.

This is a designation for external dangers such as lions and tigers, and internal dangers such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*)—that is, those calamities affecting body and mind. One endures these dangers through patience (*adhivāsanakhanti*).

It is "enduring" (*sahitā*) because it endures through qualities such as energy (*vīriya*) and so forth against the dangers (*parissaya*). It is "fearless" (*achambhī*) due to the absence of fear that causes rigidity.

What is meant? Just like those four ascetics, being content with various requisites and established here in contentment—the very foundation of practice—one is "four-directional" (*cātuddiso*) through the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] in the four directions.
Because there is an absence of fear regarding the striking back at the seven formations, he is non-reactive (*appaṭigha*).

Because he endures the aforementioned dangers due to his state of being directed toward the four quarters, and because he is non-reactive, he is undaunted (*achambhī*). Having seen this quality of practice, thinking, "By practicing wisely, I have attained Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment," he practiced with proper reflection.
Alternatively, knowing that those ascetics, being content with whatever they receive, become "one who faces in all four directions" in the manner already described,
and aspiring thus to this state of facing in all four directions, I practiced with wise attention and attained it. Therefore, another person who aspires to such a state should,
for the sake of being one who faces in all four directions, endure dangers and remain unafraid through non-resistance.
"One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.

Regarding this, in the *Niddesa*, "loving-kindness" (*mettā*) is first explained by its meaning: it is called *mettā* because it "moistens" (*mijjati*), which means it "endears. Alternatively, it is *mettā* because it exists toward friends, or because it is the activity of a friend.
"Accompanied by loving-kindness" means endowed with loving-kindness. "By the mind" means by the consciousness (*citta*).
"One direction" is said with reference to pervading beings included within one direction, beginning with a single being first grasped in one direction.
"Having pervaded" means having touched and made it the object. "Dwells" means he maintains a mode of conduct established in the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
"Likewise the second" means that just as he pervaded any one direction among the directions such as the east, [he does so for the others].
He dwells; the meaning is that immediately after that, he dwells likewise in the second, third, and fourth [directions].
By the phrase "above" (*uddhaṃ*), it is stated by this same method that he dwells in the upper direction. "Below" (*adho*) and "across" (*tiriyam*):
in the downward direction and the horizontal direction as well, it is exactly the same. In this context, "below" means beneath; "across" means the intermediate directions. Thus, in all directions—
"In the circle of the hermitage, he directs and also brings back the mind associated with loving-kindness, as if it were a horse.

Up to this point, the directed pervasion of loving-kindness has been shown by encompassing each direction individually. However, the passage beginning with "in all places" (sabbadhi) is stated for the purpose of showing the non-directed pervasion.

Therein, "in all places" (sabbadhi) means everywhere. "In all respects" (sabbattatāya) means toward all [beings]—without distinction among the categories of inferior, middling, superior, friends, enemies, neutrals, and so forth.
"By means of selfhood" (*attatāya*) means that, without making a distinction such as "this is another being," one acts through equality with oneself (*attasamatāya*); this is what is meant.
Alternatively, "by means of all-selfhood" (*sabbattatāya*) means by means of the entire state of mind, which is to say, without wavering even slightly toward the outside.
"Possessing all" (*sabbāvantaṃ*) means possessing all beings; the sense is "associated with all beings. "The world" (*lokaṃ*) refers to the world of beings (*sattalokaṃ*).
Furthermore, because this is seen through such modes of expression as "vast" (*vipula*) and so forth, it is stated here again as "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagatena*).

Alternatively, since the word "thus" (*tathā*) or the word "in this way" (*iti*) is not repeated here—as it was in the case of the specific pervasion—therefore it is stated again as "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.
Or else, this is stated by way of conclusion. And in this context, regarding the term "vast," it refers to the manner of pervading.

Its vastness is to be seen. In terms of its plane, however, it is "exalted" (*mahaggata*). In terms of its proficiency and its having immeasurable beings as its object, it is "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*).

Through the abandoning of the adversary that is ill-will (*byāpāda*), it is "free from enmity" (*avera*); through the abandoning of mental distress (*domanassa*), it is "free from affliction" (*abyāpajja*)—meaning it is free from suffering.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) has already had its meaning explained above. Those who possess it rejoice by means of it.
*Muditā* (appreciative joy) is so called because one rejoices oneself, or because it consists merely in rejoicing.

*Upekkhā* (equanimity) is so called because one looks on with indifference through the abandoning of ill-will (*vyāpāda*) by means of thoughts such as “May they be free from enmity,” and through the attainment of a state of neutrality.

As for its characteristics and so forth: here, *mettā* has the characteristic of proceeding in a manner that is beneficial; its function is to provide benefit; and it is manifested as the subduing of malice.
Compassion has as its proximate cause the perception of the endearing nature of beings. Its excellence is the pacification of ill-will; its failure is the arising of affection.
Compassion is characterized by the manifestation of the mode of removing suffering; its essence is the inability to endure the suffering of others; it is manifested as non-cruelty;
and its proximate cause is the perception of the helplessness of those overwhelmed by suffering. The pacification of cruelty is its excellence; the arising of sorrow is its failure.
Failure. Sympathetic joy (muditā) has the characteristic of being free from envy; its function is non-opposition; it is manifested as the removal of discontent;
its proximate cause is the sight of the prosperity of beings. The cessation of discontent is its success; the arising of abandonment is its failure.

Equanimity (upekkhā) has the characteristic of proceeding with an attitude of neutrality toward beings; its function is seeing beings with impartiality; it is manifested as the subsiding of aversion and attachment.

“Beings are owners of their kamma; by whose whim could they become happy, or be released from suffering, or not fall away from the attainment they have reached?”—this is the basis for the vision of beings as owners of their kamma.
The subsiding of aversion and attraction is its success; the arising of household-based equanimity rooted in ignorance is its failure.
"Content therein" means he is content by way of contentment with requisites.
"With whatever kind of robe" means not with just any robe—whether coarse, fine, rough, excellent, firm, or worn-out—but rather he is content with whatever he obtains, with whatever kind of robe;
this is the meaning. For regarding robes, there are three kinds of contentment: contentment with what is obtained, [contentment with what is received, and contentment with what is available].
Contentment according to one's strength and contentment according to what is appropriate. This same method applies to alms-food and the other requisites as well.
Thus, with reference to these three types of contentment, it is said: "He is content with any kind of robe whatsoever; he is content with whatever robe he has obtained."
And here, the robe must be understood; the field for robes must be understood; the rag-robe must be understood;
contentment with robes must be understood; and the ascetic practices connected with robes must be understood.

Therein, "the robe must be understood" means that the six types of robes beginning with linen (*khoma*) and the six types of secondary robes beginning with *dukūla* must also be understood. These are twelve.

Permissible robes are as follows: a robe made of kusa grass, a robe made of bark, a robe made of wood-shavings, a blanket of human hair, a blanket of animal fur, a cloth of *potthaka* fibers, leather, an owl’s wing, tree-bark cloth, vine-cloth, *eraka*-grass cloth, plantain-bark cloth, and bamboo-cloth—these and others like them are permissible robes.
However, those such as the following are impermissible robes: [the list of forbidden materials].

Regarding "the field for robes" (*cīvarakkhetta*): one should understand that there are six fields based on how [robes] arise—namely, from the Saṅgha, from a group, from relatives, from friends, from one’s own wealth, or as a rag from a dust heap—and there are eight fields according to the eight headings (*mātikā*).
As for "rag-robe" (*paṃsukūla*), it refers to [robes found at] a charnel ground, a shop, a street, a rubbish heap, a weaver’s workshop, a bathing place, or a ford.

The twenty-three kinds of rag-robes (*pamsukūla*) should be understood as follows: one discarded after being worn, one burnt by fire, one gnawed by cattle, one gnawed by ants, one gnawed by rats, one torn at the edges, one torn by mice, one carried away as a banner, one from a funeral monument (*thūpa*), one belonging to a recluse (*samaṇa*), one from the sea, one from a consecration ceremony, one from a traveler, one blown there by the wind, one produced by supernormal power (*iddhimaya*), and one given by a deity. And herein, "from a physician" means...

*Gabbhamalaharaṇaṃ*: cloth brought back after having been wrapped around a corpse and carried to the charnel ground. *Gatapaccāgataṃ*: cloth brought back after having been wrapped around a dead body, taken to the cemetery, and then returned.
*Dhajāhaṭaṃ*: cloth brought back from a place where a banner has been raised.

*Thūpaṃ*: cloth worshipped at a burial mound (*vammika*). *Sāmuddiyaṃ*: cloth washed ashore by the waves of the ocean. *Panthikaṃ*: [cloth] [found] by those traveling on a road out of fear of robbers, [using] stones...
Having cut it, he put on the robe. "Made by psychic power" refers to the robe [given] to one who has come as a monk (*ehibhikkhu*). The rest is self-evident.
Regarding contentment with robes, there are twenty forms of contentment with robes:

contentment with thoughts regarding robes, contentment with going, contentment with seeking, contentment with acquisition, contentment with receiving a moderate amount, contentment with avoiding greediness, and contentment with whatever is obtained.
Contentment according to one's strength, contentment according to suitability, contentment with water, contentment with washing, contentment with making [robes], contentment with measure,
contentment with sewing, contentment with dyeing, contentment with allowable things, contentment with use, contentment with avoiding hoarding, and contentment with relinquishing. In this regard,
after a monk who is seeking [robes] has lived for three months in a fixed residence, for about one month...

It is permissible to reflect upon it. For one who has performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) makes a robe during the month of the robe season; a wearer of rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*), however, makes it in just half a month.
This reflection for the duration of a month or half a month is called "contentment with reflection. Furthermore, when going for the sake of a robe, not thinking "Where shall I obtain it?
but going with the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) as the primary focus, is called "contentment with going."

Furthermore, for one who is searching, "searching with contentment" means not searching with just anyone at all, but rather taking a modest and virtuous bhikkhu as one's companion when conducting the search.
For one searching in this manner, upon seeing the robe-material being brought from afar,
one does not speculate, thinking, "This will be pleasing," or "That will be unpleasing," but rather [regards it] regardless of whether it is coarse, fine, or otherwise.

Contentment with what has been obtained is called *paṭilābhasantos*. Likewise, for one who takes what has been obtained, contentment with only what is sufficient for oneself—thinking, "this much will be for the double-layered robe" and "this much for the single-layered robe"—is called *mattapaṭiggahaṇasantoṣa*.
Furthermore, for one seeking a robe, [the thought] "at such-and-such a person's door there is something pleasing..."
Not thinking, "I shall obtain [this]," but wandering from door to door in sequence is called contentment through the avoidance of greed.
For one who is able to subsist with whatever—whether coarse or refined—the subsisting with just what has been obtained is called contentment with what is received.
Knowing one's own strength and subsisting with that by which one is able to live is called contentment according to one's capacity.
Contentment with what is appropriate is the name for maintaining oneself with whatever one has, even if it is anything at all, after having given what is pleasing to another.
Not considering whether water is pleasing or unpleasing, but washing with whatever water is fit for washing, is called contentment with water.
Likewise, in order to avoid turbid mud, red ochre, moldy leaf-juice, or dirty waters—
It is permissible. However, for one who washes, "washing with contentment" means washing by crushing it with the hands rather than striking it with clubs or similar objects.
Likewise, if it does not become clean in that way, it is permissible to wash it by adding leaves and using boiled water.
Having washed it in this manner, when preparing it, one should prepare it in a sufficient quantity without discriminating, "this is coarse" or "this is fine."
Making [the robe] is called "satisfaction with the making. Making it merely to conceal the three circles is called "satisfaction with the measure.

However, making it by taking any thread whatsoever—whether brought from the streets and such, or from a shrine of a deity, or placed at the feet [of a donor]—without deliberating, "I shall seek out pleasing thread," for the purpose of making a robe, is called "satisfaction with the thread."
However, when binding the cord, it must not be pierced even once at the mere width of a finger.
For one who acts in this way, there is no breach of the observance even if he has no companion. But at the width of three fingers, it must be pierced seven times.
For one who acts in this way, he must indeed have a companion traveling along the path; if he does not have one—
There is a breach of his rule regarding this; this is what is called "contentment with sewing. However, one who dyes [robes] must not seek out *kāḷakacchaka* (black-ear) and the like;
rather, he should dye them with whatever he obtains from *somavakkala* (white-bark) and other such materials.
But if he does not obtain these, he may take grass-dye discarded by people in the forest, or he may take the dregs discarded by monks after they have boiled it.

It should be dyed. This is called contentment with dyeing. Taking any of the blue, mud-color, black, or mixed colors and making it appear appropriate while sitting on the back of an elephant is called contentment with the robe-making.
Using it merely for the purpose of concealing the private parts is called contentment with use. As for the cloth...
If one has obtained thread, needle, or a maker, but is unable to find them, it is permissible to set [the robe] aside; if they can be found, it is not permissible.
Even if one has finished [the robe] and wishes to give it to a pupil or others, but they are not present, it is permissible to set it aside until their arrival;
as soon as they have arrived, it must be given. If one is unable to give it, one must make a formal determination (adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ). In another case...
When there is a robe-cloth, it is permissible to determine it as a rug; for that which is not determined constitutes "storing up" (*sannidhi*), whereas that which is determined does not.
Thus said the Elder Mahāsīva. This is called "contentment in avoiding storing up.

Furthermore, when distributing [robes], one should not give by looking at the face; rather, one should distribute while abiding in the *sāraṇīya-dhamma* (duties of courtesy). This is called "contentment in distribution."
The ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) connected with robes are the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice and the three-robe-wearer’s practice.

Thus, fulfilling the noble lineage of contentment with robes, the Paccekabuddha guards these two ascetic practices; by guarding them, he is content by way of the noble lineage of contentment with robes.
Regarding "one who speaks in praise": one person is content but does not speak in praise of contentment; another is not content... [and so forth].
One praises contentment. One is neither contented nor praises contentment. Another is both contented and praises contentment.
It is to show that such a person is a Paccekasambuddha that it is said: "one who speaks in praise of contentment with whatever robe one happens to have."
"Improper search" (*anesanā*) refers to various kinds of improper seeking, such as engaging in the practice of acting as a messenger or running errands. "Unbecoming" (*appatirūpa*) means unsuitable.
"And not having obtained" (*aladdhā ca*) means without having acquired [robes]. For example, someone might think, "How indeed shall I obtain a robe?
and, joining company with meritorious monks, acts with hypocrisy and becomes anxious and agitated.
A Paccekasambuddha, having not obtained a robe in this way, does not become agitated. "Having obtained" means having acquired it through lawful and righteous means.
"Attained" means free from greed and craving. "Uninfatuated" means not having fallen into a state of intoxication by excessive craving.
"Unburnt" means not overwhelmed or enveloped by craving. "Seeing the danger" refers to the fault of improper search (*an-esanā*).

Seeing the danger in the enjoyment of what has been craved for, and being one whose wisdom consists in the way of escape, he understands that very escape as it is stated: "only for the warding off of cold.
"Contentment with whatever robe" means contentment with any kind of robe whatsoever. "He does not exalt himself" means...
Just as someone here might engage in self-exaltation, thinking, "I am a wearer of rag-robes; I took up the practice of wearing rag-robes at the very moment of my full ordination;
who is there equal to me?", he does not exalt himself in this way.
Nor does he disparage others, [thinking], "But these other monks are not wearers of rag-robes," or "They do not possess even the mere quality of being a wearer of rag-robes."

Or he does not disparage another by saying, "He has nothing. For "one who is skillful therein" means one who speaks in praise of contentment with robes, or one who is skillful, clever, and competent in those matters. "Diligent" means free from laziness through constant application.
"Clearly comprehending and mindful" means endowed with both clear comprehension and mindfulness. "Established in the noble lineage" means firmly grounded in the noble lineages.

"With whatever kind of almsfood" means with any kind of almsfood whatsoever. Here too, the almsfood must be understood, the field for almsfood must be understood, contentment with almsfood must be understood, and the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) connected with almsfood must be understood.
In this context, "almsfood" refers to boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, meat, milk, curd, ghee, and fresh butter.
Oil, honey, molasses, rice gruel, solid food, soft food, and syrups—these are the sixteen kinds of almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*). The field for almsfood (*piṇḍapātakhettam*) consists of:

a meal provided for the Saṅgha, a designated meal, an invitation, a meal by ticket, a fortnightly meal, a meal on the Uposatha day, a meal on the first day of the lunar fortnight, a meal for newcomers, a meal for those departing, a meal for the sick, and a meal for those attending the sick.
The fifteen fields for alms-food are: food from a designated house (*dhurabhatta*), food from a fixed hut (*kuṭibhatta*), food by turn (*vārabhatta*), and food from a monastery (*vihārabhatta*).
Contentment with alms-food consists of: contentment with the thought regarding alms-food; contentment with the journey; contentment with the search;
contentment with the acquisition; contentment with the receiving; contentment with receiving a moderate amount; contentment with avoiding greediness; and contentment with whatever is obtained.

There are fifteen kinds of contentment: contentment with whatever strength one has, contentment with whatever is suitable, contentment with what is helpful, contentment with moderation, contentment with the use [of requisites], contentment with avoiding hoarding, and contentment with relinquishing.
In this regard, a monk who is seeking [requisites] reflects after washing his face.
However, for one who wanders together with a group of alms-collectors at the time of evening service to the elders:
Thinking only this much—“Where shall we go for alms today? and “To such-and-such a village, venerable sirs”—one should not engage in further thought from that point onward.
One who wanders alone may engage in thought while standing at the thought-hut;

however, from that point on, if one continues to think, one has fallen away from and is excluded from the Noble Lineage. This is called contentment with thought. When entering for alms, [one should maintain this].
However, one should go under the heading of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) without thinking, "Where shall I find it? This is called contentment in going.
While searching, one should not take just anyone, but should search specifically for one who is modest and virtuous. This is called contentment in searching.
Upon seeing someone being brought from afar, one should not think, "This one is pleasing; this one is unpleasing."
One should not give rise to such thoughts. This is called contentment with what is obtained.

Without thinking, "I will take this which is pleasing" or "I will not take that which is unpleasing," one should simply take whatever is sufficient for sustenance. This is called contentment in receiving.
In this regard, however, if the gift to be given is abundant but the donor wishes to give little, only a small amount should be taken. [If] the gift to be given...
If there is much [to give] and the donor wishes to give much, one should accept only a moderate amount.

If the object to be given is not much and the donor wishes to give little, one should accept little. If the object to be given is not much but the donor wishes to give much, one should accept a moderate amount.
For one who does not know the proper measure in receiving sullies the confidence of people.
He squanders what has been given in faith and does not carry out the Teaching. He is even unable to win the heart of his own biological mother.
Thus, one should accept only after knowing the proper measure; this is called "contentment in accepting with moderation.

One should go from door to door in regular order, rather than going only to wealthy families; this is called "contentment in avoiding greed. [The others] are contentment with whatever is obtained, and so forth.
The method regarding the robe is exactly as previously stated.
Having consumed almsfood, to consume it while recognizing its benefit by thinking, "I shall maintain the duty of a recluse," is called contentment with what is beneficial.
One should not accept food brought after the bowl has been filled. If there is one who is not fully ordained...
He should have it brought; if it is not there, he should have it fetched and take only the amount required for acceptance. This is called contentment regarding measure (*parimāṇasantosa*).
Eating with the thought, "This is not the escape from this [craving]," in order to dispel hunger, is called contentment regarding enjoyment (*paribhogasantosa*).
One must not eat after having stored it away. This is called contentment regarding the avoidance of hoarding (*sannidhiparivajjanasantosa*). The mouth—
Having reflected thus, one who stands firm in the qualities conducive to mindfulness should respond. This is called "satisfaction with response.
Furthermore, there are five ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) connected with almsfood:

the practice of eating only almsfood, the practice of wandering for alms from door to door, the practice of eating at a single sitting, the practice of eating only from the bowl, and the practice of not accepting food after starting to eat. Thus is the noble lineage of contentment with almsfood.

The Paccekasambuddha, fulfilling [his duties], guards these five ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). Guarding them, he is content by way of the great noble lineage of contentment with alms-food (piṇḍapāta-santosa).
"One who speaks in praise" and so forth should be understood in the manner already stated.
Regarding "lodgings" (senāsana): here, the lodging itself must be known, the field for lodgings must be known, and contentment with lodgings must be known.
It should be known; the ascetic practice connected with lodgings should be known.

In this context, "lodging" refers to these fifteen types of lodgings: a bed, a bench, a mattress, a pillow, a monastery, a gabled house, a mansion, a cell, a cave, a rock shelter, a hut, a bamboo thicket, the foot of a tree, or wherever else monks go for their retreat.
The "field for lodgings" (*senāsanakhettam*) consists of six fields: from the Saṅgha, from a group, from relatives, from friends, from one's own wealth, or as a rag-robe (*paṃsukūlam*).

"Contentment with lodgings" (*senāsanasantoso*) refers to the fifteen kinds of contentment, such as contentment with thoughts regarding lodgings; these are to be understood in the same manner as those explained in the section on almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*).

Furthermore, there are five ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) connected with lodgings: the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññikaṅgam*), the tree-root-dweller’s practice (*rukkhamūlikaṅgam*), and so forth.

The practice of living in the open air, the practice of dwelling in a charnel ground, and the practice of accepting whatever seat is offered—thus fulfilling this great noble lineage of contentment with lodgings, the Paccekabuddha guards these five ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas). By guarding these, he is satisfied by way of the great noble lineage of contentment with lodgings.
Thus, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, the General of the Dhamma, like one spreading out the earth, [fills] the belly of the ocean...
Having first taught the noble lineage of contentment with robes as if filling the sky and expanding it,
and having taught the second noble lineage of contentment with almsfood as if raising up the moon and leaping over the sun,
and having now taught the third noble lineage of contentment with lodgings as if lifting up Mount Sineru— now...

In order to explain the noble lineage of contentment with requisites for the sick, he said: “He is content with whatever medicinal requisites for the sick are obtained. This follows the same pattern as the section on almsfood.

In this context, one should be satisfied simply by whatever is obtained, however it is obtained, and whatever is appropriate. However, the noble lineage of delighting in meditation (*bhāvanārāma-ariyavaṃsa*) is not included here;
rather, the factor of being a sitter (*nesajjikaṅga*) pertains to the noble lineage of delighting in meditation. And this has also been stated:
“Five are said to concern lodgings, five are based on food;
one is associated with energy, and two are based on robes.
Regarding the phrase “established in the ancient, foremost noble lineage”: here, “ancient” means not newly arisen. “Foremost” means by those at the head.
It should be understood. "Noble lineage" (*ariyavaṃsa*) means the lineage of the noble ones (*ariya*).

For just as there is the lineage of kshatriyas, the lineage of brahmins, the lineage of vaiśyas, the lineage of śūdras, the lineage of ascetics, the lineage of clans, and the lineage of kings—so too this is the eighth noble lineage;

it is called a noble stream or a noble tradition. Furthermore, among these lineages, this [noble lineage] is like the kālānusāri fragrance and so forth among the lineages of root-fragrances and so forth.
It is declared to be supreme. But who are those Noble Ones (ariya) whose lineage this is?
"Noble Ones" refers to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata; the lineage of these Noble Ones is the "Ariyavaṃsa" (Noble Lineage).
For previously, at the head of four incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand kappas, there appeared Taṇhaṅkara and Medhaṅkara.
The four Buddhas who appeared—Saraṇaṅkara and Dīpaṅkara—are the Noble Ones (Ariya).
The lineage of these Noble Ones is the Ariyavaṃsa. After the final Nibbāna of those Buddhas, after the passing of an incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyya), the Buddha named Koṇḍañña appeared...
[and so on] ...in this present aeon, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One.

"Gotama": four Buddhas have arisen; the lineage of those Noble Ones is the "Ariyavaṃsa" (Noble Lineage). Furthermore, the lineage of all the Noble Ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha—of the past, future, and present, is the Ariyavaṃsa;
[he is] "standing" (ṭhita) in that Ariyavaṃsa, meaning firmly established. The rest should be understood in the manner already explained.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Eighth Stanza. 129.
The application [of the words] in the ninth [stanza] is as follows: "Some who have gone forth are difficult to restrain, being overcome by non-contentment;
and likewise, those householders living at home are of the same nature. Loathing this state of being difficult to restrain, I [apply] insight (*vipassanā*).
"Having undertaken [the practice], I have attained *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment). The remainder should be understood in the same manner as before.
In the *Niddesa*, "not obedient" (*anassava*) means those who do not listen to what is said. "Those who do not speak [what they are told]" (*avacanakara*) means those who are difficult to speak with.

"Those who act contrarily" (*paṭilomavuttino*) means those whose habit is to speak in opposition; the meaning is that they proceed as rivals. "They turn their faces away" means [they turn away] from the one giving advice.
Having seen it, they turn their faces away and look toward another direction. "Being unattached" means being unbound.
"Being without longing" means being without clinging.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of the ninth verse.

130. "Having removed" (*oropayitvā*) means having taken away. "Householder's emblems" (*gihibyañjanāni*) refers to hair and beard, bathing, clothing, ornaments, garlands, perfumes, ointments, wives, sons, female and male slaves, and so forth.
These manifest the state of a householder; therefore, they are called "householder's emblems. "One whose bowl is broken" (*sañchinnapatta*) means one whose bowl has fallen [from the path].

"Having cut off" (*chetvāna*) means having severed with the knowledge of the Path (*maggañāṇa*). "A hero" (*vīra*) means one endowed with the vigor of the Path. "Householder's bonds" (*gihibandhanāni*)...
The fetters of sensual desire. For sensual desires are indeed the fetters of householders; such is the literal meaning of the words.
But this is the underlying intention: "O, that I too might lay aside the marks of a householder and become like a kovilāra tree with its leaves completely stripped away!
Thinking thus, I applied myself to insight and attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
The remainder should be understood in the same manner as before. Regarding the commentary on the *Niddesa*:

"And a seat of essence" (*sārāsana*) means a seat made of essence. "Cut off" (*chinnāni*) means fallen away. "Completely cut off" (*sañchinnāni*) means lying prostrate. "Fallen" (*patitāni*) means released from the stalk. "Completely fallen" (*paripatitāni*) means fallen upon the ground.
This concludes the commentary on the explanation of the tenth verse.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Chapter 131–2.
Regarding the first two [suttas] of the Second Chapter: "Nipaka" means naturally clever and wise in the preliminary work for the kasiṇas and so forth.

"Wholesome" (kusala). "One who dwells well" means one endowed with either the state of absorption (appanā-vihāra) or the access state (upacāra). "Wise" (dhīra) means one possessed of steadfastness (dhiti).

Therein, the perfection of steadfastness was stated by way of being prudent (nipaka); here, however, the meaning is simply "one possessed of steadfastness. Steadfastness is the quality of unflagging exertion;
it is a designation for energy (vīriya) that proceeds in such a manner as: "Even if my skin and sinews [should waste away]."

Moreover, the wise one should even despise his own evil deeds. "Like a king abandoning a conquered kingdom" means that just as a rival king, realizing "this conquered kingdom brings no benefit," abandons his realm and wanders alone, so too should one abandon the company of fools and wander alone.
Alternatively, "like a king abandoning a kingdom" refers to how King Sutasoma abandoned his conquered kingdom and wandered alone.

And just as with "the great multitude," so too does one "wander alone"—this is its meaning. The remainder can be understood according to what has already been stated, and thus it is not elaborated upon.
There is nothing further to be said in the Niddesa.
This concludes the first pair.

133. The meaning of the third verse is plain. However, regarding the phrase "perfection of companions" (*sahāyasampadā*), here it should be understood that "companions" refers specifically to those endowed with the aggregates of virtue and so forth belonging to the *asekkha* (those beyond training), and this alone constitutes "perfection of companions.
This is the construction here: we certainly praise, indeed we extol in every way, this aforementioned perfection of companions.
This has been said. How so? "One should associate with the best of companions.

Why? Because for one who associates with those superior to oneself in virtue and other qualities, those dharmas such as virtue that have not yet arisen do arise, and those already arisen reach growth, increase, and fullness.
For one who associates with equals, [virtue and the rest] are obtained through mutual support and the dispelling of remorse.

[They] fall away. But having found neither such superior nor equal companions, a clansman who desires his own welfare should avoid wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy and the like, and instead eating food obtained through righteous and fair means, without giving rise to aversion or attachment toward it, he should live alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, being one who eats blameless food. For I too am thus...
“While wandering, I have attained this prosperity”—the detailed explanation follows the method already stated. This is the third [section]. 134.
In the fourth [verse], *disvā* means having looked upon. *Suvaṇṇassa* means of gold (*kañcana*). The word *valayāni* (bracelets) is to be supplied as a remainder of the text.
This meaning is expressed with a remainder [of words]. "Radiant" (*pabhassarāni*) means having the nature of shining; it is said to mean "possessing luster.
The rest has its word-meanings (*padattha*) already explained. This, however, is the construction:
having seen the golden bracelets on his arm, and reflecting thus—"When living in a group there is clashing, but when living alone there is no clashing"—he began insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
"I have attained paccekabodhi. The rest is exactly as previously stated. "Nūpurāni" means bracelets;
some say it means "niyurā. "Ghaṭṭenti" means they strike one another.
This is the fourth [chapter].
135. The meaning of the words in the fifth verse is quite plain. However, the intended sense here is as follows:

if, through my dwelling together with this second prince who informs me of the cold, heat, and so forth, there has arisen in me a verbal expression directed toward him, or an outburst of anger born of affection for him; and if I do not renounce him, then even in the future...
"It will be exactly so. Just as it is now, so too shall there be verbal exchange or provocation with my second [companion].
Both of these are obstacles to the attainment of distinction.
Foreseeing this danger for the future, I abandoned that [distraction], practiced with wise reflection (*yoniso*), and attained Pratyekabuddhahood. The rest is according to the method already stated.
The fifth [section]. 136.

In the sixth [section], "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) refers to two kinds of sensual pleasure: sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāma*). Therein, sensual pleasures as objects are agreeable phenomena such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth;
sensual pleasures as defilements are all the various types of lust (*rāga*), beginning with desire (*chanda*). However, here it is sensual pleasures as objects that are intended.
[They are] intended [here]. They are variegated (*citrā*) by way of the many modes such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth. They are sweet (*madhurā*) by way of worldly gratification.

They are "delightful" (*manoramā*) because they delight the minds of foolish worldlings (*bālaputhujjana*). "In various forms" (*virūparūpena*) means by way of a disfigured form; what is meant is that they exist in manifold natures.
For they are variegated by way of form and so forth, and even within form and so forth, they possess diverse appearances by way of blue and so forth. Thus...
By assuming various hideous forms and displaying such-and-such gratification, they agitate the mind and do not allow one to delight in the going-forth (pabbajjā).
The rest here is self-evident. The conclusion should also be understood by joining two or three phrases according to the method stated in the preceding verses.
“Strands of sensual pleasure” (*kāmaguṇā*): they are *kāmā* in the sense of being objects of desire; they are *guṇā* in the sense of being fetters.
In the passage, “I allow you, monks, a double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) of unwashed cloth,” the sense of *guṇa* is that of a layer.

In the passage, “Time passes, nights fly by, and the strands of youth are gradually abandoned,” the sense of *guṇa* is that of a collection. [In the phrase] “A gift hundredfold... [the sense is that of a multiplier].

In the phrase “to be expected,” the meaning of *guṇa* is the sense of benefit or advantage. In the phrase “one might make an end, a cord for the end, and many cords for a garland,” the meaning of *guṇa* is the sense of binding.
Here too, this same sense is intended; therefore it is said: “*Guṇas* in the sense of binding.
“Cognizable by the eye” means they are to be seen by visual consciousness. By this same method, [the terms] “cognizable by the ear,” and so forth, are also explained.

The meaning should be understood as follows: "Desirable" (iṭṭhā) means whether they have been sought after or not, they are objects that are desirable. "Pleasant" (kantā) means worthy of being desired. "Charming" (manāpā) means increasing the mind's delight. "Of a lovely nature" (piyarūpā) means born of what is dear.

"Connected with sensual desire" (kāmūpasaṃhitā) means connected with the sensual desire that arises by taking them as its object. "Lust-inducing" (rajanīyā) means capable of inducing lust; the meaning is that they are the causes for the arising of passion.
Regarding the passage beginning with "If by means of signs" (*muddāya*): "signs" (*muddā*) refers to hand-gestures (*hatthamuddā*) formed by placing symbolic marks on the finger joints.

"Counting" (*gaṇanā*) refers to counting without gaps. "Calculation" (*saṅkhāna*) refers to calculation by summation. By means of which, having looked at a field, one thinks, "There will be this much rice here";
having looked at a tree, "There will be this many fruits here"; or having looked at the sky, "These birds in the sky are this many."
...will come to be. *Kasī* means agricultural work. *Vaṇijjā* refers to trade, such as trading on foot or by land.
*Gorakkha* is the livelihood of maintaining cattle, either one’s own or those of others, and making a living through the sale of the five products of the cow.
*Issattha* is said to be the service of attending [to a king] while taking up weapons. *Rājaporisa* is royal service performed without weapons.
"Having performed attendance upon the king. "One of the crafts" refers to the remaining crafts such as elephant-riding, horse-riding, and so forth, which were not previously mentioned.
"Placed in front of the cold" means standing before the cold as one stands before a target; the meaning is that he is being afflicted by the cold.
The same method applies to heat as well. Regarding "gadflies and so forth": *daṃsa* refers to the brown fly (*piṅgalamakkhikā*); *makasa* refers to all types of flies.
“Crawling creatures” refers to those that move by crawling. “Being vexed” means being oppressed, afflicted, struck, or touched.
“Dying” means perishing. “This, monks,” means, monks, this affliction consisting of cold and other conditions arising from making a living through palmistry and such means.
“The danger in sensual pleasures” means the calamity or misfortune within sensual pleasures; this is the meaning. “Visible here and now” means—
It must be seen for oneself through direct experience (*paccakkha*). "The mass of suffering" (*dukkhakkhandha*) means a heap of suffering.

Regarding the phrases "with sensual desire as its cause" (*kāmahetu*) and so forth: in the sense of a condition, sensual desires are its cause, thus it is "caused by sensual desire" (*kāmahetu*). In the sense of a root, sensual desires are its source, thus it is "originated from sensual desire" (*kāmanidāna*);

however, it is expressed as "originated from sensual desire" (*kāmanidāna*) due to a change in grammatical gender. In the sense of a reason, sensual desires are its basis, thus it is "based on sensual desire" (*kāmādhikaraṇa*); [this too is expressed] precisely through a change in grammatical gender.

But it is called "having sensual pleasures as its basis. The phrase "for the sake of sensual pleasures alone" is a restrictive statement; the meaning is that it arises only with sensual pleasures as its condition.
"Exerting himself" means exerting himself with the energy that initiates one’s livelihood. "Striving" means joining that energy together from before to after.
"Making an effort" means making an exertion, a striving, and an application. "Not being accomplished" means...
They do not come to fruition; they do not reach the hand. "He sorrows" means he sorrows with the powerful sorrow arisen in the mind.
"He is exhausted" means he is exhausted by the pain arisen in the body. "He laments" means he laments with speech.
"Beating his breast" means having struck his chest. "He wails" means he weeps. "He falls into delusion" means he becomes utterly bewildered, as if unconscious. "In vain" means...
"Empty" means void. "Fruitless" means without result.
"On account of guarding" means for the sake of protection. "How might I... means by what means indeed might I... "Even that which is mine...
means even that wealth of mine which was produced by performing work such as plowing and so forth—"even that is not ours. Even that... [is gone].
"We have none now.
Furthermore, monks, by means of the passage beginning "with sensual desire as cause" (*kāmahetu*), he demonstrates the danger (*ādīnava*) after first showing the reason.

In that context, "with sensual desire as cause" (*kāmahetu*) means that because of sensual desire as a condition (*kāmapaccayā*), even kings quarrel with other kings. "With sensual desire as source" (*kāmanidāna*) is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*).
The meaning is: "They dispute, making sensual pleasures the cause. *Kāmādhikaraṇa* is likewise a neuter noun; the meaning is:
"They dispute, making sensual pleasures the basis (*adhikaraṇa*). "For the sake of sensual pleasures alone" means:
"They dispute for the sake of sensual pleasures such as those pertaining to villages, market towns, military commanders, chaplains, positions, and so forth. "They attack" means they strike.
*Sasicamma* means swords as well as shields made of hide and so forth.
*Sannayhitvā dhanukalāpaṃ* means having taken up a bow and fastened on a quiver.
*Ubhatobyūḷhaṃ* means drawn up in battle array on both sides. *Pakkhandanti* means they enter. *Usūsu* means in arrows. *Vijjotalantesu* means while they are whirling about.
"Te tattha" means "they there," that is, in that battle.
Regarding the phrase "addāvalepanā upakāriyo": here, people build the foundations of the ramparts out of bricks in the shape of horse-hooves and then plaster them over with lime.
Those rampart foundations thus constructed are called "upakāriyo. They [are covered] with that which is moist...

Being drenched with *kalala* (mud), they are called "smeared with mire. They "leap forward" because, although they are pierced from below by sharp iron spikes, wooden stakes, and the like, they run right toward the wall, unable to climb it due to its slippery condition. "With dung" means with boiled cow-dung.
"With a hundred-fold edge" means with a hundred teeth; having fashioned that in the shape of eight teeth, [it is placed at] the city gate.
Thinking, “We shall break [the door] and enter,” they come and, standing at the upper door, cut his binding ropes and crush him with that very mass.
“They break into a house” means they break into the house’s opening. “They commit a raid” means they strike the village and carry out a great plundering.
"Living as a house-dweller alone": even fifty or sixty people surround him, seize him by the neck, and force him to bring back wealth.
"They stand on the road": they perform the work of highwaymen. "With half-staffs": with clubs.
The rest has the meaning already explained.
The sixth. 137.
In the seventh [verse], *īti* means "calamity" (*eti*). This is a designation for adventitious causes of misfortune that partake of the unwholesome.

Therefore, these strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) are also called *īti*, in the sense that they bring about manifold misfortunes and in the sense of being a violent outbreak. A boil (*gaṇḍa*) is also...

It oozes impurity; it is swollen, ripened, and burst. Therefore, these defilements are called "boils" because they ooze impurity and because they are in a state of being swollen, ripened, and burst by way of arising, aging, and dissolution. It "assails" (upaddavati), thus it is an "assault" (upaddava);
the meaning is that it produces harm, overcomes, and overwhelms. This is a designation for the boil of lust and the other [defilements].
Therefore, these strands of sensual pleasure are a calamity because they bring about the cause for not attaining the goal of Nibbāna and because they serve as the basis for all misfortunes.

Furthermore, since these [sensual pleasures] produce a state of affliction by the defilements—or, by giving rise to greed, plunder the natural health known as virtue—they are thus a "disease" in the sense of plundering health. In the sense of having entered within...

Furthermore, it is a "dart" (*salla*) in the sense of internal piercing and in the sense of being difficult to extract. It is a "fear" (*bhaya*) because it brings about fear pertaining to both the present life and the future life.
The word "me" (unto me) and the rest here are already evident. The conclusion should also be understood according to the method already stated.
"Kāmarāgarattāyaṃ" means this one is colored by sensual lust. "Chandarāgavinibaddho" means bound by the affection of desire-lust (*chandarāga*).
"Bound. "Wombs pertaining to this present life" refers to the wombs of the six sense-bases existing within this current personal existence (*attabhāva*).
"Wombs pertaining to future lives" refers to the wombs of the six sense-bases in the world beyond. "Is not liberated" means he is unable to be released.

"Plunged into what appears pleasant" means he has descended into or entered [the cycle] through passion for its sweet nature. "Quagmire" refers to the path of the mire of sensual desire. "Difficult" means difficult to traverse.
The seventh [chapter]. 138.
In the eighth [chapter], cold is of two kinds: that caused by internal disturbance of the elements and that caused by external disturbance of the elements;
likewise for heat. Therein, "stinging insects" refers to *piṅgala* flies. "Reptiles" refers to any long-bodied creatures that move by crawling.
They go. The remainder is already clear. The conclusion should also be understood according to the method already stated.
This is the eighth [chapter]. 139. The word-meaning of the ninth verse is indeed clear. However, the intended connection here is as follows: and that indeed...

This is by way of reasoning, not by way of hearsay. Just as this elephant is called a "Nāga" because he does not descend to the level of the undisciplined due to his being tamed in the virtues dear to noble ones,
or because of the greatness of his body, so too, when shall I also— by being tamed in the virtues dear to noble ones,
by not descending to the level of the undisciplined, by not committing transgressions, and by not returning again to this state of existence— be called a Nāga?
Or perhaps I might become a Nāga because of the greatness of my body and virtues.

Just as this [elephant], having avoided the herds, dwells in the forest according to his pleasure in the bliss of solitary wandering—when indeed shall I too, having avoided the crowd, dwell in the forest according to my pleasure in the bliss of solitude and the bliss of *jhāna*, like the rhinoceros horn? My own...
"In whatever way there is happiness, in that same way, for as long as I desire, for that long may I dwell alone in the forest;
'may I wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros'—this is the meaning.

And just as this [elephant] has developed a great trunk through the excellence of its well-formed trunk, when will I too likewise develop a great trunk through the excellence of the aggregates of the virtues of one beyond training (asekkha-sīlakkhandha)?

"May I become like him. Just as he is called 'Lotus' because his limbs resemble a lotus or because he was born in the lotus family, when indeed shall I too become a 'Lotus' because of the greatness of my enlightenment factors which resemble a lotus, or because of being born in the noble birth-lotus?
And just as he is sublime through his strength, power, speed, and so forth, when indeed shall I too [become so] through my perfectly pure bodily conduct and so forth?"
"Or perhaps I might become superior through virtue, concentration, penetrative wisdom, and so forth. Thinking thus, he applied himself to insight and attained the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha.
This is the ninth [chapter].
140. Regarding the phrase *dasame aṭṭhānanti*: it is an impossibility (*aṭṭhāna*); it is stated as a reason (*tanti*), meaning "there is no cause.
The nasalization (*anunāsika*) has been elided, as in the case of expressions such as *ariyasaccāna dassanaṃ*. *Saṅgaṇikārattassa* means "of one who delights in company.
*Yaṃ* is a word expressing a reason, as in expressions such as *yaṃ hirīyati hirīyitabbena*. *Phassaye* means "he would attain."
"Temporary liberation" (*sāmayikā vimutti*) refers to a mundane attainment (*lokiya-samāpatti*).
For that [attainment] is called "temporary liberation" because it is liberated from opposing states only at the very moment it is entered.

That temporary liberation—[regarding] that, there is no possibility, no such cause exists, for one who delights in social company, by which cause he might touch [the path] of that Paccekabuddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
“Having heard his words and abandoned delight in social company, by practicing with systematic application, I have attained it,” he said. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

In the *Niddesa*, “the bliss of renunciation” (*nekkhammasukha*) is the bliss of going forth (*pabbajjā*). “The bliss of seclusion” (*pavivekasukha*) is the bliss in the seclusion of body, mind, and acquisitions (*upadhi*).

“The bliss of peace” (*upasamasukha*) is the bliss of the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*) through the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa*). “The bliss of enlightenment” (*sambodhisukha*) is the bliss of the path (*magga*).
"Obtaining at will" means obtaining according to one's own preference. "Obtaining without difficulty" means obtaining without suffering. "Obtaining without hardship" means obtaining in abundance.
"Not occasional" refers to the supramundane. "Unshakable" refers to the supramundane path, which is free from fluctuation and immovable. This is the tenth [chapter].
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3. Commentary on the Third Chapter. 141.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the Third Chapter, "the snares of views" refers to the sixty-two types of speculative views (*dvāsaṭṭhi-diṭṭhigatāni*). For these are [opposed] to the right view of the Path (*maggasammādiṭṭhi*).

They are "divergences" (*visūka*) in the sense of being contradictory, in the sense of piercing, and in the sense of being contrary. Thus, "divergences of views" (*diṭṭhivisūka*) means divergences that are views;
or alternatively, the views themselves are the divergences, hence "divergences of views. "One who has transcended" means one who has passed beyond by means of the path of seeing.

"Attained to certainty" (*niyāma*) means one who has reached the state of certainty through the nature of not falling into the lower realms and through having enlightenment as the ultimate goal; that which is designated as the "certainty of rightness" (*sammattaniyāma*).
Or, "the first path. Up to this point, both the accomplishment of the function of the first path and its acquisition have been described.

Now, by the phrase "having acquired the path," he shows the acquisition of the remaining paths. "I am one whose knowledge has arisen" means that I am one who has arisen in the knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekabodhi).
By this, he shows the fruit (phala). "Not to be led by others" means not to be led by others [with the thought], "This is truth, this is truth."

By this, he illustrates the state of being self-become (*sayambhu*). Alternatively, because there is an absence of dependence on others for the knowledge of individual enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*) once it has been attained, it is "self-determined.

Or, having transcended the thorns of views through serenity and insight, having entered the certainty of rightness (*niyāma*) by means of the first path, having acquired the remaining paths, and having produced knowledge through the knowledge of fruition—all that has been realized by himself alone; thus, he is not to be led by another.
The rest is to be understood in the manner already stated.

"Not led by others" means he is not to be led by others. "Not made to believe by others" means that because the Dhamma is directly verifiable (*paccakkha*), he is not to be made to have faith by others.
"Not dependent on others" means that another is not his condition; he does not act according to the faith of another.
"Not dependent on others": he is not one whose wisdom proceeds in dependence on others.
First. 142.
In the second [verse], "free from greed" (*nillolupa*) means without longing. For whoever is overcome by craving for flavors is greatly plundered (*luppati*).
Because one is repeatedly plundered [by greed], one is called "lolu-po" (greedy). Therefore, rejecting that, he said "nillolupo" (free from greed).

Regarding "nikkuho" (free from deceit): although one who lacks the three bases of deceit is called "nikkuho," the intended meaning here is that one is "nikkuho" because of not falling into wonder or delight at pleasant food and such things.

"Free from thirst" (*nippipāsa*): here, "thirst" (*pipāsā*) is the desire to drink; by the absence of that, he is "free from thirst," meaning he is devoid of the longing to eat driven by greed for delicious flavors.
"Free from hypocrisy" (*nimmakkha*): here, "hypocrisy" (*makkha*) is characterized by the destruction of another's virtues; by the absence of that, he is "free from hypocrisy.
He says this with reference to his lack of hypocrisy regarding the cook's virtues during his time as a householder. "Having cleansed the stain of delusion" (*niddhantakasāvamoha*):...

In this context, the six factors—namely, the three beginning with lust (rāga) and the three beginning with bodily misconduct (kāyaduccarita)—should be understood as "astringents" (kasāva) in the sense that, according to their occurrence, they cause one to abandon one's own nature and take on another’s nature by way of being unappealing, by way of inducing a change of state, and by way of being a sediment. As it is said:

"In this regard, what are the three astringents? The astringent of lust, the astringent of hatred, and the astringent of delusion—these are the three astringents. In this regard, what are the other three astringents? The astringent of body, the astringent of speech, and the astringent of mind."
Among these, having removed delusion, he is one who has "wiped away the stain of delusion" because of the removal of the five stains and of that delusion which is the root of them all;
or alternatively, he is one who has "wiped away the stain of delusion" because of the removal of the three stains of body, speech, and mind, as well as delusion itself.
In the other cases, by means of non-covetousness and so forth, there is the removal of the stain of lust, and by means of non-malice, the removal of the stain of hatred.
The state of having shaken off [defilements] is indeed established. "Free from longing" (*nirāsa*) means without craving. "In the whole world" (*sabbaloke*) means in the entire world;

the meaning is that one should be devoid of craving for existence and non-existence within the three realms of being or the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*). The rest should be understood according to the method already explained.
Alternatively, after stating the three feet [of the verse], "one should wander alone" (*eko care*) may also mean that one is able to wander alone.
Here, the connection should be made.
Second. 143.
In the third [section], this is the summarized meaning: because he is possessed of the ten-based evil view...
He is evil. He shows what is harmful even to others, thus he is "one who sees harm. He is established in the unevenness of bodily misconduct and so forth.
A clansman desiring his own welfare should avoid such an evil companion—one who sees harm and is established in the uneven.
He should not associate with him by his own volition; but if he is under the power of another, what can be done?
"Kātuṃ" means to do. "Pasutaṃ" means attached; the meaning is that they are stuck here and there by way of [wrong] views.
"Pamattaṃ" means one whose mind is abandoned to the strands of sensual pleasure, or one who is devoid of the cultivation of the wholesome.
One should not associate with, frequent, or attend upon such a person; rather, one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
In the *Niddesa*: "One should not pursue it oneself" means one should not approach it personally. "One should not pursue it oneself" means one should not even approach it with the mind.
"One should not pursue" means one should not associate with it. "One should not cultivate" means one should not go near it.
"One should not frequent" means one should remain at a distance. "One should not dwell among" means one should retreat from it.
The third [section].

144. In the fourth [section], this is the summary of the meaning: "One who is learned" (*bahussuta*) is of two kinds: one who is learned in the scriptures (*pariyatti-bahussuta*), having mastered the entirety of the three Piṭakas in their meaning;
and one who is learned through realization (*paṭivedha-bahussuta*), because of having penetrated the paths, fruits, clear knowledges (*vijjā*), and superknowledges (*abhiññā*).
Furthermore, one who has mastered the traditional scriptures and upholds the Dhamma is "one who has come to the tradition" (*āgatāgama*) and "a bearer of the Dhamma" (*dhammadhara*).

One who is endowed with sublime deeds of body, speech, and mind is "exalted" (*uḷāra*). One who possesses inspired eloquence is "eloquent" (*paṭibhānavā*), being either possessed of appropriate eloquence, liberated eloquence, or both appropriate and liberated eloquence.

Alternatively, one may understand the term "eloquent" as threefold according to study, inquiry, and realization. For he in whom the scriptures shine forth is "eloquent in the scriptures" (*pariyattipaṭibhānavā*).
One for whom an inquiry regarding the meaning, the method, the characteristic, and the possible and impossible occurs as a ready response is one possessed of ready response through inquiry.
One by whom the Path and so forth have been penetrated is one possessed of ready response through realization.
One should associate with such a person who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, a noble friend possessed of ready response. From him—
By the power of that [knowledge], having understood the manifold kinds of benefits— distinguished as those pertaining to oneself,
others, or both, or as those pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal—
he dispelled doubt and eliminated uncertainty regarding the points of doubt such as, "Did I exist in the past? Having thus performed all his duties, he [attained].
"One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.
This is the fourth [verse].

145. In the fifth, "play" (*khiḍḍā*) and "delight" (*rati*) have already been explained previously. "Sensual pleasure" (*kāmasukha*) refers to sensual pleasure based on material objects (*vatthukāmasukha*). Material objects (*vatthukāmā*) also...
For indeed, things are called "pleasure" because they serve as the objects and conditions for pleasure. As it is said: "There is form that is pleasant, associated with pleasure.

Thus, without adorning this world-sphere with play, delight, and sensual pleasure, and without treating them as "enough," or failing to grasp them as "this is what satisfies" or "this is the essence";
[the phrase] "without looking back" refers to that lack of adornment.
One who is by nature free from longing, without desire, and devoid of craving; one who abstains from the grounds for adornment and speaks the truth—such a person should wander alone.

In this context, adornment is twofold: the adornment of the householder and the adornment of the homeless one. Therein, the adornment of the householder consists of head-dresses, garlands, perfumes, and so forth;

the adornment of the homeless one consists of the decoration of the alms-bowl and such. Adornment itself is the "ground for adornment" (*vibhūsaṭṭhāna*); therefore, [the phrase is] "from the grounds for adornment."
He is abstinent from all three kinds of abstinence. Because his speech is not false, he is a "speaker of truth"—thus the meaning should be understood.
This is the fifth [chapter]. 146. In the sixth, "wealth" refers to gems such as pearls, jewels, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, silver, and gold.
"Grains" (*dhaññāni*) refers to the seven types of grains—namely rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, panicled millet, and kudrūsa—as well as other remaining foods.
"Relatives" (*bandhavāni*) refers to the four kinds of relatives: by birth, by clan, by friendship, and by craft.
"As they are" (*yathodhikāni*) means exactly as they exist according to their respective categories. The rest is just as previously stated.
The sixth [section]. 147.
In the seventh [verse], "this is a snare" (*saṅga*) indicates one's own enjoyment;

for living beings cling there, like an elephant sunk in mud—thus it is a "snare. "Therein, happiness is meager" (*parittaṃ ettha sukhaṃ*): herein, at the time of enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure...
Because it must be produced through perverted perception, or because it is included among the phenomena of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), pleasure is "inferior" in the sense of being base;
it is "limited," meaning it is short-lived like the joy of watching a dance illuminated by the light of a lightning flash—this is what is meant.
Regarding the statement, "There is little gratification, but suffering here is more," this refers to those five [aggregates] which, O monks, [are thus described].
"Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on the strands of sensual pleasure—this is the gratification of sensual pleasures.
Having stated this, the suffering therein is described by way of such passages as: "And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in sensual pleasures?
Here, bhikkhus, a clansman earns his living by some craft or trade, whether by calculation or accounting," and so forth.
Compared to that, [the pleasure] is merely the size of a drop of water; rather, suffering alone is greater and more abundant, being like the water in the four oceans.
Therefore it was said: "The gratification here is slight, but suffering is greater.
"This is a hook"—having shown the gratification, this refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure which, by way of dragging one in, are like a fishhook. Knowing this thus, the wise man...
Knowing this, a wise and intelligent person, having abandoned all this, should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
(The Seventh) In the second line of the eighth verse, "jāla" refers to a net made of thread. "Ambu" means water; therein—
"One who moves in water" (*ambucārī*) is a designation for a fish. "One who moves in water in the water" (*salilambucārī*) means one who has gone into that river-water after breaking through the net;
thus it is said. In the third line, "burnt" (*daḍḍha*) refers to a place that has been burnt.
Just as fire does not return again to a place that has been burnt, nor does it come there again in greater measure.
Thus, having burned the locus of the strands of sensual pleasure with the fire of path-knowledge, he does not turn back;
it is said that he does not return there again. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Regarding "fetters" (*saṃyojanāni*): they are called fetters because they fetter and bind the person in whom they exist to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Furthermore, it is appropriate to present these fetters (saṃyojana) either according to the sequence of the defilements (kilesa) or according to the sequence of the paths (magga).
The fetters of sensual lust (kāmarāga) and aversion (paṭigha) are abandoned by the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga); the fetter of conceit (māna) by the path of arhatship (arahattamagga);

the fetters of views (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), and adherence to rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa) by the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga); the fetter of lust for existence (bhavarāga) by the path of arhatship; and the fetters of envy (issā) and avarice (macchariya) by the path of stream-entry.

Ignorance [is abandoned] by the path of arahantship. According to the sequence of the paths: wrong view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, envy, and avarice are abandoned by the path of stream-entry; sensual lust and ill will by the path of non-returning; and conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance by the path of arahantship.
"Having broken" means having brought about a breach. "Having split apart" means having cut through. "Having shattered" means having split open. "Having completely shattered" means...
"Having taken. "Having caused to be gathered": the word has been expanded by means of a prefix (*upasagga*). The eighth [section]. 149.
In the ninth, "with downcast eyes" (*okkhittacakkhu*) means with eyes cast downward; having placed seven neck-bones in a row...
It is said that he "looks only a plough’s length ahead" for the purpose of seeing what must be avoided;
however, it does not mean that he strikes the heart-bone with the jaw-bone. For if it were so, his downcast gaze would not be in accordance with the character of a recluse.
Nor is he "fidgety with his feet," meaning that he does not scratch his feet out of a desire to enter the midst of a group, such as when there is a second person for one, or a third for two.
"Being as if non-existent," or "one who abstains from long journeys and unsettled wandering. "Guarded in the sense-faculties" (*guttindriyo*):
since the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) has been mentioned separately here among the six faculties, he is one whose remaining faculties are guarded according to what has been stated.
