"One whose mental stream is protected" (*rakkhitamānasāno*): "mental stream" (*mānasāna*) is just another term for the mind itself; he is one whose mind-stream is protected, thus "one whose mental stream is protected. [He is so called] because he is not plundered by the defilements (*kilesa*).
Thus, it is said that "the mind is guarded. "Untainted" (*anavassuta*) means being free from the influx of defilements (*kilesa-anvāssava*) toward various objects by means of this practice.
"Not burning" (*apariḍayhamāna*) means not being scorched by the fires of the defilements precisely because one is thus free from their influx;
that is, untainted externally and not burning internally. The rest is exactly as previously explained.

"Having seen a visible form with the eye" means: having seen a visible form by means of eye-consciousness, which is capable of seeing forms and is conventionally designated as "the eye" in the sense of being its instrument.
The Ancients, however, have said: "The eye does not see the form because it is devoid of mind; the mind does not see because it is devoid of the eye;

rather, it is the mind, based upon the sensitive organ (pasāda), that sees when there is a conjunction of the door and the object. This [process] is like [saying] 'one pierces with a bow' and so forth."
This is called a discourse on the requisites; therefore, the meaning here is simply "having seen a form with eye-consciousness.

"One who grasps at signs" (nimittaggāhī) means that one grasps a sign—such as the sign of a woman or a man, or a sign of beauty and so forth—which serves as a basis for defilements, by way of desire and lust, and does not remain settled merely upon what is seen.
"One who grasps at secondary characteristics" (anubyañjanaggāhī) refers to [the grasping] of defilements...

Because it makes [the intention] manifest through its secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*), that which is conventionally termed "secondary characteristic" takes on the form of various manifestations such as hand, foot, smile, speech, and gaze.
In the passage beginning with "By reason of which," the word "which" refers to the cause, namely the lack of restraint of the eye-faculty;
and because this person dwells with the eye-faculty unrestrained by the door-leaf of mindfulness—having left the eye-door open—these states of covetousness and so forth [arise].
“Dhammas might flow in after him. “He does not practice for its restraint” means he does not practice for the purpose of closing the door of mindfulness upon that eye-faculty.
And one who is thus disposed is said to be: “He does not guard the eye-faculty; he does not attain restraint over the eye-faculty.”
In this context, although there is neither restraint nor non-restraint regarding the eye-faculty—
for mindfulness or forgetfulness does not arise depending on the sensitive materiality of the eye— nevertheless, when a visible object comes into the range of the eye,
after the life-continuum has arisen and ceased twice, the functional mind-element performs the function of adverting.
Having arisen, it ceases; then eye-consciousness arises and ceases, performing the function of seeing; then the resultant mind-element arises and ceases, performing the function of receiving;

then the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element arises and ceases, performing the function of investigating; then the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element arises and ceases, accomplishing the function of determining; immediately after that, the impulsion (javana) occurs.
Even there, restraint or non-restraint does not exist during the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), nor during any of the moments such as adverting (āvajjana) and so forth;

however, in the moment of impulsion (javana), if immorality, forgetfulness, ignorance, impatience, or laziness arises, there is non-restraint. When it exists in this way, it is called "non-restraint in the eye-faculty."
It is so called. Why? Because when that [door] exists, the door itself remains unguarded, as do the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the adverting consciousness, and the other process-consciousnesses.

How is this? Just as when the four gates of a city are left unsecured, even though the inner house doors, gate-towers, chambers, and so forth are well-secured, nevertheless all the goods within the city remain unprotected and unguarded. By means of the city gate...
For once thieves have entered, they may carry off whatever they desire.

In the same way, when restlessness, immorality, and so forth arise, and there is that lack of restraint (*asaṃvara*), the door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), and the other process-consciousnesses (*vīthicitta*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Having seen a form with the eye, one does not grasp at its signs," the phrase "does not grasp at its signs" refers to [grasping] by way of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*).
One does not grasp the sign of the kind described above. In this way, the remaining phrases are also to be understood by means of the negations stated.

And just as it was said below: "When unwholesome states such as misconduct arise in the impulsion, because that lack of restraint exists, the door is unprotected, as are the life-continuum and the cognitive-series consciousnesses beginning with adverting," so too here, when virtue and the rest [are present]...
When [the doors] have arisen, the door itself is guarded, as are the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the adverting consciousness (āvajjana), and the other process-consciousnesses.

How is this so? Just as when the city gates are closed, even though the houses and so forth within are not themselves closed, nevertheless all the goods within the city remain well-guarded and well-protected. When the city gates are shut, there is no entry for thieves.

There is none. In the same way, when the [wholesome] states such as virtue (*sīla*) arise during the impulsion (*javana*), the sense door is guarded, as are the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), and the other process-consciousnesses.
Therefore, even though it arises at the moment of impulsion, it is called "restraint of the eye-faculty" (*cakkhundriye saṃvara*).

"And by the method of being drenched" (*avassuta-pariyāya*) means by reason of being soaked with defilements (*kilesa*). "And by the method of not being drenched" (*anavassuta-pariyāya*) means by reason of not being soaked with defilements.

"Pleasant form" (*piyarūpe rūpe*) refers to a visible object (*rūpārammaṇa*) of a desirable nature. "Unpleasant form" (*appiyarūpe rūpe*) refers to a visible object of an undesirable nature. "It becomes corrupted" (*byāpajjati*) means it reaches a state of putrefaction through the influence of hatred (*dosa*). "An opening" (*otāra*) means a flaw or a vulnerability. "An object" (*ārammaṇa*) means a condition. "They overwhelmed" (*adhibhaṃsu*) means they crushed.

"He did not overwhelm" (*na adhibhosī*) means he did not crush. "Thick clay" (*bahalamattikā*) refers to thick clay applied repeatedly by way of successive offerings. "Plastering with lime" (*addāvalepanā*) refers to the application of clay that is not yet dry. The rest here is self-evident. The ninth [chapter].

150. Regarding the tenth [verse], "having gone forth clad in saffron robes": the meaning of this line should be understood as "having gone forth from his home and being clad in saffron robes. Since the remainder can be understood according to the method already stated, it has not been elaborated upon.
The tenth [chapter] is finished. The commentary on the third section is completed.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Chapter 151.
In the first [sutta] of the Fourth Chapter, "in tastes" (*rasesu*) refers to various kinds of things to be relished, such as sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, salty, alkaline, and astringent.
"They did not crave" (*gedham akaruṃ*) means they did not become greedy; what is meant is that they did not give rise to craving (*taṇhā*). "Without longing" (*alolo*)...
“I will taste this, I will taste that”—thus one is undisturbed by various flavors. “Not nourishing others” means being devoid of those who must be supported, such as co-residents;
what is meant is that one is content with merely sustaining the body. Or, having not been as one was previously in the park—greedy and longing for flavors, nourishing others—one does not become so;
rather, one abandons that craving by which, being greedy, one creates a grasping for flavors.
By abandoning craving, he shows that he is "not nourished by others" through the non-production of any other future personal existence rooted in craving.
Alternatively, the defilements are called "others" in the sense that they destroy one's welfare;

thus, the meaning here is that he is "not nourished by others" because he does not nourish them. "One who goes on a regular round" means one who does not skip houses and proceeds in successive order, following the sequence of households.
The meaning is: having abandoned both wealthy families and poor families, he enters among them without interval for alms.
"With a mind unattached to family after family" means that his mind does not cling to any place whatsoever—such as the kṣatriya caste and so forth—due to the influence of defilements;
the meaning is that he remains ever-new like the moon. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
First. 152.
In the second [verse], "obstructions" (*āvaraṇāni*) refers specifically to the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). These are explained in terms of their meaning in the *Uragasutta*.
However, because they obstruct the mind—just as clouds and so forth obscure the moon or the sun—they are called "obstructions of the mind."

These have been stated. Having abandoned them by means of access (upacāra) or absorption (appanā). "Corruptions" (upakkilesa) refers to unwholesome states that approach and afflict the mind, or alternatively, to covetousness and so forth as described in the *Vatthūpama-sutta* and other texts.

"Having dispelled" (byapanujja) means having driven away, destroyed, or abandoned by way of insight (vipassanā-magga); this is the meaning. "All" (sabba) means without remainder. Thus, one who is perfected in both serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā)—
Because the reliance on views has been abandoned by the first path, he is "independent. By the remaining paths, he has severed the fault of attachment pertaining to the three realms;
what is meant is that he has severed the "craving-fetter. For it is attachment itself, being the opposite of virtue, that is called the "fault of attachment.
The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The second [section]. 153.

In the third [verse], "having turned one's back" (*vipiṭṭhikatvāna*) means having placed behind oneself; the meaning is having discarded or abandoned. "Pleasure and pain" (*sukhaṃ dukhañca*) refers to bodily agreeable and disagreeable [feeling].
"Joy and grief" (*somanassadomanassaṃ*) refers to mental agreeable and disagreeable [feeling]. "Equanimity" (*upekkhā*) refers to the equanimity of the fourth jhāna.
"Tranquility" (samatha) refers specifically to the tranquility of the fourth jhāna.

"Purified" (visuddha) means exceedingly pure because it is liberated from the nine opposing states known as the five hindrances, initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), and pleasure (sukha); the meaning is that it is free from adventitious defilements like refined gold.
This, however, is the construction: having already turned one's back on both pleasure and pain even before [entering the first jhāna], right there on the access stage of the first jhāna...
The intention is that [mental] pain exists in the preliminary stage of the first jhāna, and pleasure exists in the preliminary stage of the third jhāna.
Furthermore, by carrying forward the word "and" (ca) mentioned at the beginning, the governing phrase is: "having turned one's back on both joy and grief, as before.

By this, it is shown that joy exists specifically in the preliminary stage of the fourth jhāna, and grief exists only in the preliminary stage of the second jhāna. For these [factors] belong to these [stages].

These are the bases for abandoning in a figurative sense. But in the non-figurative sense, the first jhāna is the basis for abandoning suffering, the second jhāna for abandoning grief, the third jhāna for abandoning pleasure, and the fourth jhāna for abandoning joy.
As it is said: "Having entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, the arisen faculty of suffering there ceases without remainder."
“Ceases,” and so forth—all of this is to be understood according to the method explained below. “Prior to that” means:

having turned one’s back on pain, mental grief, and pleasure in the first three jhānas, and having likewise turned one’s back on mental joy (*somanassa*) right here in the fourth jhāna, one [attains] the serenity (*samatha*) obtained through this practice, which is purified equanimity (*upekkhā*). Alone...
"Care" means: the remainder is exactly as explained by the method already stated. This is the third [section]. 154.
In the fourth, "one who has initiated energy" (*āraddhaviriyo*) means one whose energy has been undertaken. By this, his own undertaking of energy is shown as the initial energy (*ādivīriya*).

He shows this. "The ultimate goal" (paramattha) is said to be Nibbāna; for the sake of attaining that is "for the attainment of the ultimate goal. By this undertaking of energy, he shows the fruit to be attained.
By the phrase "with an undaunted mind," he shows the lack of dejection in the mind and mental factors that are supported by energy.
By the phrase "of unwearied conduct," he shows the non-collapse of the body in standing, sitting, walking, and so forth. "Firm in exertion" (daḷhanikkama).
By this, he shows the energy of exertion as it occurs in the passage: “Willingly, let skin and sinews [be consumed]...”.
For one who exerts himself in the gradual training and so forth is said to be “one who realizes the ultimate truth with the body and sees it by piercing through it with wisdom.
Alternatively, by this he shows the energy associated with the Path; for that is firm because it has reached the fullness of cultivation.

“Exertion” (*nikkama*) is so called because it has completely departed from all opposing factors; therefore, a person endowed with that [exertion] is also said to be “firmly exerted” (*daḷhanikkama*).
“Endowed with strength and power” (*thāmabalūpapanna*) means endowed with physical vigor at the moment of the Path and with the power of knowledge.
Alternatively, one is “endowed with strength and power” in the sense of being endowed with power that has become firm—that is, endowed with the power of steadfast knowledge.
This has been said. By this, while demonstrating the association of that energy with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), he establishes the state of wise exertion (*yoniso padahana*).
Alternatively, all three feet may be joined according to the categories of initial, intermediate, and intense energy. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
This is the fourth [section].
155. In the fifth [case], *paṭisallāna* means having withdrawn from those various conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), it is secluded;

the meaning is that it is solitude of body, consisting in the cultivation of oneness and the state of being alone. *Jhāna* is called solitude of mind because it burns away (*jhāpana*) the adverse factors and because it closely contemplates (*upanijjhāna*) the characteristics of the object.

In this context, the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) are so called because they burn away the adverse factors such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and because they closely contemplate objects such as the kasiṇas.

And it is called "jhāna. Insight, the path, and the fruit are called "jhāna" because they burn away (jhāpana) opposing states such as the perception of a self, and because they closely contemplate characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna).
However, in this context, only close contemplation of the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) is intended.

Thus, "not neglecting this seclusion and jhāna" means not abandoning, not relinquishing them. "In phenomena" refers to the phenomena comprised within insight, such as the five aggregates and so forth.

"Constantly" (*niccaṃ*) means always, continuously, and uninterruptedly. "One who practices in accordance with the Dhamma" (*anudhammacārī*) means one who practices the Dhamma of insight (*vipassanā*) that has followed along with those [nine] states (*dhammā*).
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "in the states" (*dhammesu*): here, "states" (*dhammā*) refers to the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhammā*).
That which is in conformity with those states is "conformity-Dhamma" (*anudhamma*), which is a designation for insight. In that context, "of the states... [the text continues].

Where it should have been said, "constantly practicing in accordance with the Dhamma," the form "in phenomena" (*dhammesu*) may have been used for the sake of metrical convenience through a change in case ending.
"Having comprehended the peril in states of existence" (*ādīnavaṃ sammasitā bhavesu*):

thus, while contemplating the defects such as the aspect of impermanence within the three realms of existence by means of that insight known as "practice in accordance with the Dhamma," he likewise does not neglect this physical seclusion and mental seclusion.
The construction should be understood thus: "One should say that he has attained the path known as insight that has reached its culmination; therefore, he 'should wander alone.
This is the fifth [verse].
In the sixth, "the destruction of craving" (*taṇhakkhaya*) refers to Nibbāna, which is the non-arising of that very craving whose dangers have been thus seen.

“Diligent” (*appamatta*) means one who acts with persistence. “Not a chatterer” (*aneḷamūga*) means one whose mouth does not drool; or alternatively, one who is both not a chatterer and not deaf—that is, one who is wise and competent.
“Learned” (*sutavā*) means one who possesses the hearing that brings about welfare and happiness;

that is, one who is endowed with the *āgama*. “Mindful” (*satimā*) means one who recollects things done long ago and so forth. “One who has scrutinized the Dhamma” (*saṅkhātadhamma*) [means one who has done so] through the investigation of the Dhamma.

One who has fully understood the Dhamma. "Destined" (niyata) means one who has entered the path of certainty (niyāma) by means of the Noble Path. "Exerting" (padhānavā) means endowed with the energy of the right efforts (sammappadhāna).
This reading should be construed in reverse order. Thus, being possessed of these qualities such as heedfulness (appamāda), one is "exerting" through the exertion that brings about certainty;
because of having attained certainty through that exertion, one is "destined"; and from that, through the attainment of Arahatship—
One who has fully understood the Dhamma. For an Arahant is called "one who has fully understood the Dhamma" because there is nothing further to be understood. As it is said:
"Those who have fully understood the Dhamma, and those various trainees here. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The sixth [section].
157. Regarding "lion" (*sīha*) in the seventh [case]: there are four kinds of lions—the grass lion, the pale lion, the black lion, and the maned lion (*kesarasīha*).
Of these, the maned lion is declared to be the foremost; it is this one that is intended here. "Wind" (*vāta*) is of many kinds according to its directions, such as the east and so forth.
"Lotus" (*paduma*) is of various kinds according to its colors, such as red, white, and so forth. Among those, any wind whatsoever and any lotus whatsoever are quite suitable. In that regard:

Since fear arises from self-attachment, and self-attachment is the clinging of craving, and that [clinging] occurs through greed—whether associated with or dissociated from views—and that too is simply craving;
whereas the shunning [of the object] occurs there through delusion for one devoid of investigation, and delusion is ignorance.
In this regard, the abandoning of craving occurs through serenity (samatha), and that of ignorance through insight (vipassanā).
Therefore, having abandoned self-attachment through serenity (*samatha*), one does not tremble at sounds—such as impermanence and suffering—just like a lion;
and having abandoned delusion through insight (*vipassanā*), one is unattached to the aggregates, bases, and so forth, just like the wind in a net.
Having abandoned greed and the views associated with greed by means of serenity alone, one remains unsullied by greed for all the enjoyments of existence, just as a lotus is unsullied by water.

And here, since virtue is the proximate cause of serenity (*samatha*), serenity is concentration (*samādhi*), and insight (*vipassanā*) is wisdom (*paññā*), when these two states are established, all three aggregates are thereby established. In that regard, by means of the aggregate of virtue, one is gentle;
like a lion, because of the desire not to be provoked by objects of resentment, one does not tremble amidst sounds. By means of the aggregate of wisdom—
Having penetrated their true nature, he does not cling to the various phenomena such as the aggregates, just as the wind does not cling to a net;
being free from passion through the aggregate of concentration, he is not smeared by passion, just as a lotus is not smeared by water.

Thus, by means of serenity and insight, and through the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, he is "not restless" (asanta-santo) by way of abandoning ignorance and craving, as well as the three unwholesome roots, according to their respective possibilities.
He should be understood as one who is unattached and unsmeared. The rest is exactly as previously stated. This is the seventh [section]. 158.
In the eighth, a *sīha* is so called because of its endurance, its slaying, and its swift speed; here, it is specifically intended to mean the maned lion (*kesarasīha*).
One who possesses the strength of tusks is called *dāṭhabalī*. Both terms, *pasayha* (forcibly) and *abhibhuyya* (having overcome), should be construed with the word *cārī* (roaming):

thus, *pasayhacārī* (one who roams by force) and *abhibhuyyacārī* (one who roams having overcome). In this context, he is a *pasayhacārī* because of his roaming after having seized, restrained, and driven away [his prey].
He is an *abhibhuyyacārī* because of his roaming after having overcome, terrified, and brought under his control. This [elephant], by means of his bodily strength...
“Moving by force, moving having overcome by splendor. In this regard, if someone were to ask, “What does ‘moving by force, moving having overcome’ mean? one should reply:
“Having taken the genitive case ‘of deer’ (migānaṃ) in the sense of the accusative, [it means] ‘moving by force, moving having overcome the deer.
“Remote” (pantāni) means far away. “Dwellings” (senāsanāni) means places for staying. The rest can be understood according to the method already explained above, and thus it is not elaborated here.
The eighth. 159.
In the ninth [section], loving-kindness (*mettā*) is the desire to bring about welfare and happiness for all beings by way of the formula beginning, "May all beings be happy.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the desire to remove harm and suffering by way of the formula beginning, "O, may they be freed from this suffering!"

Compassion (*karuṇā*). Joy (*muditā*) is the desire for the non-separation of beings from welfare and happiness, expressed by such phrases as, “May these worthy beings rejoice; they rejoice well and truly.
Equanimity (*upekkhā*) is the state of looking on with impartiality toward pleasure and pain, thinking, “They will fare according to their own karma.

However, for the sake of the ease of the verse composition, loving-kindness (*mettā*) was mentioned first and equanimity stated last, while joy was mentioned later. As for “liberation,” all four [immeasurables] are included.
These are indeed liberations (*vimutti*). They are called "liberations" because they are liberated from their own respective opposing states (*paccanīkadhamma*). Therefore it was said:
"Cultivating at the proper time loving-kindness, equanimity, compassion, and gladness as liberations.
In that context, "cultivating" means developing them by way of the three triplets and fourfold jhānas; "equanimity" [is cultivated] by way of the fourth jhāna.
While developing [it]: having practiced loving-kindness at the appropriate time, he emerges from that and practices compassion; emerging from that, he practices gladness;

or, emerging from that or from another jhāna devoid of rapture, he practices equanimity. It is in this sense that he is said to be "practicing at the appropriate time," or practicing at a time when it is convenient to practice.
"Not in conflict with the whole world" means not being in conflict with anyone in the ten directions.
"Unopposed by the world of beings": because of the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], beings become non-repulsive;
furthermore, the hostility that constitutes opposition toward beings is pacified. Therefore it is said: "unopposed by the entire world.
The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The ninth. 160.
In the tenth [verse], "the fetters" (*saṃyojanāni*) refers to the ten fetters; and having torn them apart by means of this or that path.
"Without fear at the end of life" (*asantasaṃ jīvitasaṅkhayamhīti*): the "end of life" (*jīvitasaṅkhaya*) is said to be the dissolution of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*); and in that...
Because attachment to life has been abandoned at the exhaustion of life, there is no more becoming.

Having thus demonstrated to himself the element of nirvana with residue (*saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) up to this point, he attained final nirvana (*parinibbāyi*) in the element of nirvana without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) at the conclusion of the verse.
The tenth [chapter].
161. "They honor" (bhajanti) means they attend upon [the teacher] by remaining close to his body.

"They serve" (sevanti) means they attend to him through such acts as raising the hands in salutation and by being ready to carry out whatever is commanded. "Those for whom the purpose is the cause" (kāraṇatthā) means those whose purpose is the cause;
there is no other cause for their honoring and serving than the purpose itself. Their very purpose is the cause; thus it is said that they serve for the sake of the purpose.

“Today, friends without cause are hard to find. Thus, by means of obtaining oneself—that is, for the sake of one's own acquisition—one thinks, “We shall receive something from this [person],” and so there are those without cause.
Only such a friend as is said: “A friend who is a benefactor, a companion in both happiness and suffering;”
“And the friend who explains what is beneficial, and the friend who is compassionate toward friends.
Friends endowed with such noble friendship as described are rare today. Their wisdom is established within themselves;

they look only to themselves and not to others—thus they are called “those whose wisdom is for their own sake” (*attaṭṭhapaññā*). “Those whose wisdom is for the seen goal” (*diṭṭhatthapaññā*)—this too...
This is indeed the ancient reading. What is meant is that their wisdom perceives only what is presently seen, and does not look toward the future.
"Impure" means they are possessed of impure, ignoble actions of body, speech, and mind. The rest should be understood according to the method already explained.
Whatever was not stated here and there for fear of excessive prolixity, all of that should be supplied by following the text itself.
This should be understood. The eleventh [chapter].
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is finished.
From the *Saddhammappajjotikā*, the commentary on the *Cūḷaniddesa*.
The commentary on the exposition of the Khaggavisāṇasutta is finished.
Concluding Remarks:
He who, being the sovereign among the sons of the Sugata, [acted] for the sake of welfare and joy;
This great commentary (*Mahā-ṭīkā*), well-analyzed by the Elder who possesses steadfast virtues, and its explanation of the meaning—
which I have undertaken based on the method of the ancient commentaries and logical reasoning— has now reached its conclusion.
That city, the most excellent of cities, known by the name Anurādhapura;
on its southern side stands the Mahāvihāra.
And that which was its ornament, the Great Stupa, a heap of stone;
In the western part of that city was a man known as Lekha-Kathika;
by the name Kittisena, he was a living person highly esteemed by the king,
endowed with pure conduct, and a scribe skilled in his craft.
The great elder Upasena had a monastic courtyard constructed, provided with trees casting cool shade,
endowed with excellent water sources, and enclosed by a beautiful perimeter wall;
he also established residents for the great courtyard.
To him, Lekha, a skilled craftsman, provided a workshop.
While residing here with the Elder named Upasena—
who was firm in virtue and equanimous— this *Saddhammajotikā* was composed.
In the twenty-sixth year of King Sirinivāsa, the glorious Saṅgha Bodhi, this commentary on the Niddesa was completed,
following the tradition of the Elders who illuminate the lineage of the Theras.
Just as this commentary, which generates welfare for the world, has reached its conclusion,
may the aspirations of all beings likewise reach fulfillment as they follow the True Dhamma and accomplish their own welfare and the welfare of others.
In this *Saddhammappajjotikā* commentary, those skilled in calculation have calculated that there are forty-two and a half recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*).
When these are counted according to the *anuṭṭhubha* meter, they are composed in verse.
It should be understood that there are more than ten thousand verses.

Whatever abundant and no small merit has been acquired by me in composing this work with devotion for the sake of the long endurance of the Dispensation and for the welfare of the world— [may it lead to the same goal].
By that merit, may the world, having enjoyed the stainless elixir of the True Dharma of the One Possessing Ten Powers, easily attain happiness through happiness.
Thus ends [the commentary] named *Saddhammapajjotikā*.
The Commentary on the Cūḷaniddesa is finished.
